In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Tafsir of Surah an-Nahl (The Bee). It is Meccan entirely, according to al-Hasan, Ikrimah, Ata' and Jabir. It is also called Surat an-Ni'am (the Surah of Blessings) because of the blessings of Allah upon His servants that He enumerates in it. It was said: it is Meccan except for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if you punish, then punish with the like of that with which you were punished﴾ [see vol. 20, and pp. 202, 192, 106, 173 of this part], the verse revealed at Medina concerning the mutilation of Hamzah and the slain of Uhud; and except for His saying: ﴿And be patient, and your patience is not but through Allah﴾ [same references]; and except for His saying: ﴿Then indeed your Lord, for those who emigrated...﴾ [same references], the verse. As for His saying: ﴿And those who emigrated for Allah after they had been wronged﴾ [same references], it is Meccan, concerning the emigration to Abyssinia. Ibn Abbas said: it is Meccan except for three verses of it, which were revealed at Medina after the killing of Hamzah, and they are His saying: ﴿And do not exchange the covenant of Allah for a small price... to His saying... what they used to do﴾ [same references].

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿The command of Allah has come, so do not seek to hasten it. Exalted is He and high above what they associate with Him.﴾ (16:1)

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿The command of Allah has come, so do not seek to hasten it﴾. It was said: "atā" (has come) means "ya'tī" (will come), so it is like your saying: "If you honour me, I will honour you." It has already been mentioned that Allah's reports about the past and the future are the same, because it will certainly come, as in His saying: ﴿And the companions of the Garden will call out to the companions of the Fire﴾ [see vol. 7, p. 209]. "The command of Allah" is His punishment for those who persist in polytheism and in denying His Messenger. Al-Hasan, Ibn Juraij and al-Dahhak said: it is what the Qur'an brought of His obligations and rulings. This is far-fetched, because it is not reported that any of the Companions hastened the obligations of Allah before they were imposed upon them; whereas those who hastened the punishment and retribution are reported of many of the disbelievers of Quraysh and others, to the extent that al-Nadr ibn al-Harith said: "O Allah, if this is indeed the truth from You..." (the verse), so he sought to hasten the punishment. I say: al-Dahhak may cite the saying of Umar, may Allah be pleased with him: "I agreed with my Lord in three matters: the station of Ibrahim, the veil, and the prisoners of Badr," which Muslim and al-Bukhari recorded. It has already been mentioned in Surat al-Baqarah [see vol. 2, p. 112]. Al-Zajjaj said: it is what He promised them of recompense for their disbelief, as in His saying: ﴿until when Our command came and the oven gushed forth﴾ [see vol. 9, p. 30]. It was said: it is the Day of Resurrection, or what indicates its nearness of its signs. Ibn Abbas said: when the verse ﴿The Hour has drawn near and the moon has split﴾ [see vol. 17, p. 125] was revealed, the disbelievers said: "This man claims that the Resurrection has drawn near. So refrain from some of what you were doing." They refrained and waited, but they saw nothing, and they said: "We see nothing." Then the verse was revealed: ﴿The reckoning of people has drawn near for them﴾ [see vol. 11, p. 266], the verse. So they grew anxious and waited for the nearness of the Hour, but the days lengthened and they said: "We see nothing." Then ﴿The command of Allah has come﴾ was revealed, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the Muslims started up and feared, so ﴿so do not seek to hasten it﴾ was revealed, and they were reassured. Then the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I and the Hour have been sent like these two," and he pointed with his two fingers: the index finger and the one next to it, meaning: "It nearly outran me, but I outran it." Ibn Abbas said: the sending of the Prophet (ﷺ) was among the signs of the Hour, and when Jibril passed by the inhabitants of the heavens, sent to Muhammad (ﷺ), they said: "Allah is greatest, the Hour has come."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Exalted is He and high above what they associate with Him﴾. That is, glorification of Him above what they attribute to Him, namely that He is not able to bring about the Hour. For they say: "No one can resurrect the dead," so they describe Him with the incapacity that is only ascribed to a created being, and that is shirk. It was said: "what they associate" means "their association (of partners)." It was also said: "mā" means "alladhī" (that which), i.e., He is exalted above those who associate partners with Him.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 16, verse 2:

Al-Mufaddal related from ʿAsim: "tanazzalu al-malaikatu" (تَنَزَّلُ الْمَلَائِكَةُ), and the original form is tatanazzalu, so the verb is attributed to the angels. Al-Kisa'i related from Abu Bakr, from ʿAsim, with a variation from him, and al-Aʿmash (read): "tunazzalu al-malaikatu" (تُنَزَّلُ الْمَلَائِكَةُ), in the passive voice (ghayr musamma al-fa'il, the verb whose subject is not named). Al-Ju'fi related from Abu Bakr, from ʿAsim: "tanazzala al-malaikata" (تنزل الْمَلَائِكَةَ) with the nun, in the active voice (musamma al-fa'il, the verb whose subject is named). The rest (of the readers) read "yunazzilu" (يُنَزِّلُ) with the ya', in the active voice, and the pronoun in it refers to the Name of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. It is related from Qatadah: "tunzilu al-malaikata" (تُنْزِلُ الْمَلَائِكَةَ) with the nun and without the tashdid. Al-Aʿmash read "tanzilu" (تَنْزِلُ) with a fatha on the ta' and a kasra on the za', from al-nuzul (descent), with "al-malaikatu" in the nominative, like "tanazzala al-malaikatu" [[See vol. 20, p. 133.]].

(bil-Ruh) means: with the revelation, which is prophethood, as Ibn ʿAbbas said. Its parallel is: "He sends down the Spirit by His command upon whom He wills of His servants" [[See vol. 15, p. 299.]]. Al-Rabiʿ ibn Anas said: with the word of Allah, which is the Qur'an. It was also said: it is the clarification of the truth that must be followed. It was also said: the souls of creation, as Mujahid said, meaning that no angel descends except with a spirit accompanying him. Similarly, it is related from Ibn ʿAbbas that the Spirit is a creation of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, in the likeness of the sons of Adam, and that no angel descends from the heaven except that one of them is with him. It was also said: with mercy, as al-Hasan and Qatadah said. It was also said: with guidance, because hearts are given life by it just as bodies are given life by spirits, and this is the meaning of the statement of al-Zajjaj. Al-Zajjaj said: the Spirit is that in which there is life from the command of Allah through guidance to His command. Abu ʿUbaydah said: the Spirit here is Jibril. The "bi" in His saying "bil-Ruh" carries the meaning of "ma'a" (with), as in your saying: "He went out with his clothes," meaning with his clothes.

(min amrihi) means: by His command.

(ʿala man yashaʾu min ʿibadihi) means: upon those whom Allah has chosen for prophethood. This is a rebuttal of their saying: "Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a man of importance from the two cities?" [[See vol. 16, p. 82.]]

(an andhiru annahu la ilaha illa ana fattaquni) is a warning against the worship of idols, and for this reason the word "al-indhar" (warning) came, because its origin is a warning against what is feared. This is indicated by His saying: "so fear Me." "An" is in a position of nasb (accusative) by the removal of the preposition, meaning: "warn the people of disbelief that there is no god but Allah," so "an" is in a place of nasb by the dropping of the preposition, or by the action of warning falling upon it.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 16, verse 3:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He created the heavens and the earth with truth﴾, meaning: for cessation and annihilation. It was also said: "with truth" means as a proof of His power, and that He has the right to make His servants worship Him through obedience, and to bring the creation back to life after death.

(Exalted is He above what they associate with Him), meaning: above these idols, which are not able to create anything.

Al-Qurtubi, *al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran*, on surah 16, verse 4:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He created man from a drop of sperm﴾. When He mentioned the proof of His oneness (*tawhid*, the affirmation that God is one), He then mentioned man, his contentiousness, and his overstepping of his station. "Al-insan" (man) is a noun for the species. It is narrated that the one meant by it was Ubayy ibn Khalaf al-Jumahi, who came to the Prophet ﷺ with a decayed bone and said: "Do you think Allah will bring this back to life after it has crumbled?" In connection with this, the following was also revealed: "Does man not see that We created him from a drop of sperm, and behold, he is an open adversary?" That is, He created man from water that issues from between the loins and the ribs, then moved him through stages until he was born and grew up to the point where he disputes about matters. So the meaning of the statement is an expression of wonder at man, ﴿and he makes a comparison for Us and forgets his own creation﴾. His saying, ﴿behold, he is a disputer﴾ means a *khasim*, a one who disputes, like *nasib* in the sense of *munasib*: he disputes with Allah, mighty and majestic, regarding His power. And ﴿open﴾ means clearly contentious. It was said: he makes his contention evident through falsehood. *Al-mubin* is the one who expresses clearly what is in his mind through his speech.

**Third**, *Question* 1: the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And the cattle He created for you﴾. When He mentioned mankind, He mentioned the favours He bestowed upon them. *Al-an'am* (cattle) are camels, cows and sheep. Most often *na'am* and *an'am* are used for camels, and the term is applied to the collective, but it is not used for sheep in the singular. Hassan said:

*"The Dhat al-Asabi' and al-Jiwa' have become desolate,
to 'Adhra' whose dwelling is empty."*
[[Dhat al-Asabi' and al-Jiwa': two places in Syria. 'Adhra': a village in the Ghouta of Damascus.]]

*"Abodes of the Bani al-Hasḥas, a barren waste,
which the winds that sweep the sand and the rain have effaced."*
[[al-Hasḥas: the name of a man. al-Rawamis: winds that stir up dust and bury traces.]]

*"And there was never a time when there was company in them,
amid their pastures, of na'am and sheep."*

Here *na'am* refers specifically to camels. Al-Jawhari said: "*Al-na'am* is the singular of *al-an'am*, and it is livestock that grazes. This term is used most often for camels." Al-Farra' said: "It is masculine and is not feminized; they say, 'This is a na'am coming to water.' Its plural is *nu'man*, like *haml* and *hulman*. *Al-an'am* may be masculine or feminine. Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿of what is in their bellies﴾ [[See p. 122 of this part.]], and in another place: ﴿of what is in their bellies﴾ [[See vol. 12, p. 117.]]." *Al-an'am* is in the accusative either as a conjunction with *al-insan* (mankind), or by a verb understood from context, and the latter is the more preferred view.

**Second question**: the words of Allah, the Exalted: (﴿warmth﴾). *Al-dif'* means warmth. It is what one is warmed by from their wool, fleece and hair: garments, quilts and *qutuf* [[*al-qutuf* (plural of *qatifa*): a cloak with a nap, i.e., fleece.]].

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: "*Dif'uha* is their offspring," and Allah knows best. Al-Jawhari said in *al-Sihah*: "*Al-dif'* is the young of camels, their milk, and whatever benefit is derived from them." Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿For you therein is warmth﴾. In a hadith: "We have from their *dif'* what they have guaranteed by covenant." *Al-dif'* also means heat. One says from it: *dafi'a al-rajul dafa'atan*, like *karaha karahatan*. Likewise *dafi'a dafa'an*, like *zami'a zama'an*. The noun is *al-difu'* (with a kasra), which is that which warms you, and its plural is *al-adfa'*. One says: *ma 'alayhi difu'* (he has no warm clothing), because it is a noun; and one does not say *ma 'alayka dafa'a* (with the verbal noun), because that is a *masdar*. And one says: *uq'ud fi difi' hadha al-ha'it* (sit in the warmth of this wall), meaning in its shelter. A man is *dafi'* on the pattern *fa'il* if he wears what warms him; likewise *rajul daf'an* and *imra'a dafa'a*. He warmed him with the garment (*adfa'ahu al-thawb*), and he warmed himself with it (*tadaffa'a bi-al-thawb*), and he was warmed by it (*istadfa'a bihi*). *Adda'a bihi* is of the *ifta'ala* form, meaning he wore what warmed him. *Dafu'at laylatuna* (our night was warm), and a warm day is *dafi'* on the pattern *fa'il*; a warm night is *daflyah*, and likewise a garment and a house. *Al-mudfi'a* is a large herd of camels, because some of them warm others with their breath, and it may be intensified. *Al-mudfi'a* is also a herd of camels with abundant wool and fat, from al-Asma'i. Al-Shammakh recited:

*"And how could one lose the owner of warm herds,
upon whose backs there is frost?"*
[[*athbaj*: plural of *thabaj*, the middle of something; it is said to be the space between its belly and its back.]]

**Allah's words**: ﴿And benefits﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: "The benefits are the offspring of every animal." Mujahid said: "Riding, carrying loads, milk, meat and ghee."

(﴿And of them you eat﴾) He singled out the benefit of eating for mention, because it is the greatest of the benefits. It was also said: the meaning is "and from their meat you eat at slaughter."

**Third question**: This verse indicates the wearing of wool, which was worn by the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and by the prophets before him, such as Musa and others. In the hadith of al-Mughira: "He washed his face, and he was wearing a Syrian woollen cloak with narrow sleeves..." the hadith. Muslim and others transmitted it. Ibn al-'Arabi said: "It is the emblem of the pious, the garment of the righteous, the distinguishing mark of the Companions and the Successors, and the choice of ascetics and those who know Allah. It is worn soft, coarse, good, moderate and poor. Certain people ascribed the Sufis to it, because it is generally their clothing; so the *ya'* is for the relative ascription and the *ha'* is for the feminine." One of their shaykhs recited to me in Bayt al-Maqdis, may Allah purify it:

*"People disputed about the Sufi and differed concerning him,
and they thought he was derived from* al-suf *(wool).*
I do not confer this name on anyone except a youth
who is pure, so he is called Sufi until he is named al-Sufi."*

Al-Jamal (beauty) is that by which one is adorned and made attractive. Al-Jamal means al-husn (goodness, fineness of form). It is said: the man became beautiful (jamula, with a damma on the jim) with jamal, so he is jamil (beautiful); the woman is jamila, and also jamla', according to al-Kisa'i. He recited:

"So she is jamla', like a rising full moon, who has surpassed all creation in beauty."

And the saying of Abu Dhu'ayb:

"Your beauty, O heart, which is wounded! [[This is the first half of the verse; its second half, as in Lisan al-Arab, is:

'We shall meet the one you love, and you will find rest.']]"

He means: keep to your dignity and modesty, and do not lament with an ugly lament.

Our scholars said: beauty exists in form and in the composition of creation, it exists in inner character, and it exists in actions. As for the beauty of creation, it is something the eye perceives and conveys to the heart as pleasing, so the soul becomes attached to it without knowing its cause or attributing it to any human being. As for the beauty of character, it is that one possesses praiseworthy qualities such as knowledge, wisdom, justice, chastity, restraining anger, and wishing good for everyone. As for the beauty of actions, it is their being suited to the interests of creation, bringing about benefits for them and averting harm from them. The beauty of livestock and beasts of burden is part of the beauty of creation; it is visible to the eyes and agreeable to insight. Among their beauty is their abundance, and people's saying when they see them, "These are the camels of so-and-so," as said by al-Suddi. And because when they are brought back in the evening their beauty becomes complete, their worth grows, and hearts become attached to them, for at that time they are at their fattest and their udders are fullest, as said by Qatadah. For this reason (God) mentioned the returning (in the evening) before the going out (in the morning), because at that time their milk is complete and the soul is delighted by them. And God knows best.

Ashhab related from Malik who said: God, Mighty and Majestic, says, "And for you in them is beauty when you bring them back and when you send them out to pasture" (16:6), and that refers to livestock when they return to the pasture and are sent out to graze upon it. Al-Ruwah (returning) is their return in the evening from the pasture, and al-Sarah is in the morning. You say: sarahat al-ibil asrahuha sarhan wa surudan, when you go out with them to the pasture in the morning and leave them there; and sarahat hiya (the camels went out on their own). The transitive and intransitive forms are the same.

This passage contains three issues (masa'il).

The first: Allah's words ﴿And it carries your burdens﴾. Al-athqal (the burdens) are the loads of people, of goods, food and other things, that is, whatever is heavy for a person to carry. It is said that what is meant is their bodies. This is supported by His words: ﴿and the earth brings forth its burdens﴾ [[See vol. 20, p. 147; perhaps the burdens in al-Zalzalah are the treasures.]]. "The land" (al-balad) is Makkah, according to the view of Ikrimah. It is also said that the verse is general, applying to every land where the traveller's route is on the back (of the animal). Shiqq al-anfus means their hardship and the utmost of their effort. The common recitation is with a kasrah on the shin. Al-Jawhari said: al-shiqq means hardship, and from it is His words: ﴿you would not have reached it except with great hardship to yourselves﴾. This may also be pronounced with a fatha, as transmitted by Abu Ubaydah. Al-Mahdawi said: the kasrah and fatha of the shin in "shiqq" are close in meaning; both mean hardship, and it derives from the splitting (shiqq) of a staff or the like, because it suffers from it as a person suffers hardship. Al-Tha'labi said: Abu Ja'far recited "illa bi-shiqq al-anfus", and both are two dialects, like riqq and raqq, jiss and jass, ritl and ratl. The verse of the poet is recited with both the kasrah and the fatha:

"And one with camels who strives for them, and reckons them his own; a brother of toil and labour, and one who is persistent."

It may also be a verbal noun from "shaqqqtu 'alayhi shaqqan" (I burdened him). Al-shiqq, with a kasrah, also means half: one says "akhadhtu shiqq al-shah" and "shiqqat al-shah" (I took half of the sheep). The meaning of the verse may also be this: you would not reach it except with a loss of strength and the going of a portion of it, that is, you would not reach it except with half the powers of your selves and the loss of the other half. Al-shiqq also means a side of a mountain. In the hadith of Umm Zar': "He found me among the people of a small flock in a Shiqq." Abu Ubayd said: it is the name of a place. Al-shiqq also means the shaqiq (full brother), one says: "He is my brother and the shiqq of my self." Shiqq is also the name of a soothsayer among the soothsayers of the Arabs. Al-shiqq also means the side, and from it is the words of Imru' al-Qays:

"When she weeps from behind her, she turns to him with a side, and beneath me is her side, unturned."

So it is a homonym.

The second: Allah, glorified is He, favoured us with livestock in general, and here He singled out camels for mention in carrying burdens over the other livestock, for sheep are for pasture and slaughter, cattle for ploughing, and camels for carrying. In the Sahih of Muslim, from Abu Hurairah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "While a man was driving a cow that he had loaded, the cow turned to him and said: 'I was not created for this; I was created only for ploughing.' The people said: 'Glory be to Allah!' in wonder and alarm: 'A cow speaks?' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'I believe in this, and so do Abu Bakr and Umar.'" This hadith indicates that cattle are not to be loaded or ridden, but are for ploughing, for eating, and for milk and offspring (al-nasl wa al-rasl) (al-rasl: milk).

The third: This verse is evidence for the permissibility of travelling with animals and loading burdens on them, but only in proportion to what they can bear, without excess in loading, together with gentleness in travel. The Prophet (ﷺ) commanded kindness towards them, giving them rest, and attending to their fodder and water. Muslim related from the hadith of Abu Hurairah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When you travel in fertile seasons, give the camels their share of the land; and when you travel in a year of drought, hasten with them to their marrow [[His words "in the drought" mean in dearth, when the land's plants have dried. Al-naqy (with a kasrah on the nun and sukun on the qaf) is the marrow. Its meaning: hasten the camels on their journey so that you reach the destination while they still have some strength, since there is nothing on the land to strengthen them for travel.]]." Malik related it in the Muwatta' from Abu Ubayd from Khalid ibn Ma'dan. Mu'awiyah ibn Qurrah related: Abu al-Darda' had a camel called Damun, and he used to say: "O Damun, do not dispute with me before your Lord." Animals are dumb; they cannot devise for themselves what they need, nor can they express their needs. Whoever benefits from their services and then neglects their needs has neglected gratitude and exposed himself to being disputed against before Allah, the Exalted. Matar ibn Muhammad related: Abu Dawud told us, saying: Ibn Khalid told us, saying: al-Musayyab ibn Adam told us, saying: "I saw Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, strike a camel-driver and say: 'Do you load on your camel what it cannot bear?'"

**Ch. 16, v. 8 (Part 1 of 2)**

There are three issues concerning this verse.

The first concerns His saying, ﴿and horses﴾. It is in the accusative (*wal-khayla*) as a conjunction, meaning: "and He created the horses." Ibn Abi 'Abla recited "*wal-khayla wal-baghala wal-hamir*" with the nominative (*raf'*) in all of them. The horse (*khayl*) was so named because of its *ikhtiyal*, its proud and swaggering gait. The singular of *khayl* is *khā'il*, like *da'in* being the singular of *da'n*. It is also said that it has no singular. This was mentioned earlier in Surat Al 'Imran,[[See vol. 4, p. 32.]] and we cited the hadiths there. When God, glorified is He, singled out the horses, mules and donkeys for mention, this indicates that they were not included under the term *al-an'am* (livestock). It has been said, however, that they were included, but were singled out for mention because of what relates to them of riding, for riding is common with horses, mules and donkeys.

The second issue: The scholars said: God, exalted is He, made the livestock and the beasts subject to us and tamed them for us, and permitted us to make them serve us and to benefit from them, out of His mercy toward us. Whatever a person owns and is permitted to put to use among animals, its hire (*kira'*) is permissible by the *ijma'* (scholarly consensus), with no disagreement among them about this. The ruling on hiring mounts and beasts is mentioned in the books of jurisprudence (*fiqh*).

The third issue: There is no disagreement among the scholars about hiring beasts and mounts, and travelling on them, due to His saying, ﴿and they carry your loads﴾ [16:7], and the verse goes on. They permitted a man to hire out a beast or a mount to a specific city, even if he does not specify where along the way he will stop, or how many watering places (*manhal*)[[*Al-manhal*: the watering place; then the term came to be used so widely that the stopping places by the waters on the route became known as *manahil*.]] he will stop at, the manner of his travel, or how many stops he will make on the road. They relied on what is customary among people in such matters.

Our scholars said: Hiring (*al-kira'*) follows the rules of sales (*al-buyu'*) in what is lawful and unlawful in it. Ibn al-Qasim said, concerning one who hires a beast to a certain place in exchange for a woven garment (*thawb marwi*) without describing its dimensions or length: it is not permitted, because Malik did not permit this in sales, and he does not permit in the price of hire anything except what is permitted in the price of a sale. I say: there is no disagreement about this, God willing, because this is a lease (*ijarah*).

Ibn al-Mundhir said: All the scholars whose transmissions are known have agreed that if a man hires a beast in order to load ten *qafizah* of wheat onto it, and he loads what was stipulated, and it perishes, then there is no liability on him. The same holds if he loads ten *qafizah* of barley. They differed concerning one who hires a beast to load ten *qafizah* onto it, and he loads eleven *qafizah*. Al-Shafi'i and Abu Thawr said: he is liable for the value of the beast, and he owes the hire. Ibn Abi Layla said: he owes its value, and he owes no hire. And there is a third view: that he owes the hire, and owes a portion of the rent and a portion of the value of the beast in proportion to the extra load. This is the view of al-Nu'man (Abu Hanifa), Ya'qub and Muhammad. Ibn al-Qasim, the companion of Malik, said: there is no liability on him according to Malik's view if the extra *qafiz* does not overburden the beast, and it is known that such a load does not cause the beast to die; and the owner of the beast is owed the hire for the extra *qafiz* along with the original hire, because its death was not caused by the extra load. This differs from exceeding the agreed distance, because exceeding the distance is entirely a transgression (*ta'addi*), so he is liable if it perishes, whether the excess is small or large. The extra load beyond what was stipulated combines permission and transgression; so if the extra load does not usually cause death to such a beast, it is known that its perishing is from what he was permitted to do.

The fourth issue: The scholars differed concerning a man who hires a beast for a set fee to a specified place, then transgresses and goes beyond that place, and then returns to the place he was permitted to reach. One group said: if he goes beyond that place, he is liable, and he owes no hire for the transgression; this is what al-Thawri said. Abu Hanifa said: he owes the hire for what he stipulated, and he owes no hire for what he did not stipulate, because he acted contrary (to the agreement), so he is liable; and Ya'qub agreed with this. Al-Shafi'i said: he owes the hire that was stipulated, and the customary hire (*kira' al-mithl*) for the distance beyond that; and if the beast dies, he must pay its value. The seven jurists of Madina, the elders of the people of Madina, said something similar: if he reaches the distance and then goes further, he owes the hire for the extra distance if the beast survives, and if it perishes he is liable. Ahmad, Ishaq and Abu Thawr said: he owes both the hire and liability for damage. Ibn al-Mundhir said: we also hold this view. Ibn al-Qasim said: if the hirer reaches the destination for which he hired the beast and then goes a mile or so further, or a few miles, or a considerable distance further, and the beast dies, then its owner is owed the original hire, and he has the choice of taking the hire for the extra distance, however far it goes, or the value of the beast on the day of the transgression. Ibn al-Mawwaz: it has also been related that he is liable even if he goes a single step further. Ibn al-Qasim also reported from Malik concerning the extra mile or the like: "As for what people deviate to during a day's march, he is not liable." Ibn Habib reported from Ibn al-Majishun and Asbagh: if the excess is slight, or he exceeds the agreed time by a little, then he returns with the beast safe to the place he hired it to, and it dies, or dies on the way to that place, then he owes only the hire for the excess, just as one returns what he borrowed of a deposit (*wadi'ah*). If he exceeds by a great deal, such that in that many days the beast's condition would change, then he is liable, just as if it had died while exceeding the time or the distance. This is because when the excess is slight, it is known that such an excess does not contribute to killing it, so its death after it has been returned to the place he was permitted to reach is like the death of what he borrowed of a deposit after he has returned it, without doubt. But if the excess is great, then that excess has contributed to its death.

The fifth issue: Ibn al-Qasim and Ibn Wahb said: Malik said: God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And horses and mules and donkeys, for you to ride and as an adornment﴾ [16:8]. So He made them for riding and adornment, and did not make them for eating. Ashhab said something similar. For this reason our companions said: it is not permitted to eat the flesh of horses, mules or donkeys, because when God specified riding and adornment, this indicates that what is other than these is excluded. Concerning livestock He said: ﴿and some of them you eat﴾ [16:5], together with what God bestowed upon us from them of warmth and benefits; so He permitted us to eat them through the lawful slaughter (*dhakah*) prescribed for them. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hakam ibn 'Uyayna also argued from this verse. Al-Hakam said: the flesh of horses is forbidden in the Book of God, and he recited this verse and the one before it, and said: "This is for eating, and this is for riding." Ibn 'Abbas was asked about the flesh of horses and disliked it, and he recited this verse and said: "This is for riding," and he recited the verse before it, ﴿And the livestock He created for you, in them is warmth and benefits﴾ [16:5], and then said: "This is for eating." Malik, Abu Hanifa and their companions, al-Awza'i, Mujahid, Abu 'Ubayd and others held this view as well. They relied on what Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, al-Daraqutni and others transmitted from Salih ibn Yahya ibn al-Miqdam ibn Ma'd Yakrib, from his father, from his grandfather, from Khalid ibn al-Walid, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) forbade on the day of Khaybar the eating of the flesh of horses, mules and donkeys, and every animal with a fang among beasts of prey or a talon among birds. This is the wording of al-Daraqutni. Al-Nasa'i also has, from Khalid ibn al-Walid, that he heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say: "The eating of the flesh of horses, mules and donkeys is not lawful."

The majority of jurists and hadith scholars said: it is permissible. This is also reported from Abu Hanifa. A small group deviated and said it is forbidden, among them al-Hakam as we mentioned, and this is also reported from Abu Hanifa. Al-Ruyani, in *Bahr al-Madhhab* according to the Shafi'i school, reported three narrations from him.

I say: the correct view, which reason and the reports indicate, is the permissibility of eating horse flesh, and that neither the verse nor the hadith is a binding proof against it. As for the verse, there is no evidence in it for forbidding horses; for if it indicated this, it would indicate the forbidding of donkey flesh, and the surah is Meccan. What need was there to renew the prohibition of donkey flesh in the year of Khaybar, when the permissibility of horses is established in the reports, as will come? Also, when God mentioned the livestock, He mentioned the most prevalent of their benefits and their most important aspect, which is carrying loads and eating; He did not explicitly mention riding, ploughing with them, or anything else, though they are ridden and used for ploughing. God said: ﴿It is He who made the livestock for you, that you may ride some of them and some of them you eat﴾ [see vol. 15, p. 334]. And about horses He said: ﴿for you to ride and as an adornment﴾, so He also mentioned their most prevalent benefit and their main purpose, and did not mention carrying loads on them, though they are indeed used to carry loads, as is observed. For this reason He did not mention eating. And the Prophet (peace be upon him), to whom was entrusted the explanation of what was revealed to him, has clarified it, as will come. It does not follow from their having been created for riding and adornment that they may not be eaten. Consider this cow: its Creator, who made everything speak, made it speak, and it said: "I was only created for ploughing." So whoever reasons that horses may not be eaten because they were created for riding must also reason that cows may not be eaten because they were created for ploughing. The Muslims have agreed on the permissibility of eating cows; so likewise horses, by the established Sunna concerning them. Muslim related from the hadith of Jabir, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) forbade on the day of Khaybar the flesh of domestic donkeys, and permitted the flesh of horses." And al-Nasa'i reported from Jabir: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) fed us the flesh of horses on the day of Khaybar and forbade us the flesh of donkeys." In another narration from Jabir he said: "We used to eat the flesh of horses during the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ)."

If it is said: the report from Jabir that they ate them at Khaybar is a report of a situation and a specific incident, so it is possible that they slaughtered them out of necessity, and one cannot argue from incidents of circumstance. We say: Jabir's report and his informing that they used to eat horse flesh during the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) removes that possibility. And even if we concede it, we have the hadith of Asma', who said: "We slaughtered a horse during the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) while we were in Madina, and we ate it." Muslim related it. Every interpretation without preponderance (*tarjih*) set against an explicit text is mere assertion, not to be paid attention to or turned to. Al-Daraqutni also related a fine addition which overrides every interpretation in the hadith of Asma': Asma' said: "We had a horse during the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) which was about to die, so we slaughtered it and ate it." So its slaughter was only out of fear that it would die, and not for any other of the circumstances. And success is from God.

If it is said: an animal with solid hooves, so it should not be eaten, like the donkey? We say: this is analogy by resemblance (*qiyas al-shabah*), and the scholars of the principles of jurisprudence differed concerning whether it is valid to rely on it. And even if we concede it, it is refuted by the pig, for it has a cloven hoof, yet it differs from the cloven-hoofed animals. Moreover, when analogy is set against an explicit text, it is invalid in its foundation and not to be paid attention to.

Al-Tabari said: In their consensus on the permissibility of riding what is mentioned, there is evidence for the permissibility of eating what is mentioned for riding.

**Sixth:** As for mules, they are classed with donkeys if we hold that horses are not eaten. A mule is then born of two animals that are not eaten. If we hold that horses are eaten, a mule is an animal born of an edible and a non-edible parent, so prohibition takes precedence, following what applies in the principal sources. Likewise, the slaughter (*dhakah*, ritual slaughter) of an offspring born to two disbelievers, one of whom is among those eligible to perform *dhakah* and the other not, is not a valid *dhakah*, and the animal is not lawful through it. The discussion of the prohibition of wine has already passed in *al-An'am* [[See vol. 7, p. 115 onward.]], so there is no point in repeating it. The prohibition of eating the donkey has been explained by the reason that it displays its foul essence when it mounts a male and engages in sodomy, and so it is called *rijs* (filth).

**Seventh:** The verse indicates that there is no *zakah* (obligatory alms, *zakat*) on horses, because Allah, glorified is He, has bestowed favour upon us by permitting them to us and honouring us with their benefits. It is not permissible to impose a burden upon them except by evidence. Malik narrated from ʿAbdullah ibn Dinar, from Sulayman ibn Yasar, from ʿIrak ibn Malik, from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "There is no *sadaqah* (charity) on a Muslim for his slave or his horse." Abu Dawud narrated from Abu Hurayrah, from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who said: "There is no *zakah* on horses or slaves, except the *zakat al-fitr* on slaves." This is the view of Malik, al-Shafiʿi, al-Awzaʿi, al-Layth, Abu Yusuf and Muhammad. Abu Hanifah said: If they are all females, or males and females, then for every horse grazing freely there is one dinar, and if he wishes he may value them and pay from every two hundred dirhams five dirhams. He argued with a report from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "On grazing horses, one dinar for every horse," and with his saying ﷺ: "Horses are of three kinds..." the hadith. In it is: "and he has not forgotten Allah's right in their necks or their backs."

As for the first, the answer is that it is a hadith that no one narrated except Ghurak [[He is Ghurak ibn al-Hadrami, Abu ʿAbdullah.
(From al-Daraqutni.)]] al-Saʿdi, from Jaʿfar, from Muhammad, from his father, from Jabir. Al-Daraqutni said: Ghurak alone transmitted it from Jaʿfar, and he is extremely weak, and those below him are weak. As for the hadith, the right (*haqq*) mentioned in it is going out on them (horses) when a call to mobilise (*nafir*) occurs and they become obligatory for fighting the enemy when that is required. It also concerns carrying those who are cut off (from their means) on them when they need it. This is obligatory upon him when it becomes necessary, just as it becomes obligatory for him to feed them in cases of necessity. These are Allah's rights in their necks.

If it is said: this is the right in their backs, and the right in their necks remains, the answer is: it has been narrated, "He does not forget Allah's right in them." There is no difference between his saying "Allah's right in them" and "in their necks and backs," since the meaning returns to one thing, because the right attaches to the whole of them. A group of scholars have said that the right here is to keep them in good condition, to ensure they are well fed, to treat them kindly, and to ride them without overburdening them, as came in the hadith: "Do not take their backs as chairs." The mention of their necks in particular is because necks and throats are often used figuratively in places of binding rights and obligatory duties, such as the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿freeing a believing neck﴾ [[See vol. 5, p. ...]]. Their use and figurative application of this became so common that they applied it to property and wealth. Do you not see the saying of Kuthayyir:

*"Generous of garment, when he smiles laughing,*
*the necks of wealth are shackled by his laughter."* [[Ghamr: abundant water. A man ghamr al-ridaʾ means generous of garment, and ghamr al-khuluq means broad of disposition, bountiful and munificent.]]

Also, the animal for which *zakah* is due has a *nisab* (threshold) of its own kind, and since horses are outside this, we know that *zakah* does not apply to them. Also, imposing *zakah* on females alone, excluding males, is a contradiction on his part, and there is no distinction in the hadith between them. We analogise females to males in the negation of charity, on the basis that it is an animal kept for its offspring and not for its milk, and *zakah* is not due on its males, so it is not due on its females, like mules and donkeys.

It has also been narrated from him (Abu Hanifah) that there is no *zakah* on their females if they are kept separately, just as there is none on their males when kept separately. This is the view of the majority. Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr said: The report on the *sadaqah* of horses from ʿUmar is sound, from the transmission of al-Zuhri and others. It has also been narrated through Malik's transmission, and Juwayriyyah related it from him, from al-Zuhri, that al-Saʾib ibn Yazid said: "I saw my father valuing the horses and then handing their *sadaqah* to ʿUmar." This is a proof for Abu Hanifah and his teacher Hammad ibn Abi Sulayman. I know of no jurist from the major cities who made *zakah* obligatory on horses other than these two. Juwayriyyah alone transmitted it from Malik, and he is trustworthy.

**Eighth:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and as adornment﴾ is in the accusative by an implied verb; the meaning is "and He made them an adornment." It has also been said that it is an object of purpose (*maf'ul li-ajlih*). *Zinah* (adornment) is that with which one beautifies oneself. Although this beauty and adornment are among the enjoyments of this world, Allah, glorified is He, has permitted His servants to have it. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Camels are a might for their owners, sheep are a blessing, and horses have good tied to their foreheads." Al-Barqani and Ibn Majah recorded it in the *Sunan*. It has already been mentioned in *al-An'am*.

The Prophet ﷺ gathered might in camels because they provide clothing, food, milk, carrying and warfare, even though attack and retreat reduce them. He placed blessing in sheep because of the clothing, food and drink they provide and their abundant offspring, for they give birth three times a year, besides the tranquillity that accompanies them, and they bring their owner to humility and gentleness of manner, unlike the *faddadin* (owners of many camels, who own between two hundred and a thousand camels; in another source: people of camels), the people of the wool-tent (*ahl al-wabar*). The Prophet ﷺ associated good with the foreheads of horses for as long as time endures, because of the spoils gained through acquisition and livelihood, and what is reached through subduing enemies, overcoming unbelievers, and raising the word of Allah, exalted is He.

**His saying, exalted is He:** ﴿and He creates what you do not know﴾. Al-Jumhur said: it is from the creation. It was also said: it refers to kinds of insects and vermin in the lower parts of the earth, on land and in the sea, which humans have neither seen nor heard of. It was also said: "and He creates what you do not know" refers to what Allah has prepared in Paradise for its people and in the Fire for its people, which no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and which has not occurred to the heart of any human. Qatadah and al-Suddi said: it is the creation of the weevil in clothes and the worm in fruits. Ibn ʿAbbas said: a spring beneath the Throne, related by al-Mawardi. Al-Tha'labi said: Ibn ʿAbbas said: to the right of the Throne is a river of light, like the seven heavens, the seven earths and the seven seas, seventy times over. Gabriel enters it every dawn and bathes, and his light increases upon his light, his beauty upon his beauty, his greatness upon his greatness. Then he shakes himself, and Allah brings forth from each feather seventy thousand drops, and from each drop He brings forth seven thousand angels, of whom seventy thousand enter the Bayt al-Maʿmur every day, and seventy thousand enter the Kaʿbah, and they do not return to it until the Day of Resurrection.

A fifth opinion [[So in the originals. The apparent reading is "sixth."]] is what is narrated from the Prophet ﷺ, that it is "a white land, a journey of thirty days for the sun, filled with creatures who do not know that Allah, exalted is He, is disobeyed on earth." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, are they from the children of Adam?" He said: "They do not know that Allah created Adam." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, where is Iblis among them?" He said: "They do not know that Allah created Iblis." Then he recited: ﴿and He creates what you do not know﴾. Al-Mawardi mentioned it.

(Margin note) I say: In this same sense is what al-Bayhaqi mentioned from al-Shaʿbi, who said: "Indeed Allah has servants beyond al-Andalus, as we have explained, between them and al-Andalus, who consider that the one who disobeys Him is a created being. Their pebbles are pearls and rubies, their mountains are gold and silver. They do not plough or sow, and they do no work. They have trees at their doors that bear fruit, which is their food, and trees with broad leaves, which is their clothing." He mentioned this in the beginning of creation from the *Kitab al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat* [Book of Names and Attributes]. (Note: *al-rada'd* means pebbles.) He also transmitted from the hadith of Musa ibn ʿUqbah, from Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir, from Jabir ibn ʿAbdullah al-Ansari, who said: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "I have been permitted to relate about an angel of Allah's angels, one of the bearers of the Throne, that the distance between the lobe of his ear and his shoulder is a journey of seven hundred years."

**Al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Qur'an) on Surah 16, verse 9:**

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And upon Allah is the direct way﴾. That is, upon Allah is the explanation of the direct way, so the modifier, which is the explanation, has been omitted. *Al-sabil* (the way) means the path. That is, upon Allah is its explanation through the messengers, the proofs and the evidences. *Qasd al-sabil* (the direct way) means the straightness of the path. It is said: a *tariq qasid* (a straight road), meaning one that leads to the desired goal.

(﴿And among it is the deviating﴾) That is, among the way there is one that deviates, meaning one that turns aside from the truth, so one is not guided by it. From this is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*"And of the path is a deviating one, and a guided one... the direct way, and of it is the one that bends."*

And Tarafa said:

*"Ya'dawliyya, or from the ships of Ibn Yamin... the sailor makes it deviate at times."*

*Al-'Adawliyya* is a ship attributed to 'Adawli, a village in Bahrain. *Al-'Adawli* is the sailor, as he stated in *al-Sihah*. In the revelation: ﴿And that this is My path, straight, so follow it, and do not follow the other ways﴾. This has already been mentioned [see vol. 7, p. 137].

It is also said that the meaning is: "And among them is one who deviates from the path of truth," meaning one who turns away from it, so he is not guided to it. Regarding *them* there are two opinions. The first is that they are the people of the varying desires, as Ibn 'Abbas said. The second is that they are the religious communities of disbelief: Judaism, Zoroastrianism and Christianity.

In the Mushaf of 'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud) it reads "and among you is the deviating one." 'Ali also read "minkum" with the *kaf* (you). It is also said that the meaning is "and from it (*'anha*) is the deviating one," that is, from the way. Here *min* carries the meaning of *'an* (from/away from).

Ibn 'Abbas said: whoever Allah wants to guide, He makes the path of faith easy for him, and whoever He wants to misguide, He makes faith and its branches burdensome upon him.

It is also said: the meaning of *qasd al-sabil* is "your journey and your return." The word *al-sabil* is singular in form but collective in meaning, and for this reason the pronoun is feminine, so He says: ﴿among it﴾. In the dialect of the people of the Hijaz, *al-sabil* is feminine.

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And had He willed, He would have guided you all﴾. This shows that the will belongs to Allah, the Exalted. It confirms what Ibn 'Abbas held in interpreting the verse, and it refutes the Qadariyya (the sect that affirmed human free will in the absolute sense) and those who agree with them, as has already been mentioned.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 16, verse 10:

"Al-sharab" is what is drunk. "Wa'l-shajar" is known (ma'ruf), meaning that from the rain there grow trees, vines (ʿurush) and plants.

"Tusimun" (you pasture your livestock): "tasra'una ibilakum." It is said: "sama al-sa'imah yasumu sawman," meaning she grazed, so she is "sa'imah" (a grazing animal). "Al-sawam" and "al-sa'im" have the same meaning, and it is the grazing livestock. The plural of "al-sa'im" and "al-sa'imah" is "sawa'im." "Asamtuha" I mean: I took it out to graze, so I am "musim" and it is "musamah" and "sa'imah." He said:

"Awla laka ibn musimat al-ajmal" [[This is the second half of a line; its first half, as in Tafsir al-Tabari, is: "mithla ibn bazi'ah aw ka-akhar mithlihi."]]

The root of "sawm" is distance in pasture. Al-Zajjaj said: it is taken from "al-suwmah," which is the mark, meaning that they leave marks on the ground by their grazing; or because they are marked (ta'lim) for being sent out to pasture. I say: "al-khayl al-musawwamah" may be the ones put out to pasture, and may be the ones marked (mu'allamah). As for His saying "musawwimin," al-Akhfash said: it may mean marked, and it may mean sent out, from your saying "sawwama fiha al-khayl," meaning he sent the horses into it; and from it comes "al-sa'imah." It came with the ya' and nun because the horses were marked and their riders were upon them.

**The words of the Exalted: ﴿He causes to grow for you thereby the crops, the olives, the date palms, the grapes, and of all the fruits.﴾** Abu Bakr, on the authority of 'Asim, read *nunbitu* (نُنْبِتُ) with a *nun*, as an expression of majesty (*ta'zim*). The majority (*al-'ammah*) read it with a *ya'* (يُنْبِتُ), meaning "God causes to grow for you." It is said *yunbitu al-ardu* and *anbatat* with the same meaning, and *nabata al-baqlu* and *anbata* with the same meaning. Al-Farra' recited:

*Ra'aytu dhawi al-hajati hawla buyutihim*
*qatinan biha hatta idha anbata al-baqlu*

That is, *nabata* (it grew). It is said *anbatahu Allahu fa-huwa manbut*, against the usual analogy (*qiyas*). *Anbata al-ghulamu*: his pubic hair grew. *Nabata al-shajaru gharsahu* [[In the text: *bi-nabt al-shajar gharsatuhu*.]]. It is said: *nabata ajaluka bayna 'aynayk* (your death has sprouted between your eyes). *Nabbatu al-sabiyya tanbitan*: I raised the child. *Al-manbat* is the place of growth; it is said: *ma ahsana nabitata bani fulan*, that is, what their wealth and children grow upon. *Nabatat lahum nabita* when young offspring grow up for them. *Inna bani fulanin lanabitatu sharr* (the sons of so-and-so are a bad growth). *Al-nawabit* are the foolish, inexperienced people. *Al-Nabit* is a tribe of Yemen, and its name is 'Amr ibn Malik [[Abu Hayy from Yemen, whose name is 'Amr ibn Malik.]]. *Al-yanbut* is a tree; all of this is from al-Jawhari [[In al-Qamus: *al-yanbut* is the poppy tree or another tree, the carob.]].

**(Wa-al-zaytun)** is the plural of *zaytunah*. The word is used both for the tree itself and for its fruit, *zaytunah*. The ruling on the obligatory alms (*zakat*) on these fruits has already been discussed in *Surat al-An'am* [[See vol. 7, p. 99 onward.]], so there is no point in repeating it.

**(Inna fi dhalika)**, that is, in the sending down (of water) and the causing of growth,

**(La-ayatan)**, that is, a sign (*dalalah*), **(li-qawmin yatafakkarun)**, for a people who reflect.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 16, verse 12:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He has subjected to you the night and the day﴾, meaning for rest and for work, as He said: "And out of His mercy He made for you the night and the day, that you may rest therein and that you may seek of His bounty" [see vol. 13, p. 308].

(﴿And the sun and the moon and the stars are subjected by His command﴾), meaning made subservient for knowing the times, for the ripening of fruits and crops, and for being guided by the stars in the darknesses. Ibn 'Abbas [in one report] and Ibn 'Amir and the people of Syria read "wa-al-shamsa wa-al-qamara wa-al-nujumu musakharatun" with the nominative (raf'), as an inceptive subject and predicate. The rest read it in the accusative (nasb), as a conjunction with what precedes it. Hafs, from 'Asim, read "wa-al-nujumu" with the nominative, with "musakharatun" as its predicate. It is also reported as "wa-al-shamsa wa-al-qamara wa-al-nujumu" in the accusative.

(Conjoined to "al-layla" and "al-nahar," with "wa-al-nujumu" in the nominative as an inceptive subject. "Musakharatun" in the nominative is the predicate of an elided inceptive subject), meaning: they are musakharatun. In the reading of one who put it in the accusative, it is an emphatic circumstantial clause (hal mu'akkida), as in His saying: "And it is the truth, confirming" [see vol. 2, p. 29].

(﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who reason﴾), meaning: who reflect upon what Allah has alerted them to and granted them success in.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 16, verse 13:

There are three issues in this.

The first: His, the Exalted's, statement: ﴿And what He has created (dhara'a)﴾, meaning: and He has subjected to you what He has created (dhara'a) in the earth. "Dhara'a" means "khalaqa" (created). God created the creation, yadhra'uhum dhar'an, that is, He created them, so He is Dhari'. From it comes "al-dhurriyyah" (offspring), which is the progeny of the two weighty things (jinn and humankind), except that the Arabs dropped its hamza. Its plural is "al-dharari" (offspring). It is said: "May God make your dhar'ak and dharwak grow," meaning your offspring. The root meaning of "dharw" and "dhar'" is scattering after gathering. In the hadith [[That is, in the hadith of Umar, may God be pleased with him, when he wrote to Khalid: "Indeed I think you are the family of al-Mughirah, the dhar'u of the Fire."]] "dhar'u al-nar" means that they were created for it.

The second: Whatever God, glory be to Him, has created of it is subjected and made submissive, like the beasts, the livestock, the trees and others, and other than that. The evidence for this is what Malik related in the Muwatta' from Ka'b al-Ahbar, who said: "Were it not for words I say, the Jews would have turned me into a donkey." It was said to him: "And what are they?" He said: "I seek refuge in the Face of God the Great, than which nothing is greater, and in the perfect words of God which neither the righteous nor the wicked can transgress, and in all the Most Beautiful Names of God, what I know of them and what I do not know, from the evil of what He has created, made, and scattered (dhara'a)." In it, from Yahya ibn Sa'id, who said: "The Messenger of God ﷺ was taken on the Night Journey, and he saw an 'ifrit of the jinn seeking him with a flame of fire," the hadith... And in it: "and the evil of what He has scattered (dhara'a) in the earth." We have mentioned it and what is in its meaning in another place.

The third: His, the Exalted's, statement: ﴿Its colours being diverse (mukhtalifan alwanuhu)﴾. "Mukhtalifan" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). "Alwanuhu" means its forms and appearances, meaning the beasts, the trees and others.

(Indeed in that) meaning: in the diversity of their colours.

(is a sign) meaning: is a lesson.

(for a people who take heed) meaning: who are admonished and know that in the subjugation of these created things there are signs of the Oneness of God, the Exalted, and that none other than Him is able to do that.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 16, verse 14 (part 1 of 2):**

There are nine issues in this verse.

**The first issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And it is He who subjected the sea﴾. The subjection of the sea means enabling people to make use of it and making it manageable for riding, for transport by ship, and for other purposes. This is one of God's blessings upon us. Had He willed, He could have given it power over us and drowned us. The discussion of the sea has already been covered (see vol. 1, p. 288), and so has its hunting (ṣayd). Here God calls its produce "flesh" (laḥm). According to Malik, flesh (luḥūm) comprises three kinds: the flesh of quadrupeds is one kind, the flesh of winged creatures is one kind, and the flesh of aquatic creatures is one kind. Therefore it is not permitted to sell one kind for another of the same kind with unequal amounts (mutafāḍil, i.e. riba-concern in exchange). It is permitted to sell the flesh of cattle and wild animals for the flesh of birds and fish with unequal amounts, and likewise the flesh of birds for the flesh of cattle, wild animals and fish with unequal amounts.

Abu Hanifa said: each type of flesh is a different kind, like its source. The flesh of cattle is one kind, the flesh of sheep is one kind, the flesh of camels is one kind; likewise wild animals differ, birds differ, and fish differ. This is a rejection of the two opinions of al-Shafi'i. The other opinion is that all of them, the livestock, game, birds and fish, are one kind, and exchanging them unequally is not permitted. The first opinion is the well-known position of his school among its adherents.

Our evidence is that God distinguished between the names of livestock in their living state. He said: ﴿eight mates: of the sheep two, and of the goats two﴾, then He said: ﴿and of the camels two, and of the cattle two﴾. But when He directed the whole to flesh, He said: ﴿Lawful for you are the beast of the cattle﴾, so He gathered them under one kind of flesh, because their benefits are similar, just as the flesh of sheep and goats is similar. He said in another place: ﴿and the flesh of birds of what they desire﴾, and this is the plural of ṭā'ir (bird), which is singular in form; and He said: ﴿nor a bird that flies with its two wings﴾. So He gathered all bird flesh under one name. And here He said: ﴿fresh flesh﴾, so He gathered the varieties of fish under one mention, and thus its small ones are like its large ones in this gathering.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Umar that he was asked whether the flesh of goats and the flesh of rams are one thing. He said: "No." No one disagreed with him, so it became like a consensus (ijmā'), and God knows best.

There is no proof for the opponent in his (ﷺ) prohibition of selling food except like for like, because food, in its general sense, covers wheat and other edibles, and does not cover meat. Do you not see that when someone says, "I ate food today," the understanding does not go first to eating meat? Furthermore, it is contradicted by his (ﷺ) saying: "When the two kinds differ, sell as you wish." These two are two kinds. Also, we agree on the permissibility of selling meat for bird meat with unequal amounts, not for the reason that it is the sale of food with no zakat sold for meat without zakat. Likewise, selling fish for bird meat with unequal amounts.

**The second issue:** As for locusts, the well-known position among us is that it is permitted to sell some of them for others with unequal amounts. It has been mentioned from Saḥnūn that he prohibited this, and some later scholars inclined to this view, considering it something that is stored (mudakhkhar).

**The third issue:** Scholars differ regarding one who swears that he will not eat meat. Ibn al-Qasim said: he breaks his oath by any kind of these four types. Ashhab said, in al-Majmū'a: he breaks his oath only by eating the flesh of livestock, not wild game or other kinds, out of regard for custom and common usage, and giving precedence to these over the general linguistic meaning of the word. This is better (aḥsan).

**The fourth issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and that you may extract from it ornaments which you wear﴾. It means pearls and coral, because of His saying: ﴿From both of them come out pearls and coral﴾. The extraction of ornaments is only from salt water alone. It was said that there is sea-born emerald. The Hudhali poet was faulted in his description of the pearl, when he said:

*So he brought it from a pearl of lataymiyya*
*Upon whose face is the water of the Euphrates, flowing.*

(Al-laṭīma: the camels that carry perfume. It was also said: al-laṭīma is the ambergris that is struck with musk so that its scent spreads until its fragrance is established, and it is called al-laṭīma.)

He made it from sweet water. So ornament is a right, and it is God's gift (niḥla) to Adam and his offspring. Adam was created and crowned and adorned with the crown of Paradise, and sealed with the ring which Solomon, son of David, inherited from him, may God's blessings be upon them. It was called "the ring of might," as it is related.

**The fifth issue:** God, glorified is He, bestowed a general favour upon men and women alike through what comes out of the sea, so nothing from it is forbidden to them. God forbade men only gold and silk. The authentic narration from 'Umar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb reports that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Do not wear silk, for whoever wears it in this world will not wear it in the Hereafter." Its discussion will come in surah al-Ḥajj, God willing (see vol. 12, p. 28).

Al-Bukhari narrated from Ibn 'Umar that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) made a ring of gold and placed its bezel on the side facing the inside of his palm, and engraved on it "Muhammad, Messenger of God." So the people made similar ones. When he saw that they had made them, he threw it away and said: "I will never wear it." Then he made a ring of silver, and people made rings of silver.

Ibn 'Umar said: After the Prophet (ﷺ), Abu Bakr wore the ring, then 'Umar, then 'Uthman, until it fell from 'Uthman into the well of Aris (a garden near the mosque of Quba).

Abu Dawud said: People did not differ regarding 'Uthman until the ring fell from his hand.

The scholars agreed on the permissibility of men wearing a silver ring in general. Al-Khaṭṭabi said: For women, wearing a silver ring is disliked, because it is a style of men. If they cannot find gold, they should dye it yellow with saffron or something similar.

The majority of scholars, from the early and later generations, hold that it is forbidden for men to wear a gold ring. The exception is what is reported from Abu Bakr ibn 'Abd al-Raḥman and Khabbab, but this is an anomalous opinion (khilāf shādhdh), and each of them had not received the prohibition and its abrogation (naskh). And God knows best.

As for what Anas ibn Malik narrated, that he saw on the hand of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) a silver ring for one day, then people made rings of silver and wore them, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) threw away his ring, and the people threw away their rings: this was narrated by the two Ṣaḥīḥs, and the wording is al-Bukhari's. It is, according to the scholars, a mistake (wahm) by Ibn Shihab, because what the Messenger of God (ﷺ) discarded was only a gold ring. It was narrated by 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Ṣuhayb and Qatada from Anas, and this contradicts what Ibn Shihab narrated from Anas. So the general ruling must be given in favour of the group against the single narrator who contradicts them, supported by the hadith of Ibn 'Umar.

**The sixth issue:** Once it is established that men may wear a silver ring and adorn themselves with it, Ibn Sirin and others among the scholars disliked engraving it, or having the remembrance of God on it. Some scholars permitted engraving it. Then, if the name of God, or a word of wisdom, or verses of the Qur'an is engraved on it and it is worn on the left hand, may one enter the lavatory with it and cleanse oneself with the left hand? Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab and Malik made this lenient. It was said to Malik: If there is the remembrance of God on the ring and one wears it on the left hand, may one cleanse oneself with it? He said: "I hope it is lenient." It is also narrated from him that it is disliked, and this is the preferable view. Most of his companions held the prohibition of this.

Hammam narrated from Ibn Jurayj, from al-Zuhri, from Anas, who said: When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) entered the lavatory, he would place his ring. Abu Dawud said: This is a munkar hadith. It is only known from Ibn Jurayj, from Ziyad ibn Sa'd, from al-Zuhri, from Anas, that the Prophet (ﷺ) made a ring of silver and then threw it away. Abu Dawud said: No one narrated this except Hammam.

**The seventh issue:** Al-Bukhari narrated from Anas ibn Malik that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) made a ring of silver and engraved on it "Muhammad, Messenger of God," and said: "I have made a ring of silver and engraved on it 'Muhammad, Messenger of God,' so let no one engrave upon its engraving." Our scholars said: This is evidence for the permissibility of engraving the name of the owner of the ring on his ring. Malik said: It is the practice of caliphs and judges to engrave their names on their rings. His (ﷺ) prohibition, "let no one engrave upon its engraving," is because that name is his, and describes him as the Messenger of God sent to His creation.

The people of Syria narrated that it is not permitted for anyone other than a ruler to wear a ring, and they narrated a hadith about this from Abu Rayhana, but it is a hadith with no proof due to its weakness. His (ﷺ) saying, "let no one engrave upon its engraving," refutes this, and indicates the permissibility of all people wearing a ring, provided it is not engraved with the same engraving as his ring.

The engraving of al-Zuhri's ring was "Muhammad asks God for well-being" (*Muḥammad yas'al Allāh al-'āfiya*). The engraving of Malik's ring was "God is sufficient for me, and excellent is the Guardian" (*Ḥasbiya Allāh wa ni'ma al-wakīl*).

Al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim mentioned in (*Nawādir al-Uṣūl*) that the engraving on the ring of Moses, peace be upon him, was "For every term is a Book" (*Likulli ajalin kitāb*), and this has passed in surah al-Ra'd (see vol. 9, p. 329).

It reached 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz that his son had bought a ring for a thousand dirhams, so he wrote to him: "It has reached me that you bought a ring for a thousand dirhams. Sell it and feed a thousand hungry people with its price, and buy an iron ring for a dirham, and engrave on it: 'May God have mercy on the person who knows his own worth.'"

**The eighth issue:** Whoever swears that he will not wear an ornament (ḥilya) and wears pearls does not break his oath, and this is the view of Abu Hanifa. Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: Because this, although the linguistic term includes it, was not intended by the oath, and oaths are restricted by custom. Do you not see that if someone swears that he will not sleep on a bed and sleeps on the ground, he does not break his oath? Likewise, if he swears that he will not take light from a lamp and sits in the sun, he does not break his oath, even though God has called the earth a bed and the sun a lamp.

Al-Shafi'i, Abu Yusuf and Muhammad said: Whoever swears that he will not wear an ornament and wears pearls breaks his oath, because of God's saying: ﴿and that you may extract from it ornaments which you wear﴾, and what comes out of it is pearls and coral.

**The ninth issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and you see the ships ploughing through it﴾. The mention of ships and riding the sea has already been made in al-Baqara (see vol. 1, p. 388 and vol. 2, p. 194) and elsewhere. As for His saying: *mawākhir* (ploughing through). Ibn 'Abbas said: *jawārī*, from *jarat tajrī* (they run). Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: *mu'taridha* (crossing). Al-Hasan said: *mawāqir* (laden). Qatada and al-Ḍaḥḥak said: that is, they go and come, advancing and retreating with one wind. It was also said: *mawākhir* means cutting through the depths of the sea. The root of *al-makhr* is splitting the water to the right and left. *Makhara al-safīna* (the ship ploughed), *tamkhuru* and *tamkhuru*, *makhran* and *mukhūran*, when it runs, splitting the water with a sound. From this is His saying: ﴿and you see the ships ploughing through it﴾, meaning *jawārī* (running).

Al-Jawhari said: *makhara al-sābiḥ* (the swimmer) when he splits the water with his chest; *makhara al-arḍ* means he split it for cultivation; and *makharahā bil-mā'* means when he holds water in it until it becomes fertile, that is, suitable for the good growth of crops.

Al-Tabari said: *al-makhr* in the language is the sound of the blowing of the wind, and he did not restrict it to being in water. He said: Among that is the saying of Wasil, the client of Abu 'Uyayna: "When one of you wants to urinate, let him *tamakhkhar* the wind," that is, let him look at its sound in the bodies, to see from where it blows, so that he avoids facing it, lest it return his urine upon him.

(And that you may seek of His bounty) i.e., and that you may ride it for trade and the pursuit of profit. (And perhaps you will be grateful) All of this has already been discussed in "al-Baqarah," and praise be to God.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 16, verse 15:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And He cast into the earth firm mountains﴾, meaning stable mountains. Rasa yarsu (to be firm, settled) means it became fixed and stood firm. He said:

"So I patiently restrained a noble soul in that state, while the soul of the coward rises up and is steadfast." [[The verse is by 'Antarah al-'Absi. He says: I restrained a soul that knows its duty, that is, patient. Before it is:

"And I knew that my death, if it comes to me, the swiftest flight will not save me from it."]]

(Lest it should sway with you) meaning lest it sway, according to the Kufans. And "out of dislike that it should sway," according to the Basrans. The mayd is agitation to right and left: mada al-shay' yamidu mayadan when it moves; madat al-aghsan means the branches swayed; and mada al-rajul means he strutted proudly. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: God created the earth and it began to sway and shake, so the angels said: "Indeed this earth will not keep anyone steady upon its back." So it became settled by the mountains, and the angels did not know what the mountains were created from.

'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, said: When God created the earth, it trembled and inclined, and said: "My Lord! Will You place upon me those who commit sins and transgressions, and cast upon me carrion and stench?" So God, exalted is He, set firm in it of the mountains what you see and what you do not see.

al-Tirmidhi narrated at the end of (the Book of Tafsir): Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, Yazid ibn Harun narrated to us, al-'Awwam ibn Hawshab informed us, from Sulayman ibn Abi Sulayman, from Anas ibn Malik, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "When God created the earth, it began to sway, so He created the mountains and cast them upon it, and it became firm. The angels were amazed at the strength of the mountains and said: 'O Lord, is there anything in Your creation stronger than the mountains?' He said: 'Yes, iron.' They said: 'O Lord, is there anything in Your creation stronger than iron?' He said: 'Yes, fire.' They said: 'O Lord, is there anything in Your creation stronger than fire?' He said: 'Yes, water.' They said: 'O Lord, is there anything in Your creation stronger than water?' He said: 'Yes, wind.' They said: 'O Lord, is there anything in Your creation stronger than wind?' He said: 'Yes, the son of Adam who gives charity with his right hand, concealing it from his left.'" Abu 'Isa (al-Tirmidhi) said: This is a gharib hadith; we do not know it as marfu' except through this chain.

I say: In this verse is the clearest evidence for the use of means, although He was capable of steadying it without the mountains. This meaning has already been mentioned.

(And rivers) meaning and He placed in it rivers, or cast into it rivers.

(And roads) meaning paths and routes.

(So that you may be guided) meaning to the places you intend among the lands, so that you do not go astray or become bewildered.

Third-part translation below.

There are three issues in this.

The first: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And landmarks﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "The landmarks are the markers of the roads by day," meaning He made for the road markers by which guidance is achieved.

(And by the star they are guided) meaning by night, and "the star" is intended to mean the stars. Ibn Wththab recited "wa-bin-nujum" (with a ḍammah on the nūn and the jīm). Al-Ḥasan (recited it) with a ḍammah on both the nūn and the jīm, and he intended the stars, so he shortened it, as the poet said:

Indeed the poor man among us is a judge who decides
that you should go to the water when the stars have set.

The same applies to the one who recited "an-najm," except that he lightened it by sukūn for ease. It is also possible that "an-Nujum" is the plural of najm, like suquf and saqf. There is disagreement about the stars: al-Farrāʾ said they are al-Jady and al-Farqadān. It was also said they are the Pleiades (al-Thurayyā). The poet said:

Until, when the star rose in the dim light before dawn,
and the herbage was left, some twisted and some cut down.

(Note: "istaqall" means it rose at the end of the night. In his Dīwān it reads "uḥṣida" instead of "ghudira." Uḥṣida means its time of harvest came.)

That is, some of it was twisted and some of it was cut down, and this happens at the rising of the Pleiades. Al-Kalbī said: the landmarks are the mountains. Mujāhid said: they are the stars, because among the stars there are those by which one is guided and those which are only signs and by which one is not guided. Qatādah and al-Nakhaʿī also said this. It was also said: the sentence is complete at His saying "wa-ʿalamat," then He begins and says "wa-bin-najmi hum yahtadun." According to the first view: that is, "And He made for you landmarks and stars by which you are guided." Among the landmarks are the winds, by which guidance is achieved. Regarding what guidance refers to there are two views: the first is during journeys, and this is the view of the majority; the second is regarding the qiblah. Ibn ʿAbbas said: I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about His saying, exalted is He: "And by the star they are guided," and he said: "It is al-Jady, O Ibn ʿAbbas, your qiblah is upon it, and by it you are guided on your land and your sea." Al-Māwardī mentioned it.

The second issue: Ibn al-ʿArabī said: As for all the stars, none is guided by them except one who knows their risings and settings, and the distinction between the southern and northern ones, and that is rare among people. As for the Pleiades, none is guided by it except one who is guided by all the stars. Guidance for everyone is only by al-Jady and al-Farqadayn, because they are among the stars with fixed rising points, clearly fixed direction, and stable in place, for they revolve around the fixed pole in a precise revolution. So they are always the guidance of creation on land when the roads are lost, at sea at the course of ships, and for the qiblah when direction is unknown. This is in general terms: you place the pole on the back of your left shoulder, and whatever you face is the direction of the qiblah. I say: Ibn ʿAbbas asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the star, and he said: "It is al-Jady, upon which is your qiblah, and by it you are guided on your land and your sea." That is because the last of al-Jady is the Lesser Bear (Banat Naʿsh al-Ṣughrā), and the pole around which the qiblah is aligned lies between them.

The third issue: Our scholars said: the ruling on facing the qiblah is of two kinds. The first is that one sees it and beholds it, so it is obligatory for him to face it, hit it, and intend its direction with his whole body. The second is that the Kaʿbah is in a place where he cannot see it, so it is obligatory for him to turn toward it and face it by means of indicators, namely the sun, the moon, the stars, the winds, and everything by which its direction can be known. Whoever is out of sight of it and prays, making an effort (ijtihad), toward other than its direction, while he is among those able to make the effort, has no valid prayer. But if he prays making effort and reasoning, and then after finishing his prayer it becomes clear to him that he prayed toward other than the qiblah, he repeats it if it is within its time, though this is not obligatory upon him, because he has fulfilled his duty as he was commanded. This matter has already been discussed fully in al-Baqarah [see vol. 2, p. 160], and praise be to Allah.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 16, verse 17:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Is He then who creates﴾ refers to Allah, exalted is He.

(like one who creates not) he means the idols.

(Will you not then remember?) He reports about the idols, which do not create and neither harm nor benefit, in the way the Arabs use when speaking of those who act. They used to worship them, so they were mentioned with the word "man" (من), as in His saying: ﴿Have they feet to walk with?﴾ [[See vol. 7, p. 342.]] It was also said: it is because the pronoun in the mention is joined with the Creator. Al-Farra' said: this is like the saying of the Arabs: "The rider and his camel were confused for me, so I do not know who is who (man dha wa man dha)," even though one of them is not a human.

Al-Mahdawi said: "Man" is used to ask about the Originator, exalted is He, and "ma" (ما) is not used to ask about Him, because "ma" is used to ask about kinds, and Allah, exalted is He, is not of a kind. For this reason Musa, peace be upon him, answered when he was asked: ﴿Then who is the Lord of you both, O Musa?﴾ [[See vol. 11, p. 203.]] and he did not answer when he was asked: ﴿And what is the Lord of the worlds?﴾ [[See vol. 13, p. 98.]] except with an answer using "man," and he turned away from answering with "ma" when the question was defective.

The meaning of the verse: whoever is able to create the things mentioned earlier is more worthy of worship than one who is himself created and neither harms nor benefits. ﴿This is the creation of Allah; so show me what those other than Him have created﴾ [[See vol. 14, p. 58 and p. 355.]] ﴿Show me what they have created of the earth﴾ [[See vol. 16, p. 179.]].

Al-Qurtubi's commentary on Surah 16, verses 18–19:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if you should count the favor of Allah, you could not enumerate it﴾ (Surah Ibrahim, 14:34). This was discussed previously in Surah Ibrahim [see vol. 9, p. 367].

﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful. And Allah knows what you conceal and what you declare﴾ — i.e., what you conceal within yourselves and what you show outwardly. All of this has already been discussed in full.

Al-Qurtubi's commentary on Surah 16, verses 18–19:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if you should count the favor of Allah, you could not enumerate it﴾ (Surah Ibrahim, 14:34). This was discussed previously in Surah Ibrahim [see vol. 9, p. 367].

﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful. And Allah knows what you conceal and what you declare﴾ — i.e., what you conceal within yourselves and what you show outwardly. All of this has already been discussed in full.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 16, verses 20–21:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And those whom they call upon besides Allah﴾. The reading of the common (qurra') is "tad'una" with a ta', because what precedes it is an address (in the second person). Abu Bakr narrated from ʿAsim, and Hubayra narrated from Hafs, "yad'una" with a ya', and this is the reading of Yaʿqub.
