As for his saying, "mā tusirrūna wa-mā tuʿlinūna" (what you conceal and what you disclose), all of them read it with a ta' as address, except that Hubayra narrated from Hafs from ʿAsim that he read it with a ya'.

(﴿They create nothing﴾), meaning they are not able to create anything, (﴿and they are themselves created﴾).

(﴿They are dead, not alive﴾), meaning they are dead, referring to the idols, having no spirits in them, and they do not hear or see; that is, they are inanimate objects, so how can you worship them when you are superior to them in life?

(﴿And they do not perceive﴾), meaning the idols.

(﴿when they will be raised﴾). Al-Sulami read "iyyan" with a kasra on the hamza; both are dialectal forms. Its position is in the accusative governed by "yubʿathun" (they will be raised), and it carries the sense of interrogation. The meaning: they do not know when they will be raised. It was expressed about them as it is expressed about human beings, because they claimed that the idols understand on their behalf, know, and intercede for them with Allah, the Exalted; so their address (to them) proceeded on that basis. It has also been said that Allah will raise the idols on the Day of Resurrection with spirits in them, and they will disown the worship of their worshippers, while in this world they are inanimate and do not know when they will be raised. Ibn ʿAbbas said: the idols will be raised, spirits will be placed in them, and their devils will be with them, and they will disown their worshippers; then the devils and the polytheists will be commanded to the Fire. It has also been said that the idols will be cast into the Fire along with their worshippers on the Day of Resurrection, the proof of which is ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah are fuel for Hell﴾ [see vol. 11, p. 343]. It has also been said that the speech is complete at His saying, ﴿They create nothing, and they are themselves created﴾, and then it begins, describing the polytheists as dead, and this death is the death of disbelief. ﴿And they do not perceive when they will be raised﴾, meaning the disbelievers do not know when they will be raised, that is, the time of the Resurrection, because they do not believe in the Resurrection so as to prepare for meeting Allah. It has also been said: that is, what makes them know when the Hour is, and perhaps it will be near.

Its position is in the accusative governed by "yubʿathun" (they will be raised), and it carries the sense of interrogation. The meaning: they do not know when they will be raised. It was expressed about them as it is expressed about human beings, because they claimed that the idols understand on their behalf, know, and intercede for them with Allah, the Exalted; so their address (to them) proceeded on that basis. It has also been said that Allah will raise the idols on the Day of Resurrection with spirits in them, and they will disown the worship of their worshippers, while in this world they are inanimate and do not know when they will be raised. Ibn ʿAbbas said: the idols will be raised, spirits will be placed in them, and their devils will be with them, and they will disown their worshippers; then the devils and the polytheists will be commanded to the Fire. It has also been said that the idols will be cast into the Fire along with their worshippers on the Day of Resurrection, the proof of which is ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah are fuel for Hell﴾ [see vol. 11, p. 343]. It has also been said that the speech is complete at His saying, ﴿They create nothing, and they are themselves created﴾, and then it begins, describing the polytheists as dead, and this death is the death of disbelief. ﴿And they do not perceive when they will be raised﴾, meaning the disbelievers do not know when they will be raised, that is, the time of the Resurrection, because they do not believe in the Resurrection so as to prepare for meeting Allah. It has also been said: that is, what makes them know when the Hour is, and perhaps it will be near.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 16, verses 22–23:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Your God is one God﴾. When He made clear that associating partners with God is impossible, He made clear that the One who is worshipped is one, with no lord other than Him and no one worthy of worship besides Him.

(So those who do not believe in the Hereafter, their hearts are denying,) meaning they do not accept admonition, and remembrance does not benefit them. This is a refutation of the Qadariyya (the sect that denies God's predestination).

(And they are arrogant,) meaning they are proud and consider themselves too great to accept the truth. The meaning of arrogance (istikbar) has already been discussed in al-Baqara (see vol. 1, p. 296).

(Certainly God knows what they conceal and what they reveal,) meaning what they say and do, and He will repay them accordingly. Al-Khalil said: "*La jarama* (لا جرم) is a word of affirmation and is only used as a response. It is said: 'They did that,' and then it is said: '*La jarama* they will regret,' meaning: truly, the Fire is theirs." The discussion of this has already been covered thoroughly in Hud (see vol. 9, p. 20).

(Indeed, He does not love the arrogant,) meaning He does not reward them or praise them. It is related from al-Husayn ibn ʿAli that he passed by some poor people who had set out broken pieces of bread among themselves and were eating. They said: "Come to the meal, O Abu ʿAbd Allah." So he dismounted and sat with them, and recited: (Indeed, He does not love the arrogant). When he finished, he said: "I have answered your invitation, so answer mine." They rose with him to his home, and he fed them, gave them drink, and gave them gifts, and then they departed.

The scholars said: Every sin can be concealed and hidden except arrogance, for it is a transgression that necessarily involves being made public, and it is the root of all disobedience. In the authentic hadith: "Indeed, the arrogant will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection in the likeness of ants; people will trample them with their feet because of their arrogance." Or as he (ﷺ) said: "Their bodies will be made small for them on the Gathering Place, until their smallness harms them, and they will be made large for them in the Fire, until their largeness harms them."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 16, verse 24:

His words, exalted is He: ﴿And when it is said to them, "What has your Lord sent down?"﴾ That is, and when it is said to those previously mentioned, those who do not believe in the Hereafter and whose hearts deny the Resurrection, "What has your Lord sent down?"

It is said: the one who said this was al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, and the verse was revealed concerning him. He had gone out to al-Hirah and bought the tales of (Kalilah wa-Dimnah) and would recite them to the Quraysh, saying: "Muhammad recites to his companions nothing but the fables of the ancients" (asatir al-awwalin), meaning that it is not a revelation from our Lord.

It is also said: the believers are the ones who said this to them as a test, and they answered with their words, "Fables of the ancients" (asatir al-awwalin), thereby acknowledging the denial of what is "the fables of the ancients."

Asatir (fables) means falsehoods and empty nonsense. This was already discussed in al-An'am [see vol. 6, p. 405]. The discussion of "What has your Lord sent down?" is like the discussion of "What do they spend?" [see vol. 3, p. 36]. As for His words, "(Fables of the ancients)," it is the predicate of an omitted subject; the sense is: "What He sent down is the fables of the ancients."

**The Qur'anic verse:** ﴿That they may bear their burdens in full on the Day of Resurrection, and of the burdens of those whom they mislead without knowledge.﴾ (16:25)

Al-Qurtubi's commentary on ﴿لِيَحْمِلُوا أَوْزارَهُمْ﴾ (that they may bear their burdens): It has been said that the *lam* here is the *lam al-kay* (the lam of purpose), and that it is connected to what precedes it. It has also been said that it is the *lam al-'aqibah* (the lam of consequence), as in His saying, ﴿so that it might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ (28:8). The meaning is that their statements about the Qur'an and the Prophet led them to bear their burdens, that is, their sins.

(﴿in full﴾): They did not leave any of it, because of the calamity that befell them in this world due to their disbelief. It has also been said that this is the *lam al-amr* (the lam of command), and the meaning is a threat. ﴿Because of their disbelief.﴾

(﴿and of the burdens of those who mislead them﴾) Mujahid said: they bear the burden of those whom they misled, and nothing is reduced from the sin of the one who misleads. There is a report: "Whoever calls to misguidance and is followed, upon him is the like of the burdens of those who followed him, without anything being reduced from their burdens. And whoever calls to guidance and is followed, for him is the like of their rewards, without anything being reduced from their rewards." Muslim transmitted it with this meaning. The *min* (of, from) here is *li-l-jins* (indicating the category), not *li-l-tab'id* (indicating a part), so the callers to misguidance bear the like of the burdens of those who follow them. As for His saying, ﴿without knowledge﴾, it means that they mislead people out of ignorance of what sins would be incurred upon them, for if they had known, they would not have misled.

(﴿Unquestionably, evil is what they bear﴾) That is: evil is the burden that they carry. A parallel to this verse is His saying, ﴿and they will surely bear their own burdens and other burdens along with their burdens﴾ (29:13). The explanation of His saying, ﴿and no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another﴾, has already been given at the end of *al-An'am* (see vol. 7, p. 157).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 16, verse 26:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Those before them had already plotted﴾, meaning: peoples before them had already preceded them in disbelief alongside the earlier Messengers, and the good outcome was for the Messengers.

(﴿So Allah came at their building from its foundations, and the roof fell down upon them from above them﴾) Ibn ʿAbbas, Zayd ibn Aslam and others said: it refers to Nimrod ibn Kanʿan and his people. They intended to ascend to the heaven and fight its inhabitants, so they built the tower (al-sarh) to ascend from it, after He had done what He did with the vultures, and it collapsed. As has already been explained at the end of Surah Ibrahim [see vol. 9, p. 381]. The meaning of ﴿Allah came at their building﴾ is: His command came upon the building, either as an earthquake or as a wind, which demolished it. Ibn ʿAbbas and Wahb said: the height of the tower in the sky was five thousand cubits, and its width three thousand. Kaʿb and Muqatil said: it was two farsakhs in height, so a wind blew and cast its top into the sea, and the rest fell upon them. When the tower collapsed, the tongues of people were confused from the terror of that day, so they spoke seventy-three languages; for this reason it was named Babel, and there was no language before that except Syriac. This meaning has already been mentioned in Surah al-Baqarah [see vol. 1, p. 283]. Ibn Hurmuz and Ibn Muhaysin read "al-suqufu" with a damma on both the sin and the qaf. Mujahid read the sin with a damma and sukun on the qaf, for lightening, as was mentioned before in ﴿wa-al-najm﴾ in both readings. The more likely is that it is the plural of saqf. The qawaʿid are the foundations of the building, and when the foundations are disturbed, the building falls. As for His saying: ﴿from above them﴾, Ibn al-Aʿrabi said: it is an emphasis to inform you that they were sitting beneath it. The Arabs say: "A roof fell upon us" and "a wall fell upon us" when it was owned by them even if it had not fallen upon them. So He brought the phrase ﴿from above them﴾ to remove this doubt in the speech of the Arabs, saying: ﴿from above them﴾, meaning it fell upon them while they were beneath it, so they perished and did not escape. It was also said: the intended meaning of the roof is the heaven, that is, the punishment came to them from the heaven which is above them; this is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas. It was also said: His saying ﴿So Allah came at their building from its foundations﴾ is a parable, and the meaning is: He destroyed them, so they were in the position of one upon whom his building fell. It was also said: the meaning is that Allah nullified their deeds, so they were in the position of one whose building fell. It was also said: the meaning is that He nullified their scheming and plotting, so they perished just as one upon whom the roof fell from above him perishes. Based on this, scholars differed concerning those upon whom the roof fell. Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Zayd said what has already been mentioned. It was also said: it refers to Bakht Nasr and his companions, as some exegetes said. It was also said: the intended are the Muqtasimun whom Allah mentioned in Surah al-Hijr [see p. 57 of this part], as al-Kalbi said. And according to this interpretation the sense of the parable is clear, and Allah knows best.

(﴿And the punishment came upon them from where they did not perceive﴾) meaning: from where they thought they were safe. Ibn ʿAbbas said: it means the gnat by which Allah destroyed Nimrod. [Some linguists preferred the reading with the dhal marked (dotted), and some permitted both readings.]

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 16, verse 27:

The Exalted said: ﴿Then on the Day of Resurrection He will disgrace them and say, "Where are My partners, about whom you used to dispute?" Those who were given knowledge will say, "Indeed, disgrace and misfortune this Day are upon the disbelievers."﴾ (16:27)

The Exalted said: ﴿Then on the Day of Resurrection He will disgrace them﴾, meaning He will expose them with the punishment, humiliate them with it, and debase them.

(And He will say, "Where are My partners?") meaning, according to your claim and your assertion, i.e. the deities you used to worship besides Me. This is a question of rebuke.

(About whom you used to dispute) meaning, you used to oppose My prophets on their account, so let them ward off this punishment from you. Ibn Kathir read "shurakaya" with an open yaa without hamza, while the rest read it with hamza. Nafi' read "tushaqqunni" with a kasra on the nun, as an idafa, meaning, you oppose Me concerning them. The rest read it with an open nun.

(Those who were given knowledge will say) Ibn Abbas said: they are the angels. It was also said: they are the believers.

(Indeed, disgrace) meaning, humiliation and abasement on the Day of Resurrection.

(And misfortune) meaning, the punishment, "upon the disbelievers."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 16, verse 28:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves﴾. This is among the attributes of the disbelievers. "Wronging themselves" is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: while they are wronging themselves, in that they brought themselves to the places of destruction.

(So they will offer submission) that is, surrender (al-istislam), meaning they acknowledged to Allah His lordship and submitted at death, and they said: (We did not used to do any evil) that is, any polytheism (shirk). The angels will say to them: (Yes [you did]). You used to do evil deeds.

(Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what you used to do). It was said by ʿIkrimah: this verse was revealed in Medina concerning a people who had embraced Islam in Mecca but did not emigrate. Quraysh took them out to Badr against their will, and they were killed there. So He said: (Those whom the angels take in death) by seizing their souls.

(wronging themselves) by remaining in Mecca and abandoning emigration.

(So they will offer submission) meaning in their going out with them. In this there are three views: the first is that it means reconciliation (al-sulh), as said by al-Akhfash. The second is submission (al-istislam), as said by Qutrub. The third is humility (al-khuḍūʿ), as said by Muqatil.

(We did not used to do any evil) meaning any disbelief.

(Yes, indeed Allah is Knowing of what you used to do) meaning that their deeds were the deeds of disbelievers. It was also said: when some of the Muslims saw the small number of the believers, they returned to the polytheists, and this verse was revealed concerning them. According to the first view, no disbeliever or hypocrite departs from this world until he submits, yields, is humbled and abased, and at that point neither repentance nor faith will benefit them, as He said: "Then their faith did not benefit them when they saw Our punishment." This meaning has already been mentioned. It has also been mentioned in (the commentary on) Surah al-Anfal that the disbelievers are taken in death with striking and humiliation, and likewise in al-An'am. We have mentioned this in the book al-Tadhkirah.

"The Exalted's saying: ﴿So enter the gates of Hell﴾ means: it will be said to them this at the time of death. It has also been said: it is a good-tiding of the punishment of the grave, since it is one of the gates of Hell for the disbelievers. It has also been said: the people of the second level (al-darakah al-thaniyah) do not reach it, for example, except by entering the first level, then the second, then the third, and so on. It has also been said: each level has a separate gate, so some enter through one gate and others through another. And Allah knows best.

﴿Abiding therein﴾ means: remaining in it.

﴿How wretched is the abode of the arrogant﴾ means: the place of stay of those ﴿arrogant﴾ who were proud against faith and against worshipping Allah the Exalted. He has described them in His true statement: ﴿Indeed, when it was said to them, "There is no god but Allah," they would be arrogant﴾ [[See vol. 15, p. 75.]]."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (*al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran*) on surah 16, verses 30–32:

Allah's words: ﴿And it will be said to those who were mindful of God, "What has your Lord sent down?" They will say, "Good."﴾ That is, they said: "He has sent down good," and the speech is complete. On this reading, "mādhā" (what) is a single word (functioning as one interrogative unit). A man of the Arabs would come to Makkah during the season of the pilgrimage and ask the polytheists about Muhammad, peace be upon him (ﷺ). They would say: "He is a sorcerer, or a poet, or a soothsayer, or a madman." He would then ask the believers, and they would say: "God has sent down to him good and guidance." The intended meaning is the Qur'an. It was also said that this is said to the people of faith on the Day of Resurrection.

Al-Tha'labi said: If it is asked, why is the answer in His words "tales of the ancients" in the nominative, while in His words "good" it is in the accusative? The answer is that the polytheists did not believe in the revelation, so it is as if they said: "What Muhammad says is the tales of the ancients." The believers affirmed the sending down, so they said: "He has sent down good." The meaning of this is understood from the grammatical analysis (i'rab), and praise belongs to God.

Allah's words: ﴿For those who did good in this world there is good.﴾ It has been said that this is part of the speech of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. It has also been said that it is part of the speech of those who were mindful of God. "Good" here means Paradise; that is, whoever obeys God, for him is Paradise tomorrow. It was also said: "For those who did good" today, there is good in this world, in the form of victory, conquest and spoils. (And the abode of the Hereafter is better) — that is, what they attain in the Hereafter of the reward of Paradise is better and greater than the abode of this world, because the latter perishes and the Hereafter endures.

(And excellent is the abode of the mindful) — concerning this there are two views. Al-Hasan said: the meaning is that excellent is the abode of the mindful, the world, because by working in it they attained the reward of the Hereafter and entry into Paradise. It was also said: the meaning is that excellent is the abode of the mindful, the Hereafter, and this is the view of the majority. On this reading, (Gardens of Eden) is a substitute for "abode," which is why it is in the nominative. It was also said that it is in the nominative by way of the supposition "they are gardens," so it explains His words "the abode of the mindful." Or it may be in the nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence; the estimate is: "Gardens of Eden, excellent is the abode of the mindful."

(They will enter them) is in the position of a qualifier, that is, "entered." It was also said: "Gardens" is in the nominative as the subject, and its predicate is "they will enter them," and on this al-Hasan's view is explained. And God knows best.

(Rivers flow beneath them) its meaning has been explained earlier in al-Baqarah [[See vol. 1, p. 239.]].

(For them therein is whatever they wish) — that is, of what they desired and wanted.

(Thus God rewards the mindful) — that is, God rewards the mindful with a reward like this.

(Those whom the angels take in death while they are good) Al-A'mash and Hamza read "yatawaffāhumu al-malā'ikatu" with the yā' in both places, and Abu 'Ubayd chose this, because of what is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, that he said: "Quraysh claimed that the angels are females, so you should mention them (in the masculine)." The rest read with the tā', because the intended meaning is the collective of angels. "Good" (ṭayyibīn) means: (1) pure from polytheism; (2) righteous; (3) their deeds and words are pure; (4) good of soul, confident in what they will receive of God's reward; (5) their souls are content with returning to God; (6) that their death is good, easy and smooth, with no hardship or pain in it, unlike the seizing of the soul of the disbeliever and the mixed (sinner). And God knows best.

(Saying, "Peace be upon you") This admits of two meanings: first, that the greeting is a warning to them of death; second, that it is good news to them of Paradise, because peace is security. Ibn al-Mubarak mentioned, saying: Haywa told me, saying: Abu Sakhr informed me [[In al-Tabari: Abu Sakhr that he heard.]] from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, who said: When the soul of the believing servant becomes stagnant [[To stagnate (istanqa'a) of water: to gather and settle. That is, when the soul of the believer gathers in his mouth wanting to leave, just as water stagnates in its bed; by soul he means the spirit.]], the Angel of Death comes to him and says: "Peace be upon you, friend of God, God sends you greetings of peace." Then he recited this verse: "Those whom the angels take in death while they are good, saying, 'Peace be upon you.'" Ibn Mas'ud said: When the Angel of Death comes to seize the soul of the believer, he says: "Your Lord sends you His greetings." Mujahid said: Indeed the believer is given good news of the righteousness of his child after him, so that his eye may be comforted. We have addressed this in *Kitab al-Tadhkira*, and we mentioned there the reports that come on this meaning, and praise belongs to God.

As for His words: (Enter the Garden), it admits of two meanings: first, that its meaning is "rejoice in entering the Garden"; second, that they will be told this in the Hereafter.

(For what you used to do) — meaning, in the world, of righteous deeds.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (*al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran*) on surah 16, verses 30–32:

Allah's words: ﴿And it will be said to those who were mindful of God, "What has your Lord sent down?" They will say, "Good."﴾ That is, they said: "He has sent down good," and the speech is complete. On this reading, "mādhā" (what) is a single word (functioning as one interrogative unit). A man of the Arabs would come to Makkah during the season of the pilgrimage and ask the polytheists about Muhammad, peace be upon him (ﷺ). They would say: "He is a sorcerer, or a poet, or a soothsayer, or a madman." He would then ask the believers, and they would say: "God has sent down to him good and guidance." The intended meaning is the Qur'an. It was also said that this is said to the people of faith on the Day of Resurrection.

Al-Tha'labi said: If it is asked, why is the answer in His words "tales of the ancients" in the nominative, while in His words "good" it is in the accusative? The answer is that the polytheists did not believe in the revelation, so it is as if they said: "What Muhammad says is the tales of the ancients." The believers affirmed the sending down, so they said: "He has sent down good." The meaning of this is understood from the grammatical analysis (i'rab), and praise belongs to God.

Allah's words: ﴿For those who did good in this world there is good.﴾ It has been said that this is part of the speech of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. It has also been said that it is part of the speech of those who were mindful of God. "Good" here means Paradise; that is, whoever obeys God, for him is Paradise tomorrow. It was also said: "For those who did good" today, there is good in this world, in the form of victory, conquest and spoils. (And the abode of the Hereafter is better) — that is, what they attain in the Hereafter of the reward of Paradise is better and greater than the abode of this world, because the latter perishes and the Hereafter endures.

(And excellent is the abode of the mindful) — concerning this there are two views. Al-Hasan said: the meaning is that excellent is the abode of the mindful, the world, because by working in it they attained the reward of the Hereafter and entry into Paradise. It was also said: the meaning is that excellent is the abode of the mindful, the Hereafter, and this is the view of the majority. On this reading, (Gardens of Eden) is a substitute for "abode," which is why it is in the nominative. It was also said that it is in the nominative by way of the supposition "they are gardens," so it explains His words "the abode of the mindful." Or it may be in the nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence; the estimate is: "Gardens of Eden, excellent is the abode of the mindful."

(They will enter them) is in the position of a qualifier, that is, "entered." It was also said: "Gardens" is in the nominative as the subject, and its predicate is "they will enter them," and on this al-Hasan's view is explained. And God knows best.

(Rivers flow beneath them) its meaning has been explained earlier in al-Baqarah [[See vol. 1, p. 239.]].

(For them therein is whatever they wish) — that is, of what they desired and wanted.

(Thus God rewards the mindful) — that is, God rewards the mindful with a reward like this.

(Those whom the angels take in death while they are good) Al-A'mash and Hamza read "yatawaffāhumu al-malā'ikatu" with the yā' in both places, and Abu 'Ubayd chose this, because of what is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, that he said: "Quraysh claimed that the angels are females, so you should mention them (in the masculine)." The rest read with the tā', because the intended meaning is the collective of angels. "Good" (ṭayyibīn) means: (1) pure from polytheism; (2) righteous; (3) their deeds and words are pure; (4) good of soul, confident in what they will receive of God's reward; (5) their souls are content with returning to God; (6) that their death is good, easy and smooth, with no hardship or pain in it, unlike the seizing of the soul of the disbeliever and the mixed (sinner). And God knows best.

(Saying, "Peace be upon you") This admits of two meanings: first, that the greeting is a warning to them of death; second, that it is good news to them of Paradise, because peace is security. Ibn al-Mubarak mentioned, saying: Haywa told me, saying: Abu Sakhr informed me [[In al-Tabari: Abu Sakhr that he heard.]] from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, who said: When the soul of the believing servant becomes stagnant [[To stagnate (istanqa'a) of water: to gather and settle. That is, when the soul of the believer gathers in his mouth wanting to leave, just as water stagnates in its bed; by soul he means the spirit.]], the Angel of Death comes to him and says: "Peace be upon you, friend of God, God sends you greetings of peace." Then he recited this verse: "Those whom the angels take in death while they are good, saying, 'Peace be upon you.'" Ibn Mas'ud said: When the Angel of Death comes to seize the soul of the believer, he says: "Your Lord sends you His greetings." Mujahid said: Indeed the believer is given good news of the righteousness of his child after him, so that his eye may be comforted. We have addressed this in *Kitab al-Tadhkira*, and we mentioned there the reports that come on this meaning, and praise belongs to God.

As for His words: (Enter the Garden), it admits of two meanings: first, that its meaning is "rejoice in entering the Garden"; second, that they will be told this in the Hereafter.

(For what you used to do) — meaning, in the world, of righteous deeds.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 16, verse 33:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Do they only wait for the angels to come to them?﴾

This refers to the disbelievers, meaning: they only wait for the angels to come to them to take their souls, while they are wrongdoers to themselves. Al-A'mash, Ibn Wththab, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read "yata'tihim al-mala'ikah" (﻿يَأْتِيهِمُ) with the ya' (the third person masculine prefix). The rest read it with the ta' (the second/feminine prefix), as has already been mentioned.

﴿Or the command of your Lord comes?﴾ That is, the punishment: whether by killing, like the Day of Badr, or by earthquake and sinking into the earth in this world. It was also said: the intended meaning is the Day of Resurrection.

These people did not wait for these things, because they did not believe in them; but their refusal to believe made the punishment obligatory upon them, so it was attributed to them, meaning: their end is punishment.

﴿So did those before them do.﴾ That is, they persisted in disbelief, so the command of God came to them and they were destroyed.

﴿And God did not wrong them﴾

That is, by punishing and destroying them, but they wronged themselves by associating partners with God.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 16, verse 34:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So the evil consequences of what they had done struck them﴾. It has been said: there is inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in it. The sense is: "Thus did those before them act, so the evil consequences of what they had done struck them, and Allah did not wrong them, but they were wronging themselves. So there befell them the punishments of their disbelief, the recompense for the evil of their deeds."

(﴿And there encompassed them﴾) i.e., it surrounded them and closed in on them.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 16, verse 35:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And those who associated partners with Allah said: "Had Allah willed, we would not have worshipped anything besides Him, neither we nor our fathers, nor would we have prohibited anything without His command."﴾ That is, "anything" (shay'an), and "min" (from) is extra (silah). Al-Zajjaj said: They said this mockingly, and if they had said it sincerely (an i'tiqad), they would have been believers. This has already been explained and analysed in grammatical terms in Surat al-An'am, so there is no point in repeating it. [[See vol. 7, p. 128.]]

(Thus did those before them do) That is, they did the same denial and mockery, and those who came before them dealt with the messengers in this way, and so they were destroyed.

(Is there upon the messengers anything but the clear conveyance?) That is, there is upon them only the conveying (of the message), while guidance belongs to Allah, Exalted is He.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 16, verse 36:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We certainly sent among every nation a messenger, [saying]: Worship Allah⦆, meaning: that you worship Allah and affirm His oneness.

(And avoid the Taghut) meaning: abandon every object of worship other than Allah, such as the Shaytan, the soothsayer (kahin) and the idol, and everyone who calls to misguidance. Among them are those whom Allah guided, that is, He directed them to His religion and His worship.

(And among them are those upon whom misguidance was justly decreed) meaning: by the prior decree concerning them, so that they died in their disbelief. This refutes the Qadariyya, because they claimed that Allah guided all people and enabled them to be guided, whereas Allah, may He be exalted, says: ﴿Among them are those whom Allah guided, and among them are those upon whom misguidance was justly decreed⦆. This has already been discussed in more than one place.

(So travel through the earth) meaning: so travel through the earth taking heed.

(And see how was the end of the deniers) meaning: how their final affair came to ruin, punishment and destruction.

The Almighty's statement: ﴿Even if you are eager for their guidance﴾, meaning: if you, O Muhammad, strive with all your effort to seek their guidance.

(﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide those whom He leads astray﴾), meaning: He does not guide the one whom He has led astray. That is, whoever has been predestined by Allah to misguidance, He does not guide. This is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud and the people of Kufa. Here "yahdi" (يهدي) is an imperfect verb, and its perfect is "hada" (هدى). "Man" (مَنْ) is in the accusative position, object of "yahdi" (يَهْدِي). It is also permissible that "hada yahdi" (هَدَى يَهْدِي) carries the meaning of "ihtada yahtadi" (اهْتَدَى يَهْتَدِي, to be guided). Abu 'Ubayd related this from al-Farra', who said: just as it has been recited, ﴿Is one who does not find guidance unless he is guided?﴾ [[See vol. 3, p. 342.]] with the meaning of "yahtadi" (يَهْتَدِي). Abu 'Ubayd said: We know of no one who related this except al-Farra', and he is not to be suspected in what he transmits. Al-Nahhas said: It was related to me from Muhammad ibn Yazid that the meaning of ﴿Allah does not guide those who go astray﴾ appears to be: those whom He knows to be such and for whom this has been decreed by Him. He said: "Yahdi" cannot carry the meaning of "yahtadi" unless it is "yahdi" or "yuhdi" (يُهْدِي). According to al-Farra's view, "yahdi" in the sense of "yahtadi," "man" is in the nominative position, and the returning pronoun to "man" is the omitted pronoun in the relative clause (ṣila, the clause that completes the relative pronoun), while the returning pronoun to the subject of "inna" (إِنَّ) in "fa-inna Allah" is the hidden pronoun in "yudillu" (يُضِلُّ).

The rest of the reciters read ﴿is not guided﴾ with a damma on the yā' and a fatha on the dāl, i.e., "yuhda" (يُهْدَى). Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim chose this reading, with the meaning: whomever Allah has led astray, no guide will guide him. Their proof is His statement: ﴿Whomever Allah leads astray, there is no guide for him﴾. Here "man" is in the nominative position as the subject of the passive verb (ism ma lam yusamma fa'iluhu, the grammatical subject of a passive verb), and it has the meaning of "alladhi" (الَّذِي, "the one who"). The returning pronoun from its relative clause is omitted, and the pronoun returning to the subject of "inna" in "fa-inna Allah" is the hidden pronoun in "yudillu."

(And they have no helpers), the meaning of which has already been explained.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 16, verse 38:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they swore by Allah with their most emphatic oaths﴾. This is a marvelling at their conduct, for they swore by Allah and went to great lengths in making the oath binding, that Allah does not resurrect the one who dies. The point of the marvel is that they display the glorification of Allah by swearing by Him, and then they attribute to Him inability to resurrect the dead. Abu al-'Aliyah said: A man from among the Muslims had a debt owed to him by a polytheist, and he demanded it from him. In some of his speech he said: "By Him whom I hope for after death, it is such-and-such." So the polytheist swore by Allah: "Allah does not resurrect whoever dies," and the verse was revealed.

Qatadah said: It was mentioned to us that a man said to Ibn 'Abbas: "O Ibn 'Abbas, some people claim that 'Ali will be resurrected after death before the Hour, and they interpret this verse." Ibn 'Abbas said: "Those people are liars! This verse is general for mankind. If 'Ali had been resurrected before the Resurrection, we would not have married his wives, nor divided his inheritance."

﴿Yes [bala]﴾: this is a refutation of them, meaning: Yes, indeed He will resurrect them.

﴿A promise binding upon Him, in truth﴾: a emphatic verbal noun (masdar mu'akkad), because His saying "He will resurrect them" [[i.e., the implied verb]] indicates a promise; meaning, He promised the resurrection as a true promise.

﴿But most people do not know﴾ that they will be resurrected. In al-Bukhari, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: Allah the Exalted said: "The son of Adam has denied Me, and he had no right to do so; and he has reviled Me, and he had no right to do so. As for his denying Me, it is his saying: He will not restore me as He originated me. As for his reviling Me, it is his saying: Allah has taken a son, while I am the One, the Eternal Refuge; He begets not, nor is He begotten, and there is none equal to Him."

This has been mentioned previously [[see vol. 2, p. 58]], and will come again.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 16, verse 39:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That He may make clear to them﴾, i.e., that He may manifest to them.

(That about which they differ) i.e., regarding the matter of the Resurrection.

(And that those who disbelieved may know) in the Resurrection and swore by it (that they were liars). It has also been said: the meaning is (margin) "And We certainly sent among every nation a messenger, that he might make clear to them that about which they differ." What the polytheists and the Muslims differed about comprises several matters: among them the Resurrection, among them the worship of idols, and among them that some people acknowledged that Muhammad is true, but imitation (taqlid) prevented them from following him, like Abu Talib.

He informed them of the ease of creation for Him, meaning: if We wish to resurrect those who have died, there is no toil or exertion for Us in bringing them back to life, nor in anything else that We bring into being, because We only say to it, "Be" (كُنْ), and it is (فَيَكُونُ).

The reading of Ibn 'Amir and al-Kisa'i is "فَيَكُونُ" in the accusative (naṣban), as a conjunction coordinated with "أَنْ نَقُولَ" (that We say). Al-Zajjaj said: it is permissible for it to be accusative as an answer to "كُنْ" (the imperative "Be"). The rest read it in the nominative (rafʿan), on the meaning of "فَهُوَ يَكُونُ" (so it is that it comes to be). The discussion of this has already passed in full in al-Baqara [see vol. 2, p. 90].

Ibn al-Anbari said: He applied the word "shay'" (thing) to what is known to God before creation, because it is as though it had already been found and witnessed.

In the verse is evidence that the Qur'an is uncreated (ghayr makhluq). For if His saying "كُنْ" were created, it would need a second saying, and that second one a third, and so it would regress infinitely (tasalsul), which is impossible.

In it is also evidence that God, glory be to Him, wills all events, their good and their evil, their benefit and their harm. The proof of this is that whoever sees in his dominion something he dislikes and does not will, it is for one of two reasons: either because he is ignorant and does not know, or because he is overpowered and cannot prevent it. Neither of these is permissible in describing Him, glory be to Him. The proof has been established that He is the Creator of the acquisition (iktisab) of His servants, and it is impossible that He be the agent of something He does not will, because most of our actions occur contrary to our aim and our will. So if the Truth, glory be to Him, did not will them, those actions would occur without intention. This is the view of the naturalists (al-Ṭabīʿiyyūn), and the monotheists have agreed upon its falsity and corruption.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 16, verse 41:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who emigrated for the sake of Allah after they had been wronged﴾. The meaning of hijrah (emigration) has already been discussed in "al-Nisa'" [[See vol. 5, p. 347 and what follows.]]. It is the abandoning of homelands, family and kin for the sake of Allah, or for the religion of Allah, and the abandoning of evil deeds. It is also said that "fi" here means "li-" (for), i.e., for Allah. "After they had been wronged" means they were tortured for the sake of Allah. It was revealed concerning Suhayb, Bilal, Khabbab and Ammar, whom the people of Makkah tortured until they said to them what they wanted; then, when they left them alone, they emigrated to Madinah. This is what al-Kalbi said. It is also said that it was revealed concerning Abu Jandal ibn Suhayl. Qatadah said: the intended ones are the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ), whom the polytheists in Makkah wronged and expelled, until a group of them joined the Abyssinians; then Allah, exalted is He, settled them in the abode of emigration (Madinah) and made for them helpers from among the believers. The verse encompasses all of them.

﴿We will surely settle them in this world in a good place﴾. Regarding "a good place" there are six opinions. The first: the descent into Madinah, said by Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi and Qatadah. The second: good provision, said by Mujahid. The third: victory over their enemy, said by al-Dahhak. The fourth: that it is "a tongue of truth" (lisan sidq), related by Ibn Jurayj. The fifth: what they conquered of the lands opened and the governorships they held therein. The sixth: the praise that remained for them in this world, and the nobility that came to their descendants in it. All of this was gathered for them by the grace of Allah, and praise be to Allah.

﴿And the reward of the Hereafter is greater﴾, i.e., the reward of the abode of the Hereafter is greater, meaning greater than anyone could know before witnessing it, "And when you look there, you will see bliss and a great kingdom" [[See vol. 19, p. 142.]].

﴿If only they knew﴾, i.e., if only these wrongdoers knew that. It is said that it refers to the believers, i.e., if they had seen the reward of the Hereafter and witnessed it, they would have known that it is greater than the good of this world. It is narrated that when Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, would give the stipend to the emigrants, he would say: "This is what Allah promised you in this world, and what He has stored up for you in the Hereafter is greater," and then he would recite this verse to them.

"It is said: (alladhina) is a substitute (badal) for the first (alladhina). And it is said: it is a substitute for the pronoun in (lanubawwi'annahum). And it is said: they are those who were patient in their religion.

(And upon their Lord they rely) in all their affairs. Some of the scholars of verification (ahl al-tahqiq) said: The best of creation is the one who, when a matter befalls him, is patient, and when he is unable to deal with a matter, he relies upon God. God Most High said: ﴿Those who were patient and upon their Lord they rely.﴾"

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 16, verse 43–44:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We did not send before you except men to whom We revealed⦆. The common reading is "yūḥā" with ya' and a fatha on the ha'. Ḥafṣ, from ʿĀṣim, read "nūḥī ilayhim" with the nūn of majesty (the plural of greatness) and a kasra on the ha'. It was revealed concerning the polytheists of Makkah when they denied the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) and said: "God is too great for His messenger to be a human being. Why did He not send an angel to us?" So God, the Exalted, answered them with His saying: ﴿And We did not send before you⦆, O Muhammad, to the earlier nations, ﴿except men⦆, human beings.

(﴿So ask the people of the reminder⦆) Sufyan said: it means the believers among the People of the Book.

(﴿if you do not know⦆) They will inform you that all the prophets were human. It was also said: the meaning is, ask the People of the Book; if they do not believe, they nonetheless acknowledge that the messengers were of mankind. This meaning is related from Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "the people of the reminder" are the people of the Qur'an. It was also said: they are the people of knowledge. The meanings are close.

(﴿with clear proofs and scriptures⦆) It was said: "bil-bayyināti" is connected to "arsalnā". There is an inversion in the sentence, meaning: We did not send before you, with clear proofs and scriptures, except men – that is, not men – so "illā" here means "other than", like His saying: "lā ilāha illā Allāh" (there is no god except God). This is the view of al-Kalbi – "to whom We revealed". It was also said: there is an elision in the sentence, indicated by "arsalnā", meaning: We sent them with clear proofs and scriptures. On this view "bil-bayyināti" does not depend on the first "arsalnā", because what precedes "illā" does not govern what follows it; rather it depends on the implied "arsalnā", i.e., We sent them with clear proofs. It was also said: it is an object of "taʿlamūn" with the bā' being extra, or it is put in the accusative by an implied "aʿnī" (I mean), as the poet al-Aʿshā said:

"And he is not a protector if a fearful one comes to the tribe, nor one who speaks except that he is the one who is blamed,"

meaning: I mean the one who is blamed.

"Clear proofs" (al-bayyinat) are the arguments and demonstrations. "Scriptures" (al-zubur) are the books. This has already been discussed in Āl ʿImrān.

(﴿And We sent down to you the Reminder⦆) meaning the Qur'an.

(﴿that you may make clear to the people what has been sent down to them⦆) in this Book, of rulings, promise and warning, by your words and your deeds. The Messenger (ﷺ) explains from God, the Mighty and Majestic, His intent in what He stated in summary in His Book, such as the rulings of prayer and zakat, and other matters He did not detail. This meaning has been treated fully in the introduction to this book, and praise be to God.

(﴿and that they may reflect⦆) so that they may take admonition.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 16, verse 45–47:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Do those who devise evil deeds feel secure⁠—⁠﴾ meaning: [who devise] evil deeds. This is a warning to the polytheists who schemed to nullify Islam.

(That Allah should cause the earth to swallow them up.) Ibn 'Abbas said: as He caused it to swallow Qarun. It is said: "khasafa al-makan yakhsifu khusufan" meaning it sank into the earth, and "khasafa Allahu bihi al-ard khusufan" meaning Allah made him disappear into it. From this is His saying: ﴿So We caused the earth to swallow him and his home﴾ [see vol. 13, p. 317]. Khasafa (intransitive) and khusifa bihi (passive) are both used. The interrogative here carries the sense of denial, meaning: they must not feel secure against a punishment that will overtake them, just as it overtook those who denied.

(Or that the punishment should come upon them from where they do not perceive.) As was done to the people of Lut and others. It is also said that it refers to the Day of Badr, when they were destroyed, and none of that had been in their reckoning.

(Or that He should seize them in their going back and forth.) That is, in their journeys and their activities; this is the view of Qatadah.

(Then they cannot escape.) That is, they cannot outpace Allah or escape Him. It is also said that "in their going back and forth" refers to their beds, wherever they may be. Al-Dahhak said: by night and by day.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 16, verse 48:

Ḥamzah, al-Kisa'i, Khalaf, Yahya and al-A'mash read "tarawu" with the letter tā' (you [plural] see), on the basis that the address is to all people. The rest read it with the letter yā' (they see), as a report about "those who plot evil deeds," and this is the preferred reading.

(min shay') means: from any body that stands and has a shadow, whether a tree or a mountain; this is what Ibn 'Abbas said. And this is so even though all things are in fact obedient and submissive to God, exalted is He.

(yatafayya'u zilaluhu) Abu 'Amr, Ya'qub and others read it with the letter tā', because the word "shadows" (zilal) is feminine. The rest read it with yā', and Abu 'Ubayd preferred this. It means: it inclines from side to side. At the beginning of the day it is in one state, it contracts, and then at the end of the day it returns to another state. So its turning and inclining from place to place is its prostration. From this, the shadow in the evening is called fay', because it "returned" (fa'a) from the west to the east, that is, it came back. Al-fay' means return, and from it comes: "until it returns (tafi'a) to the command of God" [[See vol. 16, p. 315.]]. The meaning of this view has been reported from al-Dahhak, Qatadah and others, and this meaning was already given in surah al-Ra'd [[See vol. 9, p. 302.]]. Al-Zajjaj said: it means the prostration of the body; its prostration is its submission, and what is seen in it of the traces of craftsmanship, and this is general for every body. The meaning of (wa-hum dakhirun) is: humbled and abased. Al-dukhur is lowliness and humiliation. It is said: "dakhara al-rajulu" (with fatḥah) so he is dākhir, and God made him dākhir (abased). Dhu al-Rummah said:

"Nothing remained but one abased in a cage (mukhayyas) ... and one hiding in a hole (mun-ḥajar) in a land not your own, in a rock-crevice."

Al-Mawardi attributed it thus to Dhu al-Rummah, while al-Jawhari attributed it to al-Farazdaq and said: al-Mukhayyas is the name of a prison that was in Iraq, that is, the place of humiliation. And the one who said it [[The speaker is our master 'Ali, may God be pleased with him. Nafi': a prison in Kufa, which was not well-built and was made of reeds, and the prisoners used to escape from it. It is said that it was breached and the prisoners escaped, so 'Ali, may God be pleased with him, demolished it and built the mukhayyas for them of clay.]]:

"Do you not see me as clever and shrewd? I built the mukhayyas after Nafi'."

He used the singular for the right side in His words "from the right" but the plural for the left, because the meaning of "right" though singular is plural in sense. Had one said: "from the right-hands and the lefts," or "the right and the left," it would be permissible, since the meaning is multiplicity. Also, it is the custom of the Arabs, when two indicators are combined in one thing, to pluralize one of them and keep the other singular, as in His words: "God has sealed their hearts and their hearing" [[See vol. 1, p. 189.]], and His words: "and brings them out of the darknesses into the light" [[See vol. 6, p. 117.]]. Had He said "their hearings" and "to the lights," it would have been permissible. It is also possible that "the right" refers to the word "mā" and "the left" to its meaning. Such usage is common in speech. The poet said:

"The arrivers, and Taym in the heights of Saba have been bitten at their necks by the hide of buffaloes."

[[The line is by Jarir. The version in his Diwan reads: "Taym calls you, and Taym in the villages of Saba..." etc.]]

He did not say "hides." It was also said: He made "the right" singular because when the sun rises while you are facing the qiblah, the shadow spreads on the right for a while, then inclines toward the left in successive states; so He called them "shamā'il" (lefts).

The Qur'an: **"And to Allah prostrates whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth of creatures (dābba)"**, meaning: of all that crawls upon the earth.

**"And the angels"**: meaning the angels who are on the earth. He singled them out for mention because of their distinguished rank, so He distinguished them by name from the category of creatures that crawl, even though they are included in it, as in His saying: ﴿In them are fruits, and palm trees, and pomegranates﴾ [See vol. 17, p. 185.]. It has also been said: they are excluded from the general category of what crawls because Allah gave them wings, so they are not included in the general term, and therefore they are mentioned separately. It has also been said: He meant, "And to Allah prostrates whoever is in the heavens" from among the angels, the sun, the moon, the stars, the winds and the clouds, "and whatever is on the earth of creatures," and the angels of the earth prostrate.

**"And they do not show arrogance"** in worshipping their Lord. This is a refutation of Quraysh, who claimed that the angels are the daughters of Allah.

The meaning of **"they fear their Lord from above them"** is: the punishment of their Lord and His chastisement, because the destroying punishment descends only from the sky. It has also been said: the meaning is that they fear the power of their Lord, which is above their power, so there is an ellipsis in the speech. It has also been said that the meaning of "they fear their Lord from above them" is: the angels fear their Lord, and they are above whatever is on the earth of creatures, and despite that they fear Him; so whoever is below them is more deserving of fear. The evidence for this view is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and they do what they are commanded﴾, meaning the angels.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 16, verse 51:

His the Exalted's saying: ﴿And Allah said: Do not take two gods﴾. It was said: the meaning is, "Do not take two gods," with "two" (ithnayn) being the object of the prohibition's emphasis. It was also said: His saying "ithnayn" came as an emphasis (tawkid). Since the true God (al-Ilah al-Haqq) does not admit of plurality, and since everything that admits of plurality is not a god, He restricted the mention to "two," because He intended the negation of plurality.

(﴿He is only one God﴾): meaning His holy essence. The rational and legal proof for His oneness has been established, as its explanation was given earlier in al-Baqarah [see vol. 2, p. 190 onward], and we mentioned it in discussing His name "the One" in the explanation of the Names, and praise be to Allah.

(﴿So fear Me, and Me alone﴾): that is, be afraid of Me. This was discussed earlier in al-Baqarah [see vol. 1, p. 332].

The Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 16, verse 52:

Allah's words: ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth, and to Him religion is due perpetually﴾. "Ad-din" (religion, here meaning submission and sincerity) means obedience and sincere devotion. "Wasiban" means "constantly." Al-Farra' related it, and al-Jawhari transmitted it: "wasaba ash-shay'u yasibu wusuban," meaning it persisted. "Wasaba ar-rajulu 'ala al-amr" means he was persistent in it. The meaning is that obedience to Allah is obligatory forever. Among those who said that "wasiban" means "constant" were al-Hasan, Mujahid, Qatada and al-Dahhak. From the same root is Allah's words: ﴿And for them is a perpetual punishment﴾ [[See vol. 15, p. 64.]], meaning enduring.

Al-Duwali said:

"I do not seek a little praise whose duration is brief,
at the cost of blame that lasts the whole of time."

Al-Ghaznawi, al-Tha'labi and others recited:

"I do not seek praise whose endurance is brief, one day,
at the cost of blaming time, entirely and perpetually."

It is also said that "al-wasab" means weariness and exhaustion, meaning that obedience to Allah is obligatory even if the servant grows weary in it. From this is the poet's saying:

"He does not grasp his shank from exhaustion or weariness,
nor does he bite upon his shursuf from hunger, pale-faced."

[[The poem is by A'sha Bahila. The first half-line is from one verse and the second from another. The two verses are:

"He does not wait for what is in the sand-hollow that he watches,
nor does he bite on his shursufa out of hunger, pale-faced.

He does not grip the shank from exhaustion or fatigue,
and he does not cease to lead the people, seeking the path."

"Ta'arra bil-makan" means he stayed at the place. "Ash-shursuf" is the cartilage of every soft bone that is eaten, attached to each rib, like the cartilage of the shoulder. "Ash-shaqr" (with vowelling) is a disease of the belly that makes the face turn yellow. It is also said that "as-safr" here means hunger. "Iftaqara al-athar" means he followed the trail.]]

Ibn Abbas said: "Wasiban" means "obligatory." Al-Farra' and al-Kalbi said: "sincere."

Allah's words: ﴿Then is it other than Allah you fear?﴾ meaning it is not fitting that you fear anyone other than Allah. The word "ghayra" is in the accusative case (nasb) and is governed by "tattaquna" (you fear).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 16, verse 53–55:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And whatever blessing you have is from Allah﴾. Al-Farra' said: "Ma" (whatever) here carries the meaning of a conditional (jaza'). The letter "ba" in "bikum" (with you) is connected to a verb that is implied, its estimate being: "wa-ma yakun bikum" (and whatever is with you). "Min ni'mah" (of blessing) means soundness of body, abundance of provision, and children, "fa-min Allah" (it is from Allah). It was also said: the meaning is, "and whatever blessing you have, it is from Allah."

(Then when harm touches you) meaning sickness, affliction and drought. Then to Him you cry out (ta'jarun), meaning you raise your voices in supplication. It is said: ja'ara yaj'aru ju'aran. Al-ju'ar is like al-khuwar (lowing), as it is said: ja'ara al-thawr yaj'aru, meaning it bellowed. Some read: "'ijlan jasadan lahuju'ar" (a calf-body that had a lowing), related by al-Akhfash. And ja'ara al-rajul ila Allah means he humbled himself in supplication to Allah. Al-A'sha said, describing a cow:

So she circled three times between a day and a night... and the denial was that she would be compassionate (tudifu) and cry out (watajar'a)

(Then when He removes the harm from you) meaning the affliction and sickness.

(Then, behold, a party of you associate others with their Lord) after the removal of the affliction and after the crying out. The meaning of the speech is an expression of wonder at associating partners after being saved from destruction. This meaning is repeated in the Qur'an, and it has preceded in al-An'am and Yunus, and it will come in "Subhan" and elsewhere. Al-Zajjaj said: this is specific to those who disbelieved.

(So that they may disbelieve in what We have given them) meaning so that they may deny the blessing of Allah which He bestowed upon them, namely the removal of harm and affliction. That is, they associated others so that they might deny. Thus the lam is the lam of purpose (kay). It was also said it is the lam of consequence (al-'aqibah). And it was said: "li-yakfuru bima atainahum" means that they make the blessing a cause of disbelief. All of this is a wicked act, as the poet said:

"And disbelief is a corruption of the soul of the benefactor" [[This is the second half of a line from the Mu'allaqa of 'Antarah, whose first half is:

Nubbi'tu 'Amran ghayra shakirin ni'mati]]

(So enjoy yourselves) is a command of threat. 'Abd Allah read: "Qul tamatta'u" (Say: enjoy yourselves).

(For you will soon know) meaning the outcome of your affair.

This meaning is repeated in the Qur'an, and it has preceded in al-An'am and Yunus, and it will come in "Subhan" and elsewhere. Al-Zajjaj said: this is specific to those who disbelieved.

(So that they may disbelieve in what We have given them) meaning so that they may deny the blessing of Allah which He bestowed upon them, namely the removal of harm and affliction. That is, they associated others so that they might deny. Thus the lam is the lam of purpose (kay). It was also said it is the lam of consequence (al-'aqibah). And it was said: "li-yakfuru bima atainahum" means that they make the blessing a cause of disbelief. All of this is a wicked act, as the poet said:

"And disbelief is a corruption of the soul of the benefactor" [[This is the second half of a line from the Mu'allaqa of 'Antarah, whose first half is:

Nubbi'tu 'Amran ghayra shakirin ni'mati]]

(So enjoy yourselves) is a command of threat. 'Abd Allah read: "Qul tamatta'u" (Say: enjoy yourselves).

(For you will soon know) meaning the outcome of your affair.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 16, verse 53–55:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And whatever blessing you have is from Allah﴾. Al-Farra' said: "Ma" (whatever) here carries the meaning of a conditional (jaza'). The letter "ba" in "bikum" (with you) is connected to a verb that is implied, its estimate being: "wa-ma yakun bikum" (and whatever is with you). "Min ni'mah" (of blessing) means soundness of body, abundance of provision, and children, "fa-min Allah" (it is from Allah). It was also said: the meaning is, "and whatever blessing you have, it is from Allah."

(Then when harm touches you) meaning sickness, affliction and drought. Then to Him you cry out (ta'jarun), meaning you raise your voices in supplication. It is said: ja'ara yaj'aru ju'aran. Al-ju'ar is like al-khuwar (lowing), as it is said: ja'ara al-thawr yaj'aru, meaning it bellowed. Some read: "'ijlan jasadan lahuju'ar" (a calf-body that had a lowing), related by al-Akhfash. And ja'ara al-rajul ila Allah means he humbled himself in supplication to Allah. Al-A'sha said, describing a cow:

So she circled three times between a day and a night... and the denial was that she would be compassionate (tudifu) and cry out (watajar'a)

(Then when He removes the harm from you) meaning the affliction and sickness.

(Then, behold, a party of you associate others with their Lord) after the removal of the affliction and after the crying out. The meaning of the speech is an expression of wonder at associating partners after being saved from destruction. This meaning is repeated in the Qur'an, and it has preceded in al-An'am and Yunus, and it will come in "Subhan" and elsewhere. Al-Zajjaj said: this is specific to those who disbelieved.

(So that they may disbelieve in what We have given them) meaning so that they may deny the blessing of Allah which He bestowed upon them, namely the removal of harm and affliction. That is, they associated others so that they might deny. Thus the lam is the lam of purpose (kay). It was also said it is the lam of consequence (al-'aqibah). And it was said: "li-yakfuru bima atainahum" means that they make the blessing a cause of disbelief. All of this is a wicked act, as the poet said:

"And disbelief is a corruption of the soul of the benefactor" [[This is the second half of a line from the Mu'allaqa of 'Antarah, whose first half is:

Nubbi'tu 'Amran ghayra shakirin ni'mati]]

(So enjoy yourselves) is a command of threat. 'Abd Allah read: "Qul tamatta'u" (Say: enjoy yourselves).

(For you will soon know) meaning the outcome of your affair.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 16, verse 56:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they assign to that which they do not know a share of what We have provided for them﴾. He mentions another kind of their ignorance, namely that they assign to that which they do not know (to harm or benefit), which is the idols, a portion of their wealth by which they seek nearness to it. This is the view of Mujahid, Qatadah and others. According to this view, "they know" (ya'lamun) refers to the polytheists. It has also been said that it refers to the idols, and that the verb, with the waw and nun ending, is treated as it would be for those who have reason (ya'qilu), so it returns to "má" (that which). The object of "ya'lamu" is then omitted, and the meaning is: these disbelievers assign a share to the idols which know something. The explanation of this meaning has already passed in "al-An'am" in His saying: ﴿They say, "This is for God," by their claim, and this is for our associates﴾ [[See vol. 7, p. 89.]]. Then the discourse shifts from the third person to the second person, and He says: ﴿By God, you will certainly be questioned﴾, and this is a question of rebuke.

(﻿﻿﻿...﻿) ﴿concerning what you used to invent﴾, that is, what you fabricate of falsehood against God, that He commanded you with this.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 16, verse 57:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they attribute to Allah daughters﴾. It was revealed concerning Khuza'ah and Kinanah, for they claimed that the angels are the daughters of Allah, and they used to say, "Join the daughters to the daughters" (alhiqu al-banat bi-al-banat).

(Subhanahu) He declared Himself far exalted above what they ascribed to Him of taking offspring.

(And for them is what they desire) meaning, they assign to themselves the sons and disdain the daughters. The place of "ma" (what) is nominative, as the subject (mubtada'), and the predicate (khabar) is "lahum" (for them), and the statement is complete at His saying, "Subhanahu." Al-Farra' permitted that it be accusative, with the implied sense: "and they assign to them what they desire." Al-Zajjaj rejected this and said: the Arabs use in such a case "wa-yaj'aluna li-anfusihim" (and they assign to themselves).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 16, verse 58:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When one of them is given the good news of a female﴾, i.e., one of them is informed of the birth of a daughter.

(Her face remains darkened) i.e., changed, and he does not mean the blackness which is the opposite of whiteness; rather it is a metaphor for his distress over the daughter. The Arabs say of everyone who encounters something disagreeable: "His face has blackened with distress and sorrow," said al-Zajjaj. Al-Mawardi related that what is meant is the blackness of color, and he said: this is the view of the majority.

(And he is ﴿kazim﴾) i.e., filled with grief. Ibn Abbas said: sorrowful. Al-Akhfash said: he is one who suppresses his anger and does not show it. It was also said: he is the grieved one who closes his mouth so that he does not speak out of grief, derived from al-kizama, which is the tying of the mouth of a water-skin, said Ali ibn Isa. This meaning has already been mentioned in the commentary on surah Yusuf [[see vol. 9, p. 249.]].

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He hides himself from the people﴾, meaning he conceals himself and keeps out of sight.

(from the evil of what he has been given good news of), meaning from the evil of the grief, disgrace and shame that befalls him because of the daughter.

(Does he keep it), where the pronoun is masculine because it refers back to "مَا" (mā, "what").

(in humiliation), meaning in disgrace (hawān). Isa al-Thaqafi likewise read "عَلَى هُونٍ" (ʿalā hūn). Al-hūn means al-hawān in the dialect of Quraysh, as said by al-Yazidi, and Abu Ubayd related it from al-Kisa'i. Al-Farra' said it means "little" in the dialect of Tamim. Al-Kisa'i said it means affliction and hardship. Al-Khansa' said:

"We hold souls cheap and humble them
On the day of dread, for that preserves them better."

Al-A'mash read "أَيُمْسِكُهُ عَلَى سُوءٍ" (ayumsikuhu ʿalā sū', "does he keep it in evil"). Al-Nahhas mentioned this. He said: al-Jahdari read "أَمْ يَدُسُّهَا فِي التُّرَابِ" (am yadussuhā fī al-turāb, "or bury her in the dust"), which refers it to His saying "بِالْأُنْثَى" (bi-al-unthā, "with the female"), and it would necessarily require reading "أَيُمْسِكُهَا" (ayumsikuhā, "does he keep her"). [[Editor's note: The variant is recorded among the irregular readings as being read thus by al-Jahdari. It seems the author did not come across it.]]

It was also said that the humiliation refers to the daughter, meaning: does he keep her while she is humiliated in his sight? It was said that it refers to the one to whom the child was born, meaning: does he keep him against his will, or bury him in the dust? This is what they used to do, burying daughters alive. Qatada said: Mudar and Khuza'a used to bury daughters alive, and the most insistent in this practice was Tamim. They claimed fear of disgrace befalling them and the desire of unequal suitors for them. Sa'sa'a ibn Najiya, the paternal uncle of al-Farazdaq, whenever he sensed something of this, would send camels to the father of the girl to keep her alive by this means. Al-Farazdaq boasted:

"My uncle, who forbade those who bury their daughters alive,
And revived the buried girl, so she was not buried."

[[Editor's note: The narration reads "wajdī" (my grandfather) instead of "ʿammī" (my uncle), and Sa'sa'a ibn Najiya was the grandfather of al-Farazdaq, as in al-Isti'ab.]]

It was also said: "dassuhā" (burying her) means concealing her from people so that she is not known, like one who is hidden in the dust by being concealed from sight. This is a possibility.

Issue: It is established in Sahih Muslim from ʿĀʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: A woman came to me with two daughters of hers and asked me, but she found nothing with me except a single date. I gave it to her, and she took it and divided it between her two daughters and did not eat any of it herself. Then she got up and left with her daughters. Then the Prophet (ﷺ) entered upon me, and I told him her story. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever is tested with daughters and treats them well, they will be a screen for him from the Fire."

In this hadith there is an indication that daughters are a trial. Then he informed that patience with them and kindness to them shields one from the Fire.

Also from ʿĀʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: A destitute woman came to me carrying her two daughters, so I fed her three dates. She gave each of her daughters a date, and she raised a date to her mouth to eat it, but her daughters asked her for food, so she split the date she was going to eat between them. I was impressed by her conduct, so I mentioned what she had done to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He said: "Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has made Paradise obligatory for her because of it, or freed her from the Fire because of it."

From Anas ibn Malik, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever supports two girls until they reach maturity will come on the Day of Resurrection, he and I," and he joined his fingers together. Muslim also related this, may Allah have mercy on him.

Abu Nuʿaym al-Hafiz related from the hadith of al-Aʿmash, from Abu Wail, from ʿAbd Allah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever has a daughter, and he educates her well and teaches her well, and lavishes upon her from the blessings of Allah with which He has lavished upon him, she will be a screen or a shield for him from the Fire."

Aqil ibn Ulfa was asked for his daughter al-Jarba' in marriage, and he said:

"Even if a bridal gift of a thousand is brought to me,
With servants and ten milch camels (khuwar),
The dearest of my in-laws to me is the grave."

[[Editor's note: Khuwar is the plural of khuwwara, irregular, meaning a she-camel that gives abundant milk.]]

Abdullah ibn Tahir said:

"Every father with a daughter who watches over her affairs
Has three in-laws, if the in-law is praised:
A husband who looks after her, a chamber that shelters her,
And a grave that covers her, and the best of them is the grave."

﴿Surely evil is what they judge﴾, meaning in attributing daughters to their Creator and attributing sons to themselves. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿Is the male for you and the female for Him? That, then, is an unjust division﴾, where "ḍīzā" means unjust. It will come later [see vol. 17, p. 102].

For those who do not believe in the Hereafter is the evil description (mathal al-saw'), i.e. the attribute of evil, of ignorance and disbelief, said of these who ascribe daughters to Allah. It was also said: it is their describing Allah, exalted is He, as having a consort and a son. And it was said: it means the punishment and the Fire.

﴿And to Allah belongs the highest description﴾ i.e. the highest attribute of sincerity and monotheism, said by Qatadah. It was also said: the highest attribute, that He is the Creator, the Provider, the All-Powerful, and the Recompenser. Ibn 'Abbas said: "the evil description" is the Fire, and "the highest description" is the testimony that there is no god but Allah. It was also said: "There is nothing like unto Him" (42:11). It was also said: "And to Allah belongs the highest description" is like His saying: "Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth; the likeness of His light..." (24:35). If it is asked: how did He attribute the "mathal" here to Himself when He said: "So do not strike for Allah examples" (16:74)? The answer: His saying "So do not strike for Allah examples" means the examples that entail resemblance and deficiency; that is, do not strike for Allah an example that implies deficiency and likening Him to creation. And "the highest description" is describing Him with what has no likeness and no equal, exalted is He far above what the wrongdoers and deniers say, a great exaltation.

﴿And He is the Mighty, the Wise﴾ its meaning has already been mentioned.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 16, verse 61:

His words, exalted is He: ﴿And if God were to take people to task for their wrongdoing﴾, that is, for their disbelief and their fabrication, and hasten their punishment.

(He would not leave upon it) means upon the earth. It is a pronoun referring to something not mentioned, but it is indicated by His words "a creature (dabba)", since a creature (dabba) only crawls upon the earth. The meaning intended is "a disbelieving creature", so it is specific. It was also said: the meaning is that if He destroyed the fathers for their disbelief, the sons would not exist. It was also said: the verse is intended in its generality, that is, if God seized the creation for what they earned, He would not leave upon the back of this earth any creature, whether a prophet or other than a prophet. This is the view of al-Hasan. Ibn Mas'ud said, reciting this verse: If God seized the creation for the sins of the sinners, the punishment would strike all of creation, even the ju'lan (ju'lan, plural of ju'al, like surad: a black creature among the creatures of the earth) in its burrow, and He would withhold the rains from the sky and the plants from the earth, and the creatures would die. But God deals with them through pardon and grace, as He said: "and He pardons much" [see vol. 16, p. 30]. (When their term comes) means the time of their death and the end of their lifespans.

(They cannot delay it an hour, nor can they hasten it) This has already been discussed [see vol. 7, p. 202]. If it is asked: how can destruction encompass all of them when among them there is a believer who is not a wrongdoer? It is answered: the destruction of the wrongdoer is made a retribution and a requital, and the destruction of the believer is compensated by the reward of the Hereafter. In Sahih Muslim, from Abdullah ibn Umar, who said: I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: "When God intends a punishment for a people, the punishment strikes whoever is among them, then they are resurrected according to their intentions" [in Sahih Muslim, "according to their deeds"]. And from Umm Salamah, who was asked about the army that would be swallowed up, and that was in the days of Ibn al-Zubayr, and she said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "A seeker of refuge will seek refuge in the House, and a force will be sent against him, and when they are in a desert of the earth, they will be swallowed up." I said: O Messenger of God, what of one who was unwilling? He said: "He will be swallowed up with them, but he will be resurrected on the Day of Resurrection according to his intention." We have treated this meaning at length in the "Kitab al-Tadhkira," and what was mentioned in al-Ma'ida and at the end of al-An'am [see vol. 6, p. 352 and vol. 7, p. 157] is sufficient, praise be to God. It was also said: (When their term comes) means when the Day of Resurrection comes. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (*al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran*) on surah 16, verse 62:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they attribute to Allah what they dislike﴾, that is, daughters.

(﴿And their tongues describe the lie, that for them is the best﴾) Mujahid said: this is their saying, "For them are the sons, and for Allah are the daughters." *Al-kadhib* (the lie) is the object of *tasif* (describe), and *anna* (that) is in the place of the accusative as a substitute (*badal*) for *al-kadhib*, because it explains it. It was also said: *al-husna* (the best) means the good recompense, related by al-Zajjaj. Ibn 'Abbas, Abu al-'Aliyah, Mujahid and Ibn Muhaysin read *al-kadhib* with a *damma* on the *kaf*, *dhal* and *ba'* (*al-kudhub*), as an adjective (*na't*) for *al-alsinah* (the tongues), and likewise in ﴿And do not say, concerning what your tongues describe as lies﴾. *Al-kudhub* is the plural of *kadhub*, like *rasul* and *rusul*, *sabur* and *sabr*, *shakur* and *shukr*.

(*La*, "no") is a rejection of their claim, and the sentence is complete here, meaning: it is not as you assert.

(﴿Without doubt, for them is the Fire﴾) That is, truly, for them is the Fire. This has already been discussed fully (see vol. 9, p. 20).

(﴿And that they are *mufritun*﴾) meaning abandoned and forgotten in the Fire. This was said by Ibn al-A'rabi, Abu 'Ubaydah, al-Kisa'i and al-Farra', and it is the view of Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Mujahid. Ibn 'Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr also said: *mub'adun*, meaning removed far away. Qatadah and al-Hasan said: hastened to the Fire and sent forward to it. *Al-farit* is the one who goes ahead to the water, and from this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "I will go ahead of you to the Pool" (*ana faratukum 'ala al-hawd*), meaning I will precede you. Al-Qutami said:

*They hastened us, and they were among our companions,*
*as the forerunners hasten the late comers.*

*Al-furat* are those who go ahead in seeking water, and *al-wurrad* are those who come later.

Nafi', in the narration of Warsh, read *mufrituna* with a *kasra* on the *ra'* and with light pronunciation (*mufritun*, from *afrata*). This is the reading of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas, and its meaning is "excessive in sins and disobedience," that is, they went to excess in them. It is said: "So-and-so exceeded (*afrata*) over so-and-so" when he surpassed him and said to him more evil than he said. Abu Ja'far the reciter read *mufarritun* with a *kasra* on the *ra'* and with doubling (*tashdid*), meaning those who neglect the command of Allah, so it is from *tafrit* (neglect) in what is obligatory.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 16, verse 63:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿By God, We indeed sent [messengers] to communities before you, but Satan made their deeds seem fair to them﴾ — i.e., their evil deeds. This is a consolation to the Prophet (ﷺ), that those prophets who preceded him were also disbelieved by their people.
