(﴿So he is their guardian today﴾) — i.e., their helper in this world, according to their assumption.

(﴿And for them there is a painful punishment﴾) — in the Hereafter.

It has been said: "So he is their guardian" means their companion in the Fire. "Today" refers to the Day of Resurrection, and it was given the name "day" because of its fame. It has also been said: on the Day of Resurrection it will be said to them, "This is your guardian; seek help from him to save you from the punishment," as a form of rebuke to them.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 16, verse 64:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We have not sent down to you the Book﴾, i.e. the Qur'an, (except that you may make clear to them that about which they differ) concerning the religion and the rulings, so that the proof is established against them by your clarification. Your conjunction "guidance and mercy" (hudan wa rahmah) is coordinated with the place (mawdi') of His saying "li-tubayyina" (in order that you make clear), because its place is in the accusative (nasb). The implied meaning of the speech is: "And We have not sent down to you the Book except as a clarification for mankind."

(And guidance) i.e. right guidance (rushd), (and mercy) for the believers.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 16, verse 65:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah sent down from the sky﴾, i.e., from the clouds.

(water, and gave life thereby to the earth after its death.) The discourse returns to enumerating blessings and demonstrating complete power.

(Indeed in that is a sign.) That is, an indication of the resurrection and of His oneness, since they know that their deity cannot do anything, so this indication is (for a people who hear) about Allah, exalted is He, with the hearts and not with the ears. (For indeed, it is not the eyes that are blinded, but it is the hearts within the breasts that are blinded [[See vol. 12, p. 76.]]).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 16, verse 66:

There are ten issues in this verse.

The first: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And indeed, in the livestock there is a lesson for you﴾. The discussion of "al-an'am" (livestock) has already passed [[See vol. 7, p. 111.]]. Here it refers to the four categories: camels, cattle, sheep and goats. "A lesson (ibrah)" means an indication of Allah's power, His oneness and His greatness. The root of ibrah is the representation of one thing by another so that its reality may be known through likeness, and from it comes His saying, "So take warning (fa'tabiru)" [[See vol. 18, p. 5.]]. Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: The lesson in the livestock is their subjection to their owners and their obedience to them, while you rebel against your Lord and oppose Him in everything. And among the greatest lessons is an innocent animal carrying a guilty one.

The second: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿nusqikum﴾ (We give you to drink). The reading of the people of Madina, Ibn 'Amir, and 'Asim in the transmission of Abu Bakr is with a fatha on the nun, from saqa yasqi. The rest, and Hafs from 'Asim, read it with a damma on the nun, from asqa yusqi, and this is the reading of the Kufans and the people of Makka. It is said: both are dialects. Labid said:

Saqa qawmi Bani Majdin wa asqa ... Numayran wal-qabaila min Hilal
(He gave my people, the Banu Majd, to drink, and gave to drink Numayr and the tribes of Hilal.)

It is also said: one says saqaytahu for what goes from your hand to his mouth, but when you provide him a drink or present it to him so that he may drink with his mouth, or water his crops, you say asqaytuhu. Ibn 'Uzayr said, and this has already been mentioned [[See vol. 1, p. 418.]]. A group read "tusqikum" with a ta', and this is weak, referring to the livestock. It was also read with a ya', meaning that Allah, mighty and majestic, gives you to drink. The readers, in both of the previous readings, the fatha on the nun is the dialect of Quraysh and the damma is the dialect of Himyar.

The third: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿from what is in their bellies﴾. People differed over what the pronoun in His saying "mimma fi butunihi" (from what is in its bellies) refers to. It is said that it refers to what precedes it, which is the plural feminine. Sibawayh said: The Arabs report about livestock using the singular predicate. Ibn al-'Arabi said: I do not think he relied upon this except from this verse, and this does not befit his standing nor suit his understanding. It is also said: since the word "al-an'am," which is a collective noun, is both masculine and feminine, one says "huwa al-an'am" and "hiya al-an'am," so it is permissible for the pronoun to return in the masculine. Al-Zajjaj said, and al-Kisa'i said: its meaning is "from what is in the bellies of that which we have mentioned," so it returns to what was mentioned, and Allah, exalted is He, has said: ﴿Indeed, it is a reminder; so whoever wills may remember it﴾ [[See vol. 19, p. 213.]]. The poet said:

Mithl al-firakh nutifat hawasiluhu
(Like the chicks whose crops have been plucked.)

And there are many like this. Al-Kisa'i said: "mimma fi butunihi" means "from what is in the bellies of some of them," since the males have no milk, and this is what Abu 'Ubayda relied upon. Al-Farra' said: "al-an'am" and "al-na'am" are one and the same, and "al-na'am" is masculine, which is why the Arabs say "hadha na'amun warid," so the pronoun returned to the word "al-na'am," which means "al-an'am." Ibn al-'Arabi said: The masculine refers to the meaning of the plural, and the feminine to the meaning of the group. So He mentioned it here as masculine with regard to the word "jam'" (plural), and made it feminine in Surat al-Mu'minun with regard to the word "jama'ah" (group), saying: ﴿We give you to drink from what is in their bellies﴾ [[See vol. 12, p. 118.]]. With this interpretation the meaning is arranged in a good order. The feminine with regard to the word "jama'ah" and the masculine with regard to the word "jam'" are more numerous than the sand dunes (ramal) whose edges cannot be reached, to the right of the rising sun from al-Hajar, al-Yamama, Yabrin and the desert of Palestine. [[Ramal: sand dunes whose extremities cannot be perceived. (Yaqut).]]

The fourth: Some of the eminent scholars, namely the judge Isma'il, derived from the return of this pronoun that the milk of a stallion (male animal) produces prohibition [of marriage], and he said: it has been brought in the masculine because it refers back to the mention of livestock, since milk is reckoned to belong to the male. For this reason the Prophet ﷺ ruled that the milk of the sire causes prohibition, when 'A'isha (may Allah be pleased with her) denied it, in the hadith of Aflah, the brother of Abu al-Qu'ays: "For the woman is the giving of drink (al-saqy) and for the man is the impregnation (al-liqah)," so sharing in it between them became established. A view on the prohibition by the milk of the sire has already passed in [the commentary on] "al-Nisa'" [[See vol. 5, p. 111.]], and praise be to Allah.

The fifth: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿from between dung and blood, pure milk﴾. He, glorified is He, drew attention to His great power by the emergence of pure milk between dung and blood. "Al-farth" is the dung that descends into the paunch (karsh); when it leaves it is no longer called farth. It is said: "afrathtu al-karsh" when I removed what is in it. The meaning is that the food contains what is in the paunch and blood comes from it, then the milk is purified from the blood, so Allah, glorified is He, informed that this milk comes out from between that and the blood in the veins. Ibn 'Abbas said: The animal eats the fodder, and when it settles in its paunch, it cooks it, so its lowest part becomes dung, its middle part milk, and its uppermost part blood. The liver is set over these categories, so it divides the blood, distinguishes it and sends it through the veins, and sends the milk into the udder, and the dung remains as it is in the paunch. ﴿Perfect wisdom, but warnings avail not﴾ [[See vol. 17, p. 128.]].

"Khalisan" (pure) means free from the redness of blood and the filth of dung, though both are contained in one vessel. Ibn Bahr said: its whiteness is pure. Al-Nabigha said:

Bikhalisat al-ardan khudr al-manakib
(With white sleeves, green at the shoulders.)

That is, white cuffs. This is a power that befits none but the one who sustains everything with what is beneficial.

The sixth: Al-Naqqash said: In this there is evidence that semen is not impure. Others also said this and argued: Just as milk comes out from between dung and blood, smooth and pure, so too semen may come out from the passage of urine, pure. Ibn al-'Arabi said: This is a great ignorance and a shameful inference. The report about milk came as a blessing and favour issuing from power, to be a lesson, so all of that requires the attribute of purity and pleasantness, and semen is not of this state, so that it could be attached to it or analogized with it. I say: This may be countered by saying: what favour is greater and more exalted than the emergence of semen by which the honoured human being comes into being, and Allah, exalted is He, has said: ﴿It comes out from between the loins and the ribs﴾ [[See vol. 20, p. 4.]], and He said: ﴿And Allah has made for you mates from among yourselves, and made for you from your mates sons and grandsons﴾ [[See p. 142 of this part.]], and this is the utmost in bestowing favour. If it is said: it becomes impure by its emergence through the urinary passage, we say: that is what we intended; the impurity is accidental and its origin is pure. It has been said that its exit in the woman is other than the exit of urine, especially since the entry of the male and the exit of the child are different from the exit of urine, according to what the scholars said. This was mentioned in al-Baqara. If it is said: its origin is blood, so it is impure, we say: this is refuted by musk, whose origin is blood, yet it is pure. Those who held its purity include al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Ishaq, Abu Thawr and others, on the hadith of 'A'isha (may Allah be pleased with her) who said: I used to scrape it from the garment of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ when it was dry, with my fingernail. Al-Shafi'i said: If it is not scraped off, there is no harm in it. Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas used to scrape semen from his garment. Ibn 'Abbas said: It is like phlegm; remove it from you with a piece of idhkhir (grass) and wipe it with a cloth. If it is said: it has been established from 'A'isha that she said: I used to wash the semen from the garment of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, then he would go out to prayer in that garment while I was looking at the trace of washing in it. We say: it is possible that she washed it out of disgust, like things that are removed from a garment, not because of impurity, and this would be a reconciliation between the hadiths. And Allah knows best. Malik and his companions and al-Awza'i said: it is impure. Malik said: Washing the wet dream from a garment is a binding matter agreed upon among us, and this is the view of the Kufans. It is narrated from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, Ibn Mas'ud and Jabir ibn Samura that they washed it from their garments. It is differed about from Ibn 'Umar and 'A'isha. On these two positions regarding the impurity and purity of semen, the Successors (tabi'un) differed.

The seventh: In this verse there is evidence for the permissibility of benefiting from milk, for drinking and other uses. As for the milk of a dead animal, it is not permissible to benefit from it, because it is a pure liquid that has come to be in an impure vessel, since the udder of a carcass is impure while the milk is pure; when it is milked, it becomes taken from an impure vessel. As for the milk of a dead woman, our companions differed about it. Whoever says that a human being [i.e., a Muslim] is pure both alive and dead, holds it is pure. Whoever says it becomes impure by death, holds it is impure. On both views the prohibition is established, because a child may be nourished by it just as he is nourished by a living woman, since the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Suckling is that which causes the flesh to grow and firms the bone." He did not specify, and this has passed in "al-Nisa'" [[See vol. 5, p. 111.]].

The eighth: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿palatable to the drinkers﴾, meaning delicious, easy, not causing choking to the one who drinks it. It is said: "sagha al-sharab yasuhu sawghan," meaning it was easy for it to enter the throat; "asaghahu sharibuhu" (his drinker made it pass); and "sughtuhu ana usighuhu and asughuhu," transitive; and the better form is "asaghtuhu isaghatan." It is said: "Asigh li ghussati," meaning give me time and do not hurry me. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿He gulps it down but can hardly swallow it﴾ [[See vol. 9, p. 349.]]. "Al-siwagh" (with a kasra on the sin) is what you make your choking pass with. It is said: "water is the siwagh of choking," and from it is the saying of al-Kumayt:

Fa-kanat siwaghan an jizat bi-ghussatin
(So it became a means of passage when it went down with a choking.)

It is narrated that no one ever choked on milk, and this is narrated from the Prophet ﷺ.

The ninth: In this verse there is evidence for the use and consumption of sweets and delicious foods. It cannot be said that this contradicts asceticism (zuhd) or distances from it, but that is when it is from its proper source and without extravagance or excess. This meaning has already been mentioned in "al-Ma'ida" [[See vol. 6, p. 260 onwards, and vol. 7, p. 191.]] and elsewhere. In the Sahih, from Anas, who said: "I gave the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to drink with this cup of mine all of the drinks: honey, nabidh, milk and water." Some readers disliked eating faluzaj [[Faluzaj: a sweet made of flour, water and honey (from the Persian loanwords).]] and milk as food, but the general body of scholars permitted it. It is narrated from al-Hasan that he was at a table with Malik ibn Dinar, and faluzaj was brought, and he refrained from eating it. Al-Hasan said to him: Eat! For you will be accountable for more than this for cold water.

The tenth: Abu Dawud and others narrated from Ibn 'Abbas who said: Milk was brought to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he drank. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "When one of you eats food, let him say: O Allah, bless us in it and feed us better than it; and when he is given milk to drink, let him say: O Allah, bless us in it and increase us from it, for there is nothing that suffices in place of food and drink except milk." Our scholars said: How could it not be so, when it is the first thing a human being is nourished by, and by it bodies and frames grow; it is a sustenance free of corruptions, by which the bodies are sustained. Allah, exalted is He, made it a sign to Jibril for the guidance of this community, which is the best of communities, as He said in the Sahih: "Jibril brought me a vessel of wine and a vessel of milk, and I chose the milk. Jibril said to me: You have chosen the natural disposition (fitrah). As for you, had you chosen the wine, your community would have gone astray [[Ghawat: went astray and became corrupt.]]." Then, in the supplication for an increase of it there is a sign of abundance, the appearance of good things, and multiplication of blessings, for it is wholly blessed.

**First question: the fruits of the date palms**

Al-Tabari said: The implied meaning is "and from the fruits of the date palms and the grapes [comes] what you take [as intoxicant]." The word *ma* (what) is omitted, and the pronoun in the phrase "from it" indicates its omission. It was also said that the omitted element is something else, but the matter is close. It was further said that the meaning of "from it" is "from what has been mentioned," so there is no omission in the sentence, and this is the better view. It is also permissible for the phrase "and from the fruits of" to be coordinated with "the cattle," meaning: "and for you there is a lesson from the fruits of the date palms and the grapes." It is also permissible for it to be coordinated with "from what," meaning: "and We also give you drinks made from the fruits."

**Second question: "intoxicant" (sakaran)**

﴿Sakaran﴾ means what intoxicates. This is the well-known meaning in the language. Ibn Abbas said: This verse was revealed before the prohibition of wine. By *sakar* he meant wine, and by "good provision" he meant everything that is eaten and drunk that is lawful from these two trees. Ibn Jubayr, al-Nakha'i, al-Sha'bi and Abu Thawr said this as well.

It has also been said that *sakar* means vinegar in the language of Abyssinia (Habasha), and that "good provision" means food. It was also said that *sakar* is sweet, lawful juice, and it was called *sakar* because it may become intoxicating if it is left to stand. When it reaches the point of intoxication, it becomes unlawful.

Ibn al-Arabi said: The most sound of these views is the view of Ibn Abbas, and it can be explained in one of two ways. Either this was before the prohibition of wine, or the meaning is: God has blessed you with the fruits of the date palms and the grapes, from which you make what God has prohibited to you by transgression, and what He has permitted to you by agreement or by intending the benefit of yourselves. The correct view is that this was before the prohibition of wine, so the verse is abrogated (*mansukhah*, i.e., its ruling has been abrogated by a later ruling), since this verse was revealed in Makkah (*makkiyyah*, i.e., before the Hijrah) by scholarly consensus, and the prohibition of wine was revealed in Madinah.

I say: If *sakar* means wine or sweet juice, then there is no abrogation, the verse is muhkam (clear and unabrogated), and this is a good view.

Ibn Abbas said: The Abyssinians call vinegar *sakar*. However, the majority hold that *sakar* means wine. Among them are Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Umar, Abu Razin, al-Hasan, Mujahid, Ibn Abi Layla, al-Kalbi and others previously mentioned. All of them said: *sakar* is what God has prohibited from these two fruits. Likewise, the lexicographers said: *sakar* is a name for wine and whatever intoxicates, and they recited:

*"Evil are the sober-minded, and evil is their drinking, when among them circulates al-muzza' and sakar."*

As for "good provision," it is what God has permitted from their two fruits.

It was also said that His saying "you make from it *sakar*" is a statement whose meaning is a question in the sense of denial: "Do you make from it *sakar*, and leave good provision, namely vinegar, raisins and dates?" This is like His saying: ﴿So are they the immortals?﴾ meaning: "Are they then the immortals?" And God knows best.

Abu Ubayda said: *sakar* means food. It is said: "This is *sakar* for you," meaning "food for you." He recited:

*"You made the faults of the noble into food."*

meaning: you made their blame into sustenance.

This is the view chosen by al-Tabari, that *sakar* is what is eaten as food and whose drinking is lawful, from the fruits of the date palms and the grapes, and this is the good provision. The wording differs but the meaning is one, like His saying: ﴿I only complain of my anguish and my grief to God﴾. This is good, and there is no abrogation.

However, al-Zajjaj said: This view of Abu Ubayda is not known, the people of tafsir hold otherwise, and he has no proof in the verse he recited, because its meaning according to others is that it describes them as becoming sour through people's faults.

The Hanafis said: The intended meaning of "*sakar*" is non-intoxicating nabidh (date-infusion drinks). The evidence is that God, glory be to Him, favoured His servants with what He created for them from this, and favour is only bestowed by something lawful, not something prohibited. Thus this is evidence for the permissibility of drinking whatever is less than intoxicating from nabidh, but when it reaches intoxication it is not permissible. They supported this from the Sunnah with what is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "God prohibited wine in itself, and intoxication from other than it." They also cited what Abd al-Malik ibn Nafi narrated from Ibn Umar, who said: "I saw a man come to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) while he was at the Corner (of the Ka'bah), and a cup was handed to him. He raised it to his mouth and found it strong, so he returned it to its owner. Then a man from the people said to him: 'O Messenger of God, is it forbidden?' He said: 'Bring me the man.' He was brought, and the cup was taken from him. Then he asked for water, poured it into it, then raised it to his mouth and frowned. Then he asked for water again, poured it in, and said: 'When these vessels become excessive (*ightalamat*, i.e., exceed their limit) over you, then break their edges with water.'" It is also narrated that he (peace be upon him) used to have nabidh prepared for him, and he would drink it that day; if it was the second or third day, he gave it to the servant when it had changed. Had it been forbidden, he would not have given it to him.

Al-Tahawi said: Abu Awn al-Thaqafi narrated from Abd Allah ibn Shaddad, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Wine was prohibited in itself, whether little or much of it, and intoxication from every drink." Al-Daraqutni also transmitted it.

Therefore, in this hadith and what is similar to it, the prohibition of other than wine does not concern its essence in the way wine was prohibited in its very substance. They said: wine is the drink of grapes, and there is disagreement about it. Among their proofs also is what Shurayk ibn ʿAbd Allah narrated: Abu Ishaq al-Hamdani narrated to us from ʿAmr ibn Maymun, who said: ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab said: "We eat the flesh of these camels, and nothing digests it in our bellies except nabidh." Shurayk said: "And I saw al-Thawri drinking nabidh in the house of the most learned man of his time, Malik ibn Mighwal."

As for the answer: their statement that God, glory be to Him, bestowed favour upon His servants, and that His favour is only by what He made lawful, is correct. However, it is possible that this was before the prohibition of wine, as we have explained, and so it is abrogated, as we have previously stated. Ibn al-ʿArabi said: If it is said, how can this be abrogated when it is a report (khabar), and a report is not subject to abrogation? We say: this is the speech of one who has not grasped the Shariʿa. We have shown that a report which is about real existence or about granting reward as a favour from God is what is not subject to abrogation. But when a report includes a legal ruling (hukm shar'i), then rulings are changed and abrogated, whether they came in the form of a report or a command. Abrogation does not apply to the wording itself but to what it contains. When you understand this, you will have left the category of the dull-witted about whom God spoke concerning the disbelievers in His words: ﴿And when We substitute one verse for another verse—and God knows best what He sends down—they say, "You are only a fabricator." But most of them do not know﴾ [see p. 176 of this part]. The meaning is that they were ignorant that the Lord commands what He wills, imposes what He wills, lifts by His justice what He wills, affirms what He wills, and with Him is the Mother of the Book.

I say: This is a severe accusation, to the point that the excellent scholars are being equated with the disbelievers in lack of understanding. The matter is one of legal theory (usul), namely whether reports about legal rulings may be abrogated or not. This has been disputed, and the correct view is that it is permissible, due to this verse and what is similar to it, and because a report about the legislated status of a ruling entails a demand for that legislated matter, and that demand is itself the legal ruling which is cited as evidence for its abrogation. And God knows best.

As for what they mentioned of the hadiths, the first and second are weak, because it has been reported from him, peace be upon him, through established transmission, that he said: "Every drink that intoxicates is forbidden," and he said: "Every intoxicant is wine, and every intoxicant is forbidden," and he said: "What in large quantity intoxicates, its small quantity is forbidden." Al-Nasai said: These are people of established reliability and integrity, well known for the soundness of transmission, and ʿAbd al-Malik cannot stand in the place of any one of them, even if a group of his peers supported him. And success is from God.

As for the third, even if it is sound, he used to give it to the servant not because it was intoxicating, but because it had a changed smell. The Prophet ﷺ disliked that an odour be found on him, and therefore he did not drink it. For this reason his wives tricked him with honey-and-raisin drink, by telling him: "We find from you the smell of maghafir," meaning an objectionable smell, and so he did not drink it afterwards. This will come in the chapter on prohibition [see vol. 18, p. 177].

As for the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbas, it has been narrated from him the opposite of that, through the transmission of ʿAtaʾ, Tawus and Mujahid, that he said: "What in large quantity intoxicates, its small quantity is forbidden." Qays ibn Dinar also narrated it from him. Likewise is his legal opinion on intoxicants, as al-Daraqutni stated. The first hadith was narrated from him by ʿAbd Allah ibn Shaddad, and the majority opposed him, so the view based on it falls away, together with what is established from the Prophet ﷺ.

As for what was reported from ʿUmar in his words: "nothing digests it in our bellies except nabidh," he meant non-intoxicating nabidh, by the evidence we have mentioned. Al-Nasai narrated from ʿUtbah ibn Farqad, who said: "The nabidh which ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab drank had been made sour (khullila)." Al-Nasai said: What indicates the soundness of this is the hadith of al-Sa'ib, which al-Harith ibn Miskin related to us by reading to him while I was listening, from Ibn al-Qasim: Malik narrated to me from Ibn Shihab from al-Sa'ib ibn Yazid, that he informed him that ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab came out to them and said: "I found from so-and-so the smell of a drink, and he claimed it was ṭilāʾ (boiled grape juice). I will ask about what he drank; if it was intoxicating, I will flog him." So ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, gave him the full hadd punishment. He also said in his sermon from the pulpit of the Messenger of God ﷺ: "As for what follows, O people, the prohibition of wine was revealed, and it is from five things: from grapes, honey, dates, wheat and barley. Wine is that which obscures the intellect." This has been discussed earlier in al-Ma'ida [see vol. 6, p. 285].

If it is said: Ibrahim al-Nakhaʿi and Abu Jaʿfar al-Tahawi permitted drinking it, and he was the imam of the people of his time, and Sufyan al-Thawri used to drink it. We say: al-Nasai mentioned in his book that the first to permit intoxicating nabidh was Ibrahim al-Nakhaʿi. This is a slip from a scholar, and we have warned against the slips of scholars. No argument lies in the statement of anyone against the Sunna. [It may be that what al-Nakhaʿi, being an imam, drank was not intoxicating nabidh, for some nabidh has not reached the level of intoxication.]

Al-Nasai also mentioned from Ibn al-Mubarak, who said: "I have not found a concession regarding intoxicants authentically from anyone except Ibrahim." Abu Usama said: "I have not seen a man more eager for knowledge than ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Mubarak in the Shamat [note in al-Sindi's commentary on Sunan al-Nasai: 'his saying al-Shamat seems to be a plural intending the Levantine lands'], Egypt, Yemen and the Hijaz."

As for al-Tahawi and Sufyan, even if that were authentically reported from them, they could not be used as evidence against those imams who differed with them concerning the prohibition of intoxicants, in the face of what is established from the Sunna. Moreover, al-Tahawi mentioned in his large book on differences the opposite of that. Abu ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-Barr said in his book al-Tamhid: Abu Jaʿfar al-Tahawi said: "The community has agreed that grape juice, when it becomes strong, foams and throws up froth, is wine, and whoever deems it lawful is a disbeliever. They differed concerning date nabidh when it ferments and intoxicates." He said: This shows you that the hadith of Yahya ibn Abi Kathir from Abu Hurayra from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said: "Wine is from these two trees, the palm and the grape," is not acted upon by them, for if they accepted the hadith they would have declared disbelievers those who deem date nabidh lawful. Thus it is established that only the grape juice that has become strong and reached the point of intoxication entered the prohibited wine. He said: Then it must be either that the prohibition is attached only to these, without analogy extending to others, or that analogy upon them is required. We found them all analogizing from them to date nabidh when it ferments and much of it intoxicates, and likewise raisin nabidh. He said: So it is obligatory by analogy to that to prohibit every intoxicating drink. He said: It has been reported from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "Every intoxicant is forbidden," and he dispensed with its chain because all accepted it; the disagreement among them is only in its interpretation. Some of them said he meant the category of what intoxicates; and some said he meant what produces intoxication in its own case, just as one is not called a killer unless killing actually occurs.

I say: This shows that it is forbidden according to al-Tahawi by his statement: "so it is obligatory by analogy to that to prohibit every intoxicating drink." Al-Daraqutni narrated in his Sunan from ʿAʾisha, may God be pleased with her, that she said: "God did not prohibit wine for its name; He prohibited it for its consequence. So every drink whose consequence is like the consequence of wine is forbidden, just as wine is forbidden."

Ibn al-Mundhir said: The people of Kufa brought defective reports, and when people differ about a matter it is obligatory to return it to the Book of God and the Sunna of His Messenger, peace be upon him. As for what is reported from some of the Successors, that he drank the drink which intoxicates in large quantity, then those people have sins for which they seek God's forgiveness. That must be one of two things: either a mistaken person who erred in interpretation of a hadith he heard, or a man who committed a sin and perhaps frequently sought God's forgiveness for it. The Prophet ﷺ is God's proof upon the earlier and later ones of this community.

It has been said concerning the interpretation of the verse that it was mentioned for reflection, i.e., whoever is capable of creating these things is capable of resurrection. This reflection does not differ whether wine was lawful or unlawful; taking intoxicants does not indicate prohibition. And this is as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿They ask you about wine and gambling. Say: In both is great sin and benefit for people﴾ [see vol. 3, p. 51]. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 16, verse 68:

There are three issues in this.

The first: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And your Lord revealed to the bee﴾. The discussion of revelation (wahy) has already passed, and that it may mean inspiration (ilham), which is what Allah, exalted is He, creates in the heart at the outset without any apparent cause. It is from His saying, exalted is He: "By the soul and Him who proportioned it, and inspired it with its wickedness and its righteousness" (91:7–8). Among this is the instinct of animals, and what Allah, glorified is He, creates in them of knowing their benefits, avoiding their harms, and managing their livelihood. Allah, mighty and majestic is He, has informed of this concerning the inanimate, saying: ﴿She will relate her news, because your Lord has revealed to her﴾ (99:4–5). Ibrahim al-Harbi said: "Allah, mighty and majestic is He, has a power in inanimate things whose nature is not known; no messenger came to them from Allah, but Allah made them know it, that is, inspired them." There is no disagreement among the interpreters that the revelation here means inspiration.

Yahya ibn Wassab read "ilā al-naḥal" with a fatha on the ḥa'. It was named naḥl because Allah, mighty and majestic is He, gave (nahala) it the honey that comes out of it; this is what al-Zajjaj said. Al-Jawhari said: "al-naḥl and al-naḥlah are the bee (al-dabr), which applies to both the male and the female, so that one says yaʿsūb (leader of the bees). The word naḥl is feminine in the dialect of the people of the Hijaz, and every collective noun whose singular differs from it only by the ta' (al-hā') ..."

It is related on the authority of Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "All flies are in the Fire, which will be a punishment for the people of the Fire, except the bee." al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim mentioned it in Nawadir al-Usul.

It is also related from Ibn ʿAbbas who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade killing the ant, the bee, the hoopoe and the ṣurad (a large-headed bird with a large beak, having great feathers, half white and half black, which hunts small birds)." Abu Dawud also narrated it. It will come in (the commentary on) Surat al-Naml, if Allah wills.

The second: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That take for yourselves houses in the mountains, and in the trees﴾. This applies when it has no ruler (malik).

(And of what they build) Allah made the bees' dwellings in these three kinds: either in the mountains and their crevices, or in the hollows of trees, or in what the son of Adam builds (ya'rishu) of hives (al-ajbah, the bee cells in a mountain in which honey is made), beehives, walls, and other things. ʿArasha here means prepared (hayya'a), and it is most often used for what is made with skill from branches and wood and the arrangement of their shade; from this comes the arish that was made for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on the day of Badr. From this is also the word ʿarsh (throne). It is said: ʿarasha, yaʿrishu and yaʿrishu (with kasra and damma of the ra'), and both are read. Ibn ʿAmir read with the damma, and the rest with the kasra, and there is a difference of report from ʿAsim on this.

The third: Ibn al-ʿArabi said: Among the wonders that Allah created in the bee is that He inspired it to build its dwellings hexagonal (musaddasah), whereby they join together until they become like a single piece. That is because shapes from the triangle up to the decagon, when each of them is joined to its like, do not connect and gaps remain between them, except the hexagonal shape, for when it is joined to its like it connects as if it were a single piece.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 16, verse 69 (part 1 of 3):

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then eat of all the fruits﴾. That is because it only eats the blossoms of trees.

(Then follow the ways of your Lord) meaning, the paths of your Lord. Subul (ways, paths) are roads, and He attributed them to Himself because He is their Creator. That is, enter the paths of your Lord to seek sustenance in the mountains and among the trees.

(Dhululan) is the plural of dhalul, meaning submissive, that is, obedient and subjugated. So "dhululan" is a circumstantial state (hal) of the bees: they submit and go wherever their keeper wills, for they follow their keepers wherever they go. This was said by Ibn Zayd. It has also been said that what is meant by His saying "dhululan" is the paths. Al-Yasub (the leader) is the chief [[Al-yasub: it is the queen bee, and the bees have no other leader. The mention of the drone is that which fertilises the queen and then dies; this is what the scholars affirm regarding this species.]] of the bees: when it stops, they stop, and when it moves, they move.

His saying, Exalted is He: "(From their bellies there comes forth a drink of varying colours, wherein is healing for mankind)". On this there are nine issues.

The first: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿From their bellies﴾. The address shifts to the third person in order to enumerate the blessing and to draw attention to the lesson, so He says: "From their bellies there comes forth a drink", meaning honey. Most people hold that honey comes forth from the mouths of bees, and it has been reported from ʿAlī ibn Abi Ṭālib, may Allah be pleased with him, that in belittling this world he said: "The finest garment of the son of Adam in it is the saliva of a worm, and the finest of its drinks is the excrement of a bee." The apparent meaning of this is that it comes from other than the mouth. In sum, it comes out, and it is not known whether from its mouth or from below it, but its wholesomeness is not complete except through the heat of its breaths. Aristotle built a house of glass to observe how it works, but it refused to work until they smeared the inside of the glass with mud; this was mentioned by al-Ghaznawi. He said: "From their bellies," because the transformation of food takes place only in the belly.

The second: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿of varying colours﴾ means its kinds: red, white, yellow, solid and liquid. The mother is one, yet the offspring differ, which is evidence that the power of God diversified it according to the diversity of its food, just as its taste differs according to the difference of pastures. From this meaning is the saying of Zaynab to the Prophet ﷺ: "Their bees grazed on the ʿurfuṭ [[Al-jars: eating. Al-ʿurfuṭ (with a damma): a tree of acacia (ṭalḥ), which has a foul-smelling gum; when bees eat it, its smell enters their honey. That is, the honey tasted of what the bee had eaten from the acacia tree.]]," when she compared its smell to the smell of maghafir.

**The third issue:** Allah's words, ﴿in it is healing for mankind﴾. The pronoun refers to honey. The majority of scholars said: that is, in honey there is healing for mankind. It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, al-Farra' and Ibn Kaysan that the pronoun refers to the Qur'an, meaning: in the Qur'an there is healing. An-Nahhas said: "This is a good view." Or it means: in what We have related to you of the signs and proofs there is healing for mankind. It has also been said: honey has healing in it. This view is also clear, because most of the drinks and electuaries (ma'ajin) used for treatment are originally made from honey. Qadi Abu Bakr Ibn al-Arabi said: "Whoever says it refers to the Qur'an is far from the truth. I do not think this is correctly transmitted from them, and even if it were transmitted, it would not be sound by reason, since the whole context of the speech is about honey, and the Qur'an is not mentioned in it." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "Some people of ignorance (ahl al-jahala) held that this verse is meant to refer to the People of the House and the Banu Hashim, that they are the bees, and that the drink is the Qur'an and wisdom. One of them mentioned this in the assembly of al-Mansur Abu Ja'far al-'Abbasi, and a man present said to him: 'May Allah make your food and drink from what comes out of the bellies of the Banu Hashim.' This made those present laugh, the other man was dumbfounded, and the frivolity of his statement became evident."

**The fourth issue:** Scholars differed concerning Allah's words, ﴿in it is healing for mankind﴾, as to whether it is general or not. One group said: it is general, in every case and for everyone. It is reported from Ibn 'Umar that he would not complain of a sore or anything without applying honey to it, even to a boil; when it came out, he would smear honey on it. An-Naqqash related from Abu Wajra that he would apply honey to his eyes as kohl, take honey as a purgative, and treat himself with honey. It is also reported that 'Awf ibn Malik al-Ashja'i fell ill, and it was said to him: "Shall we treat you?" He said: "Bring me water, for Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿And We send down from the sky blessed water﴾ [[See vol. 17, p. 6. It appears that by "blessed" is meant rainwater, for it is at the utmost purity, so it is a healing from illnesses and a purifier from germs. Edited.]]." Then he said: "Bring me honey, for Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿in it is healing for mankind﴾." Then he said: "Bring me olive oil, for Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿from a blessed tree﴾ [[See vol. 12, p. 262.]]." They brought him all of that, he mixed it together and drank it, and he was cured.

Some of them said: it is general when mixed with vinegar and cooked, so that it becomes a drink that benefits in every state, from every disease.

Another group said: this is particular and does not necessarily imply generality in every illness and for every person. Rather, it is information that it heals as other medicines heal, in some cases and in some states but not others. So the benefit of the verse is an announcement that it is a medicine, since healing by it has become abundant, and it has become a mixer and aid to medicines in drinks and electuaries. This is not the first word that has been specified, for the Qur'an is full of such usage, and in the Arabic language the general often comes in the sense of the particular and the particular in the sense of the general.

Among what shows that it is not general is that ﴿healing﴾ (shifa') is indefinite in an affirmative context, and there is no generality in it by the agreement of the people of the language, the verifying scholars, and the differing scholars of the principles of jurisprudence. However, a group of people of truthfulness and determination have taken it as general, so they sought healing with honey from all pains and diseases, and they were healed of their ailments by the blessing of the Qur'an and by the soundness of belief and certainty.

Ibn al-Arabi said: Whoever's intention is weak and whose habit has overcome his religion will take it in the sense of the physicians' opinions. Everything is from the wisdom of the Doer of what He wills.

**The fifth issue:** If someone says: "We have seen that honey benefits some people and harms others, so how can it be a healing for mankind?" It is said to him: Water is the life of everything, and we have seen that water kills a person when he takes it against an illness in the body that it opposes. We have also seen the healing of honey in most of these drinks. Az-Zajjaj said this as well.

The physicians have unanimously, every one of them, praised the general benefit of sikanjabin [[Sikanjabin: a drink arabized from Persian, i.e., vinegar and honey (from the arabized Persian terms).]] for every disease, and its origin is honey, and likewise all the electuaries. Moreover, the Prophet ﷺ settled the problem of this difficulty and removed the face of this possibility when he commanded the man who complained of his stomach to drink honey. When his brother told him that it had only increased his purging, he commanded him to return to drinking it, and he was cured. He said: "Allah has spoken the truth, and your brother's stomach has lied."

**The sixth issue:** Some of the atheist physicians objected to this hadith, saying: "The physicians have agreed that honey causes purging, so how is it prescribed for one who already has diarrhoea?" The answer is that this statement is true in itself for the one who has faith in His Prophet, peace be upon him, so he uses it in the manner he specified and in the place he commanded, with a sound intention and a good disposition. He will see its benefit and perceive its blessing, as has happened to the owner of this honey and to others, as previously mentioned. As for what is related as a consensus (ijma', scholarly agreement), it is evidence of his ignorance of the transmitted reports, since he did not restrict the statement but stated it in absolute terms.

Imam Abu 'Abd Allah al-Mazari said: It should be known that diarrhoea arises from many causes, among them diarrhoea resulting from overeating and hay-diseases (hayYat) [[Haydat: plural of haydah, meaning the loosening of the bowels.]]. The physicians agree in such a case that its treatment is to leave it to nature and its action, and if nature needs an aid for purging, it is aided as long as the strength remains. But holding it back is harmful. When this is clear, we say: it is possible that this man was afflicted with diarrhoea from fullness and hay-disease, so the Prophet ﷺ commanded him to drink honey, and it increased it until the material was exhausted, so the diarrhoea stopped, and it coincided with his drinking the honey. If this is outside the discipline of medicine, that indicates the ignorance of the objector in that discipline.

He said: We do not seek support for the words of our Prophet by having the physicians confirm them. Rather, if they denied him, we would deny them and declare them unbelievers and affirm him, peace be upon him. If they show us by observation the correctness of what they say, then we would need to interpret the words of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and bring them into line with what is correct, since the proof has been established that he does not lie.

**The seventh issue:** In Allah's words, ﴿in it is healing for mankind﴾, there is evidence for the permissibility of treating oneself by taking medicine and other means, contrary to those among the leading scholars who disliked that. This refutes the Sufis who claim that spiritual sainthood (wilaya) is not complete unless one is content with everything that befalls him of affliction, and that it is not permissible for him to seek treatment. There is no sense in one who denies this. It is related in the authentic (sahih) collection from Jabir, from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, that he said: "For every disease there is a cure, and when the cure of a disease is applied, it is healed by Allah's permission." Abu Dawud and at-Tirmidhi related from Usama ibn Shurayk, who said: The Bedouins said: "Shall we not treat ourselves, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Yes. O servants of Allah, treat yourselves, for Allah has not placed a disease without placing for it a healing or a cure, except one disease." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, and what is it?" He said: "Old age." This is the wording of at-Tirmidhi, and he said: "A hadith, good and sound."

It is also related from Abu Khuzama, from his father, who said: I asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: "O Messenger of Allah, what do you think of the incantations (ruqa) we use for healing, the medicines we treat ourselves with, and the precautions we take to guard against: do they repel anything of Allah's decree?" He said: "They are from the decree of Allah." He said: "A good hadith, and nothing is known from Abu Khuzama except this hadith."

The Prophet ﷺ also said: "If there is any good in your medicines, it is in a cupping incision, or a drink of honey, or a sting of fire; but I do not like to be cauterized." It was recorded in the authentic collection.

The hadiths on this subject are too numerous to count. The majority of scholars hold that treatment and seeking incantations are permissible.

It is related that Ibn 'Umar was cauterized for the lagwa [[Al-laqwa (with a fatha): an illness that afflicts the face and makes it lean toward one side.]] and was treated with incantation for a scorpion sting. It is related from Ibn Sirin that Ibn 'Umar used to give his child theriac [[Al-tiryaq: what is used to repel poison among medicines and electuaries; it is arabized.]]. Malik said: "There is no harm in that."

Those who disliked it argued with what Abu Hurayra related, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "A nation entered Paradise with its whole multitude and its small and great ones (qadd and qadid) [[That is, they entered gathered together, the last of them pressing upon the first. Ibn al-A'rabi said: al-qadd is small pebbles, meaning they entered with the great and the small.]], who did not seek fortune-telling, did not cauterize, did not take omens, and upon their Lord they put their trust."

They said: It is obligatory upon the believer to abandon these things, holding fast to Allah, trusting in Him, having confidence in Him, and turning to Him exclusively, for Allah, exalted is He, knows the days of sickness and the days of health. If creation were to strive to reduce or increase these, they could not do so. Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿No affliction befalls on earth or in yourselves except that it is in a Book before We bring it into being﴾ [[See vol. 17, p. 194.]].

Among those who held this view were a group of people of virtue and transmitted knowledge, and this is the view of Ibn Mas'ud and Abu al-Darda', may Allah be pleased with them both. 'Uthman ibn 'Affan visited Ibn Mas'ud during the illness in which he died, and 'Uthman said to him: "What do you complain of?" He said: "My sins." He said: "What do you desire?" He said: "The mercy of my Lord." He said: "Shall I not call a physician for you?" He said: "The physician has made me ill..." and he mentioned the hadith. It will come in full in the section on the virtues of al-Waqi'a, Allah willing.

Waki' related, saying: Abu Hilal narrated to us from Mu'awiya ibn Qurra, who said: Abu al-Darda' fell ill, and people visited him and said: "Shall we not call a physician for you?" He said: "The physician has laid me down."

This view was also held by ar-Rabi' ibn Khuthaym. Sa'id ibn Jubayr disliked incantations. Al-Hasan disliked taking all medicines except milk and honey.

The earlier scholars answered regarding the hadith that it contains no proof, because it is possible that it intends a type of cauterization that is disliked, based on the Prophet ﷺ cauterizing Ubayy on the day of the Confederates (al-Ahzab) at his forearm vein (akhal) [[Al-akhal: a vein in the middle of the forearm.]] when he was struck by an arrow. And he said: "Healing is in three things," as previously mentioned. It is also possible that it intends incantations with things that are not in the Book of Allah, although He, glorified and exalted is He, says: ﴿And We send down of the Qur'an that which is a healing﴾ [[See p. 315 of this volume.]], as will be explained. The Prophet ﷺ also used incantations for his companions and commanded them to use incantation, as will be explained.

The eighth issue: Malik and the majority of his companions held that there is no zakat on honey, even though it is a food that is eaten and used as a staple. The position of al-Shafi'i was divided, and what he firmly stated in his later view (al-qawl al-jadid) is that there is no zakat on it. Abu Hanifa said that zakat on honey is obligatory on both its little and its much, because the nisab is not a condition for it according to him. Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: there is nothing due on it until it reaches eight faraq [in manuscripts J and W: "five faraq"], and the faraq is thirty-six rotl by the Iraqi rotls. Abu Yusuf said: one ziq is due on every ten azqaq, relying on what al-Tirmidhi narrated from Ibn Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "On honey, one ziq is due for every ten azqaq." Abu Isa (al-Tirmidhi) said: there is some discussion about its chain of narration, and nothing authentic has been related from the Prophet (ﷺ) on this subject of substance. The practice according to most of the people of knowledge is in accordance with this, and Ahmad and Ishaq hold this view. Some people of knowledge said: there is nothing due on honey.

The ninth issue: His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed in that is a sign for a people who give thought﴾, meaning, who take lessons. Among the lessons in the bee is to look at it with fair consideration and to think subtly about its wondrous affairs. Thus one witnesses with certainty that the one who inspired it with that refined craftsmanship alongside its weak frame, and whose skill in devising its methods amid the variation of its conditions, is Allah, glorified and exalted, as He said: "And your Lord inspired the bee" [the verse]. Then it eats the sour, the bitter, the sweet and the salty, and the harmful herbs [this has not been confirmed by the beekeepers, verify], and Allah, the Exalted, makes it sweet honey and a cure, and in this is evidence of His power.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 16, verse 70:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah created you, then He causes you to die﴾. Its meaning is clear.

(And among you is one who is returned to the most abject age) meaning, the worst and lowest of it. It was said: it is the one whose strength and intellect are diminished, and who is reduced to senility (al-kharaf) and the like. Ibn 'Abbas said: meaning to the lowest of life, becoming like a child who has no intellect. The meanings are close to one another. In Sahih al-Bukhari, on the authority of Anas ibn Malik, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to seek refuge (yatawwadhu) saying: "O Allah, I seek refuge in You from laziness, I seek refuge in You from cowardice, I seek refuge in You from senility (al-haram), and I seek refuge in You from miserliness." And in the hadith of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas: "And I seek refuge in You from being returned to the most abject age," the hadith. Al-Bukhari narrated it.

(So that he does not know, after knowledge, anything) meaning he returns to the state of childhood, so he does not know what he knew before of matters, owing to the extreme of old age. It has been said: this does not happen to a believer, because a believer's knowledge is not taken away from him. It was also said: the meaning is "so that he does not act, after knowledge, anything," where action is expressed by knowledge because it depends on it, since the effect of old age on his action is more pronounced than its effect on his knowledge. The intended meaning is an argument against those who deny the Resurrection, i.e., the One who returned him to this state is able to cause him to die and then bring him back to life.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 16, verse 71:

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿And Allah has favoured some of you over others in provision﴾, meaning: He made some of you rich and some poor, and some free and some slaves.

(So those who have been favoured) — that is, in provision.

(will not hand over their provision to what their right hands possess, so that they become equal in it) — that is, the master does not return to what his right hand possesses any of what he has been provided, such that the slave and the owner become equal in wealth. This is a parable which Allah struck for the worshippers of idols: that is, if your slaves are not equal with you, then how do you make My slaves equal with Me? Since their slaves did not share with them in their wealth, it was not permissible for them to make others share with Allah, the Exalted, in worship—other than idols, stones set up for worship, and other things that are worshipped, such as the angels and the prophets, who are His servants and creation. Al-Tabari related this meaning, and it was said by Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah and others. It is also reported from Ibn Abbas that it was revealed concerning the Christians of Najran when they said, "Isa is the son of Allah," and Allah said to them: "So those who have been favoured will not hand over their provision to what their right hands possess, so that they become equal in it." That is, the master does not return to what his right hand possesses any of what he has been provided, so that the master and the slave are equal in wealth. How then do you accept for Me what you do not accept for yourselves, by making for Me a child from among My slaves? And its parallel is: ﴿He has struck for you a parable from yourselves: Do you have among what your right hands possess partners in what We have provided you, so that you are equal in it?﴾ [[See vol. 14, p. 22.]] as will come. This indicates that the slave does not own, as will come shortly after [[He means: shortly after. "Anfan" is used of the recent past, not the near future.]].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 16, verse 72:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And Allah has made for you mates from yourselves⦆ "Made" (ja'ala) here means "created" (khalaqa), and this has already been discussed. "Mates from yourselves" means: from Adam, He created Hawwa' (Eve) from him. It was also said: the meaning is "He made for you from yourselves," that is, from your own kind, your own species, and of your own make, as He said: ﴿There has certainly come to you a Messenger from yourselves﴾ [[See vol. 8, p. 301.]], that is, from among the children of Adam. In this there is a refutation of the Arabs who used to believe that they would marry the jinn and have intercourse with them, to the point that it is reported that 'Amr ibn Hind [[So it stands in the manuscripts of the originals and in Ibn al-'Arabi's Ahkam al-Quran; the correct name is 'Amr ibn Yarbu' ibn Handhala ibn Malik ibn Mana. 'Ulba' ibn Arqam said:

Woe to the tribe of Sa'lah, 'Amr ibn Yarbu', the most evil of creatures.

See the commentary on al-Tanwir upon Saqt al-Zand, on the verse of Abu al-'Ala' al-Ma'arri:

When a flash of lightning shines, their faces are wrinkled; as if I were 'Amr, and the camels were she-ghouls.]] married one of them, a ghoul, and he used to keep her away from lightning so that it would not see her and she would not flee. But one night lightning flashed, and the sa'lah [[al-Sa'lah: the female ghoul.]] saw it and said, "'Amr!" and fled, and he never saw her again. This is one of their lies. Although it is permissible under God's power and wisdom, it is a refutation of the philosophers who deny the existence of the jinn and claim that they do not eat.

(Mates) The "zawj" of a man is his second: he is a single one, and when another is joined to him they become two spouses. The attribution is made to him rather than to her because he is the origin of her existence, as has been discussed.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And He made for you, from your mates, sons and grandchildren⦆ In this there are five issues. The first: His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿He made for you, from your mates, sons﴾ is evident in enumerating the blessing of children. The existence of children comes from both of them together, but since the creation of the offspring is within the mother and its separation from her, it is attributed to her. For this reason it follows her in slavery and freedom and becomes like her in property. Ibn al-'Arabi said: I heard the imam of the Hanbalis in the City of Peace, Abu al-Wafa' 'Ali ibn 'Aqil, say: The child follows the mother in property and takes her ruling regarding slavery and freedom, because it separated from the father as a drop of semen, having no value, no property, and no benefit in it; it acquired what it acquired only through her and from her, and therefore it follows her. This is like a man who eats dates in another man's land, and a date pit falls from the eater's hand into the ground and becomes a palm tree: it belongs to the owner of the land and not to the eater, by the consensus of the community, because it separated from the eater and has no value.

The second: His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿and grandchildren (hafadah)⦆ Ibn al-Qasim related from Malik, who said: I asked him about His saying, may He be exalted, "sons and grandchildren," and he said: In my opinion, the hafadah are servants and helpers. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying, "and grandchildren," that he said they are helpers: whoever helps you has served you (hafadaka). It was said to him: Do the Arabs know this? He said: Yes, and they say it! Have you not heard the poet's words:

The maidservants hastened around them, and they yielded with their hands the reins of the camels.

That is, they hastened in service. The walā'id are servants, the singular being walīdah. Al-A'sha said:

I burdened with its unknown ones, Yemeni she-camels, when the drivers hastened over their rumps.[[al-Aksa': plural of kisa (with damma), the hindquarters.]]

That is, they hastened. Ibn 'Arafah said: among the Arabs the hafadah are helpers; whoever works and obeys and hastens in a task is a hafid. He said: from this is their saying, "To you we hasten and serve (nahfid)." Al-hafadan means swiftness. Abu 'Ubayd said: al-hafd is work and service. Al-Khalil ibn Ahmad said: among the Arabs the hafadah are servants, and Mujahid said the same. Al-Azhari said: it was said that the hafadah are the children of children, and this is related from Ibn 'Abbas. It was also said they are in-laws (al-akhtan), as said by Ibn Mas'ud, 'Alqamah, Abu al-Duha, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ibrahim, and from this is the poet's saying [[It is Jamil.]]:

If my soul had obeyed me, it would have had many grandchildren, countless.

But it is a soul proud against me, disdaining the in-law connections of the base, and refusing them.

Zirr related from 'Abd Allah that he said: the hafadah are in-laws (al-asbar), and Ibrahim said the same, and the meanings are close. Al-Asma'i said: the khatan is one who is from the woman's side, such as her father, her brother and those like them, and al-asbar from her side all together. It is said: "Fulan became related by marriage (asbara) to the sons of Fulan, and intermarried (sahara)." 'Abd Allah's saying that they are the akhtan may bear both meanings: it may be that he meant the woman's father and those of her relatives like him, and it may be that he meant: "and He made for you, from your mates, sons and daughters whom you marry off, so that you gain in-laws through them."

'Ikrimah said: the hafadah are the grandchildren of a man's offspring, and its root is from hafada yahfidu (with fatha in the past and kasra in the future), when he hastened in his course, as Kuthayyir said [[The mention of Ibn 'Abbas's citation of it has already passed, so it cannot be attributed to Kuthayyir 'Azzah.]]:

The maidservants hastened among them...

the verse.

It is said: hafadat and ahfadat are two dialects, when she served. It is said: hafid and hafad, like khadim and khadam, and hafid and hafadah, like kafir and kafarah. Al-Mahdawi said: whoever makes the hafadah servants makes it a separate statement from what precedes it, intending priority, as if he said: "He made for you helpers, and He made for you, from your mates, sons."

I say: what al-Azhari said, that the hafadah are the children of children, is the apparent sense of the Qur'an, indeed its explicit text. Do you not see that He said: ﴿And He made for you, from your mates, sons and hafadah﴾, so He made both the hafadah and the sons from them? Ibn al-'Arabi said: What is most apparent to me in His saying "sons and hafadah" is that the sons are a man's children from his loins, and the hafadah are the children of his sons, and the strength of the wording goes no further than this; the sense of the verse on this reading would be: "And He made for you, from your mates, sons, and from the sons, grandchildren." Al-Hasan said the same.

The third: If we follow the view of Mujahid, Ibn 'Abbas, Malik and the scholars of language that the hafadah are servants and helpers, then the service of the child and the wife has come out of the Qur'an with the most wondrous clarity, as Ibn al-'Arabi said. Al-Bukhari and others related from Sahl ibn Sa'd that Abu Usayd al-Sa'idi invited the Prophet ﷺ to his wedding feast, and his wife was their servant... the hadith, and it has already been mentioned in Surah Hud [[See vol. 9, p. 68.]]. In the Sahih, from 'A'ishah, she said: I myself braided the garlands of the Prophet's ﷺ sacrificial camels with my own hands. The hadith. For this reason our scholars said: she must spread the bedding, cook the pot, and sweep the house, according to her condition and the custom of women like her. God the Exalted said: ﴿And He made from it its mate that it might find rest in her﴾ [[See vol. 7, p. 337.]]. So it is as if He gathered for us in her tranquility, enjoyment, and a measure of service according to customary practice.

The fourth: A man serves his wife in what is light of service and helps her, because 'A'ishah related that the Prophet ﷺ used to be in service to his household, and when he heard the adhan he went out. This is the view of Malik: "and he helps her." Among the manners of the Prophet ﷺ: he used to mend his sandal, sweep the house, and sew his garment. 'A'ishah, when asked, "What did the Messenger of God ﷺ do in his house?" said: He was a human among humans; he delousing his garment, milked his goat, and served himself.

The fifth: He spends on one female servant, and it was said: on more, according to the wealth and station. This matter rests on custom, which is one of the foundations of the Sharia. The women of the Bedouins and the people of the desert serve their husbands (even in drawing sweet water and managing the animals, as Ibn al-'Arabi says), while the women of the towns, where a man of modest means serves his wife in what is light and helps her; but the wealthy serve their husbands and enjoy comfort with them when that is their rank. If the matter is problematic, the wife may stipulate this condition, having the husband acknowledge in witnessed form that he knows she is one who does not serve herself, and he commits to it; it is then enforced and the claim concerning it ends.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And provided you with good things﴾ That is, from fruits, grains and livestock.

(Then is it in falsehood) That is, the idols, as said by Ibn 'Abbas.

(They believe) The reading of the majority is with the ya'. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman read it with the ta'. (And in the favour of Allah) That is, in Islam.

(They disbelieve).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 16, verse 73–74:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they worship besides Allah that which possesses no provision for them from the heavens and the earth at all, and they are unable [to do so]﴾ [An-Nahl 16:73] ﴿So do not strike forth examples for Allah. Indeed, Allah knows, and you know not﴾ [An-Nahl 16:74].

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they worship besides Allah that which possesses no provision for them from the heavens﴾ means the rain.

(And the earth) means the plants.

(At all) Al-Akhfash said: it is a substitute (badal) for "provision." Al-Farra' said: it is in the accusative by virtue of the provision being attached to it, meaning: they worship that which does not possess the ability to provide them with anything.

(And they are unable) means they have no power over anything, referring to the idols.

(So do not strike forth examples for Allah) means do not liken these inanimate things to Him, for He is the One, the Capable, who has no like. This has already been discussed.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 16, verse 73–74:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they worship besides Allah that which possesses no provision for them from the heavens and the earth at all, and they are unable [to do so]﴾ [An-Nahl 16:73] ﴿So do not strike forth examples for Allah. Indeed, Allah knows, and you know not﴾ [An-Nahl 16:74].

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they worship besides Allah that which possesses no provision for them from the heavens﴾ means the rain.

(And the earth) means the plants.

(At all) Al-Akhfash said: it is a substitute (badal) for "provision." Al-Farra' said: it is in the accusative by virtue of the provision being attached to it, meaning: they worship that which does not possess the ability to provide them with anything.

(And they are unable) means they have no power over anything, referring to the idols.

(So do not strike forth examples for Allah) means do not liken these inanimate things to Him, for He is the One, the Capable, who has no like. This has already been discussed.

There are five issues here.

The first concerns God's words, ﴿God presents a parable﴾. He draws attention to the misguidance of the polytheists, and this is connected with what precedes it, namely the mention of God's blessings upon them and the absence of anything similar from their gods. "God presents a parable" means He sets forth a likeness. He then explained it by saying: (a slave owned) , meaning: just as there is no equality among you between a slave who owns nothing and cannot act on his own affairs, and a free man to whom God has given good provision, so too there is no equality between Me and these idols. The example in this verse is a slave with this description, who is owned, cannot control any property, and cannot control his own affairs, but is merely subjected to the will of his master. It does not follow from the verse that all slaves are of this description, for an indefinite noun in an affirmative sentence does not, according to the people of the language, imply generality, as was previously explained. It only indicates one. When it follows a command or prohibition, or is attached to a verbal noun, it carries general indefinite meaning, as in the saying: "Free a man" and "Do not humiliate a man." The verbal noun is like "freeing a neck" (i.e., freeing a slave). Whichever man is freed, the obligation of the address has been discharged, and an exception may validly be made from it.

Qatadah said: this parable is for the believer and the disbeliever. Qatadah held that the owned slave is the disbeliever, because he gains nothing from his worship in the Hereafter, and that the meaning of "and one whom We have provided with good provision from Us" is the believer. The first interpretation is the view of the majority of the people of knowledge (['ilm]) and of exegesis (ta'wil).

Al-Asamm said: the owned slave is meant, who may sometimes be stronger than his master in build and more radiant of face, yet he is humbled before his master and can only do what he is permitted to do. God said, by way of example, meaning: if this is your situation and the situation of your slaves, then how do you make lifeless stones partners of God in His creation and His worship, when they neither understand nor hear?

The second issue: Muslims understood from this verse and from what precedes it that the slave is lower in rank than the free man in regard to ownership, and that he owns nothing even if he does own something. The people of Iraq said: slavery contradicts ownership, so he owns nothing at all in any case. This is also the view of al-Shafi'i in his New (al-Jadid) opinion, and it was held by al-Hasan and Ibn Sirin. Others said: he does own, but his ownership is deficient, because his master may take it from him whenever he wishes. This is the view of Malik and those who followed him, and al-Shafi'i held it in his Old (al-Qadim) opinion. It is also the view of the Zahiris (literalists, adherents of the apparent meaning). For this reason our companions said: he is not obligated to perform financial acts of worship such as zakat (obligatory alms) and expiations (kaffarat), nor bodily acts of worship that would prevent him from serving his master, such as the pilgrimage (hajj) and jihad, and other such things.

The benefit of this question is that if the master makes him owner of a slave-girl, it is permissible for him to have intercourse with her by right of ownership (milk al-yamin). If he makes him owner of forty sheep and a year passes over them, zakat is not obligatory upon the master for them, because they belong to another, nor upon the slave, because his ownership is not secure. The Iraqi view says: it is not permissible for him to have intercourse with the slave-girl, and zakat on the threshold quantity remains obligatory upon the master as it was before. The evidence for these two positions is found in the books of legal disagreement.

The strongest proof for us is God's words: ﴿God is He who created you, then provided for you﴾. He made the slave and the free man equal in provision and creation. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Whoever frees a slave who has property..." and so he attributed the property to him. Ibn 'Umar would see his slave acquire a concubine with his property and would not object to that. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that a slave of his divorced his wife twice, and he ordered him to take her back by right of ownership. This is evidence that he owns what is in his possession and may do with it what an owner does with his property, so long as his master has not taken it from him. And God knows best.

The third issue: some scholars have used this verse to argue that the divorce of a slave is in the hands of his master, and that selling a female slave amounts to divorcing her, relying on God's words: ﴿does not have power over anything﴾. They said: its apparent meaning indicates that he has no power over anything at all, neither over ownership nor over anything else, so it applies in its general sense unless some evidence indicates otherwise. What we have mentioned from Ibn 'Umar and Ibn 'Abbas indicates a restriction (of this generality). And God knows best.

The fourth issue: Abu Mansur said in his creed ('Aqidah): [[The 'Aqidah is the title of a book by Abu Mansur al-Maturidi, Muhammad ibn Muhammad ibn Mahmud, who died in Samarqand in 333 AH. See Kashf al-Zunun and Taj al-Tarajim fi Tabaqat al-Hanafiyyah.]] "Provision is that by which nourishment occurs." This verse refutes this restriction, as does God's words: ﴿And from what We have provided them they spend﴾ and ﴿Spend from what We have provided you﴾, and other statements, including the words of the Prophet ﷺ: "My provision has been placed under the shade of my spear," and his words: "The provisions of my community are in the hooves of their horses and the points of their spears." Thus all spoils of war are provision, and everything from which benefit is validly gained is provision. It has degrees, the highest of which is that which nourishes. The Messenger of God ﷺ enumerated the ways of benefiting from property in his saying: "The son of Adam says, 'My property, my property.' But do you have of your property anything except what you ate and consumed, or what you wore and wore out, or what you gave in charity and sent ahead?" The meaning of clothing includes riding and other such things. In the language of the scholars of hadith, hearing is provision, meaning the hearing of hadith, and this is correct.

The fifth issue: God's words: ﴿and one whom We have provided with good provision from Us﴾ refer to the believer, who obeys God with his person and his property. The disbeliever, as long as he does not spend in obedience, becomes like the slave who owns nothing. ﴿Are they equal?﴾ means: they are not equal. He did not say "are they equal" in the dual because of the word "man," since it is an indefinite pronoun that suits the singular, the dual, the plural, and the masculine and feminine. It was said: "a slave who is owned" and "one whom We have provided" are both intended in the sense of generality within the category.

﴿Praise belongs to God,﴾ but most of them do not know. Meaning: He alone deserves praise, not what they worship besides Him, since the idols have no blessing upon them by way of any favor or kindness that would be praised for it. Complete praise belongs only to God, because He is the Bestower and the Creator. "But most of them": meaning most of the polytheists. "Do not know" that praise is due to Me and that all blessing comes from Me. The word "most" is used while meaning all, so it is a specific term used to indicate generality. It was said: meaning, most of creation do not know, and that is because most of them are polytheists.

Al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran), on Surah 16, verse 76:

God's words: ﴿And God sets forth a parable: two men, one of them dumb,﴾ This is another parable which God struck for Himself and for the idol. The dumb one, who has no power over anything, is the idol, and the one who enjoins justice is God, Exalted is He. This was said by Qatadah and others. Ibn 'Abbas said: The dumb one was a slave of 'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, to whom he would offer Islam, but he refused. The one who enjoins justice was 'Uthman. It is also reported from him that it was a parable for Abu Bakr al-Siddiq and a non-believing client of his. It was also said: The dumb one was Abu Jahl, and the one who enjoins justice was 'Ammar ibn Yasir al-'Ansi. ʿAns (with the letter nun) is a tribe of Madhhij, and he was an ally of the Banu Makhzum, the kin of Abu Jahl. Abu Jahl used to torture him for Islam, and he also tortured his mother Sumayyah, who was a client of Abu Jahl. One day he said to her: "You only believed in Muhammad because you love him for his beauty." Then he stabbed her in her private parts with a spear, and she died. She was the first martyr to die in Islam, may Allah have mercy on her. This is from the Book of al-Naqqash and others. This will come up in the verse on compulsion, explained in detail, God willing. [[See p. 180 and what follows of this part.]] 'Ata' said: The dumb one was Ubayy ibn Khalaf, who never spoke anything good.

﴿And he is a burden upon his master﴾ That is, upon his people, because he used to harm them and harm 'Uthman ibn Maz'un. Muqatil said: It was revealed concerning Hisham ibn 'Amr ibn al-Harith. He was a disbeliever of little good who was hostile to the Prophet (ﷺ). It was also said: The dumb one is the disbeliever, and the one who enjoins justice is the believer, sentence by sentence. This is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, and it is good, because it is general. The dumb one is the one who has no speech. It was also said: the one who does not understand. It was also said: the one who neither hears nor sees. In the tafsir it is said that the dumb one here is the idol. It shows that it has no power and no command, and that others carry it and carve it, so it is a burden upon them. God is the one who enjoins justice, the one who prevails over everything. It was also said: ﴿and he is a burden upon his master﴾ means a weight upon his guardian and his relatives, and a calamity upon his companion and his cousin. The orphan is sometimes called kall (burden) because of his weight upon the one who supports him. From this is the poet's saying:

"A glutton who devours the wealth of the kall before his youth,
when the bones of the kall are not strong."

Kall also means one who has neither child nor parent, and kall means dependents. Its plural is kulul. It is said from this: kallat al-sikkin kallan, meaning the blade of the knife became dull and did not cut.

﴿Wherever he directs him, he brings no good.﴾ The majority read يُوَجِّهْهُ, which is the script of the mushaf (the written codex), meaning: wherever his owner sends him, he brings no good, because he does not understand what he is told and does not comprehend what is said by him. Yahya ibn Wathhab read أَيْنَما يُوَجِّهْهُ with the passive verb.

[And it is reported from Ibn Mas'ud also] تَوَجَّهَ in the second person.

﴿Are they equal, he and one who enjoins justice, while he is upon a straight path?﴾ That is: are this dumb one and the one who enjoins justice, who is upon a straight path, equal?

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 16, verse 77:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And to Allah belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth﴾ Its meaning has already been mentioned [[See vol. 9, p. 177.]]. This is connected to His saying: "Indeed, Allah knows, and you do not know," meaning: the legislation of what is lawful and unlawful is only fitting from one who encompasses the consequences and the benefits, while you, O polytheists, do not encompass them, so why do you dictate?
