(And the matter of the Hour is but like a glance of the eye) and you will be recompensed in it for your deeds. The Hour (al-Sa'ah) is the time at which the Resurrection occurs; it was named "sa'ah" (hour) because it comes upon people suddenly in an instant, and creation dies by a single cry. Al-lamh is a rapid glance; it is said: lamahahu lamhan and lamahanan. The interpretive point is that since the Hour is certainly coming, it was described as being as near as a glance of the eye. Al-Zajjaj said: He did not mean that the Hour comes in the blink of an eye; rather He described the speed of His power to bring it, i.e., He says to a thing, "Be," and it is. It was also said: He used the glance of the eye as a comparison because one glances at the sky despite its distance from the earth. It was also said: it is an illustration of nearness, as a speaker says: "The year is but a moment," and the like. It was also said: the meaning is that it is so with Allah, not with created beings; the evidence is His saying: "Indeed they see it as distant, and We see it as near" [[See vol. 18, p. 283.]].

(Or it is nearer) The "or" (aw) is not for doubt; rather it is for illustration, whichever of the two the one illustrating intended. It was also said: it entered for the doubt of the addressee. It was also said: "aw" here has the meaning of "bal" (rather).

(Indeed Allah is over all things Competent) Already mentioned [[See vol. 1, p. 224.]].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (*al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Qur'an*) on Surah 16, verse 78:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And God brought you forth from the wombs of your mothers, knowing nothing﴾. He mentions that among His blessings is that He brought you forth from the wombs of your mothers as infants, having no knowledge of anything. There are three opinions concerning it:

First: You know nothing of the covenant that was taken from you in the loins of your fathers.

Second: You know nothing of what has been decreed for you of happiness and misery.

Third: You know nothing of your own benefits. The sentence is complete here. Then He begins anew and says: (And He made for you hearing, sight and hearts), meaning those by which you know and comprehend, because God made these for His servants before bringing them forth from the wombs. He gave them these after bringing them forth. That is, He made for you hearing so that you may hear the command and the prohibition, and sight so that you may see the signs of His workmanship, and hearts so that you may reach knowledge of Him.

"Al-af'idah" (hearts) is the plural of "al-fu'ad," like "ghurab" (crow) and "aghribah."

It has been said that within His saying "And He made for you hearing" is the affirmation of speech, because whoever does not hear does not speak, and when the faculty of hearing exists, speech exists.

Al-A'mash, Ibn Thabbat and Hamzah read "أُمَّهاتِكُمْ" here, and in Surah al-Nur [see vol. 12, p. 311], Surah al-Zumar [see vol. 15, p. 234], and Surah al-Najm [see vol. 17, p. 105], with a kasrah on the hamzah and the mim. As for al-Kisa'i, he read with a kasrah on the hamzah and a fatha on the mim, and this was for assimilation (*al-itba'*, vowel harmonization). The rest read with a damma on the hamzah and a fatha on the mim, according to the original form. The original form of "al-ummahat" (the mothers) is "ummat," and the ha' was added for emphasis, just as they added a ha' in "ahraqtu al-ma'" (I poured out the water), whose original form is "araqtu." This meaning has already been discussed in Surah al-Fatihah [see vol. 1, p. 148].

(So that you may give thanks): Concerning this there are two interpretations. The first: that you may give thanks for His blessings. The second: that is, that you may see the signs of His workmanship, because seeing them leads to thanks.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 16, verse 79:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Have they not seen the birds subjected in the midst of the sky? None holds them up except Allah﴾. Yahya ibn Wththab, al-A'mash, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah and Ya'qub read "tarawa" with the taa' (ta), in the address form (al-khitab), and Abu 'Ubayd (Abu 'Ubayd al-Qasim ibn Salam) preferred this reading. The rest read it with the ya' (ya), in the reporting form (al-khabar).

(Musakhkharat) meaning made subservient (muzallalat) to the command of Allah exalted is He; this was said by al-Kalbi. It was also said: "musakhkharat" means made subservient to your benefits.

(Fi jaww al-sama') al-jaww is what lies between the sky and the earth, and the jaww is attributed to the sky because of its height above the earth. And in His saying "musakhkharat" there is evidence of a Subjugator who subjected them and a Manager who empowered them to act.

(Ma yumsikuhunna illa Allah) in the states of gathering in and spreading out and of being arranged in rows. He showed them how to take lessons from them regarding His oneness.

(Inna fi dhalika la-ayat) that is, signs, lessons and indications.

(Li-qawmin yu'minun) in Allah and in what their messengers brought.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 16, verse 80 (part 1 of 3):**

In this verse there are ten issues. [The sources differ over how these issues are counted.]

**The first issue:** God's words, ﴿He has made for you﴾, mean "He made" (ṣayyara). Whatever rises above you and shades you is a roof and a sky. Whatever carries you is the earth. Whatever screens you on your four sides is a wall. When these are arranged and joined together, it is a house (bayt). This verse enumerates God's blessings upon people regarding houses. It first mentions the houses of cities, which are for long-term residence. His words, ﴿for rest (sakanan)﴾, mean that you dwell in them and your limbs become still from movement, although one may move about inside them and be still elsewhere; the statement follows what is usual. He counted this among the blessings, for if He had willed, He could have created the servant in constant agitation like the celestial spheres, and that would have been as He created and willed. Had He created him still like the earth, that too would have been as He created and willed. But He brought him into being as a creature who moves between the two states, whose condition varies between the two conditions, and who is moved about in how and where. The word "sakan" (rest) is a verbal noun that is applied to both the singular and the plural.

Then He mentioned the houses of travel and migration. **The second issue:** He said, ﴿And He made for you from the skins of livestock houses which you find light (to carry)﴾, that is, of leather mats and tanned hides. "Houses" here means tents and domes, which are light for you to carry on journeys.

﴿On the day of your departure (ẓa'nikum)﴾. The ẓa'n is the movement of the desert people in search of pasture (al-intijā', seeking grass and places where rain falls) and their shifting from one place to another. From it is the verse of 'Antara:

*"Those whose separation I anticipate have departed, and the crow with white markings has passed between them."*

The ẓa'n also means the litter (howdah) carried on a camel. Someone said:

*"Did the riding-litters (aẓ'ān) stir you when they departed, and when the crows of imminent separation fell?"*

It is read with the vowel on the letter 'ayn either sukūn or fatḥa, like "al-shi'r" and "al-sha'ar."

It has been said that it may include all tents of leather, tents of hair, and tents of wool, because these are from skins, since they are attached to them. Ibn Sallam inclined to this, and it is a good possibility. The words "and from their wool" would then be a new sentence, as if he said: "He made furnishings," meaning clothing and bedding and other things. The poet said:

*"Did the riding-litters stir you on the day they departed, with the fine adornment of furnishings?"*

It is also possible that by His words "from the skins of livestock" He means only tents of leather, as we mentioned at first. Then His words "and from their wool" would be a conjunction with "from the skins of livestock," meaning that He made houses from these as well. Ibn al-'Arabi said: "This is a practice widespread in those lands, and it has been absent from our lands, so tents here are pitched only of cotton and wool. The Prophet ﷺ had a dome of leather, and leather from Ṭā'if is enough, in its value's high price, its excellent craftsmanship, and its fine appearance. The Prophet ﷺ did not consider that luxury nor saw it as extravagance, because it is among the blessings God has favoured and permitted from His provisions, and the aspects of its benefit are manifest in shelter and shade, which the human species cannot do without." Among the strange things that happened: I visited one of the ascetics among the heedless with one of the narrators. We entered upon him in a cotton tent, and my companion the narrator offered to take him to his home as a guest, saying: "This is a place where heat is abundant, and a house is kinder to you and more pleasing to my soul concerning you." He said: "This tent is plenty for us, and in our making it is of little value." I said: "It is not as you claim, for the Messenger of God ﷺ, who was the chief of the ascetics, had a dome of Ṭā'if leather in which he travelled and sheltered." He was dumbfounded, and I saw him in a state of ignorance, so I left him with my companion and went out from him.

**The third issue:** ﴿...of their wool, their fur and their hair﴾. God permitted the use of the wool of sheep, the wool of camels, and the hair of goats, just as He permitted the greater matter, which is slaughtering them and eating their flesh. He did not mention cotton and linen because they were not in the lands of the Arabs being addressed. He only enumerated the blessings He bestowed upon them, and they were addressed concerning what they knew by means of what they understood. Whatever stands in the place of these and substitutes for them enters into use and blessing in the same way. This is like His words, ﴿And He sends down from the sky mountains of hail in them﴾ [see vol. 12, p. 289]. He addressed them with hail because they knew its frequent descent among them, and He was silent about snow because it did not exist in their lands, although it is like it in quality and benefit. The Prophet ﷺ mentioned both together regarding purification, saying: "O God, wash me with water, snow and hail." Ibn 'Abbas said: "Snow is a white thing that descends from the sky, and I have never seen it." It has been said that leaving out the mention of cotton and linen was only turning away from luxury, since the clothing of God's righteous servants is only wool. This is open to question, for He, glorified is He, says: ﴿O children of Adam, We have sent down to you clothing to cover your private parts﴾, as its explanation has already passed in *al-A'raf* [see vol. 7, p. 182]. And He says here: ﴿and made for you garments (sarabil)﴾, so He pointed to cotton and linen by the word "sarabil." And God knows best.

**"Athāthan" (furnishings):** Al-Khalil said: goods, with some of them gathered together with others, from *aththa*, meaning "it increased." He said:

*"And a branch that adorns the back, black and jet-dark, thick like the cluster of a palm, tightly intertwined."*

[The verse is from the Mu'allaqa of Imru' al-Qays. Al-far': complete hair. Al-matn and al-matna: what is beside the spine on its right and left of sinew and flesh. Al-fāḥim: intensely black. Al-qinw (with kasra or ḍamma): a palm cluster, which is a stalk. Al-mut'a'kal: that which has entered into one another because of its abundance.]

Ibn ʿAbbas said: "athāthan" means garments.

This verse implies the permissibility of benefiting from wool, fur and hair in every case. For this reason our companions (the Shafiʿis) said: the wool and hair of a dead animal are pure and may be used in every case, but they should be washed for fear that some filth has adhered to them. Likewise Umm Salamah related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "There is no harm in the hide of a dead animal once it has been tanned, nor in its wool and hair once they have been washed." [[The well-known hadith "Any hide that has been tanned has become pure" is related by Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasaʾi and Ibn Majah.]] Because it is among the things that death does not affect, whether or not the animal's flesh is eaten, like the hair of a human being or of a pig, which is entirely pure. This is also the view of Abu Hanifa, but he went further than us and said: horn, tooth and bone are like hair, because all these things have no life in them and are not made impure by the death of the animal. Al-Hasan al-Basri, al-Layth ibn Saʿd and al-Awzaʿi said: all hair is impure but becomes pure by washing. Three reports are transmitted from al-Shafiʿi: First, it is pure and is not made impure by death. Second, it is impure. Third, a distinction is made between human hair and other hair: human hair is pure and everything else is impure.

Our evidence is the generality of God's words: ﴿and of their wool﴾ and so on. He bestowed a favour upon us by making its benefit lawful for us, and He did not single out the hair of a dead animal from that of a slaughtered one. So it is general, unless some evidence restricts it. Also, the original state of these animals is purity before death, by consensus, so whoever claims that it has changed to impurity must provide the proof. If it is objected that God's words ﴿Forbidden to you is carrion﴾ [[See vol. 6, p. 47.]] are a general statement, we reply: we specify it by what we have mentioned, since it is explicitly stated in the mention of wool, whereas your verse does not explicitly mention it, so our evidence is preferable. And God knows best.

Shaykh Imam Abu Ishaq, the imam of the Shafiʿis in Baghdad, relied on the argument that hair is a part joined to the animal by creation, so it grows with its growth and becomes impure with its death, like the other parts. It is answered that growth is not proof of life, because plants grow and are not alive. And if they rely on continuous growth as found in animals, we rely on separation, which indicates the absence of sensation, which indicates the absence of life. As for what the Hanafis mentioned about bone, tooth and horn being like hair, the well-known view among us is that these are impure like flesh. Ibn Wahb said the same as Abu Hanifa's view. We also have a third view: whether the tips of horns and hooves are joined to their roots or to hair, there are two opinions. Likewise, the feathered part of a bird's plumage has the ruling of hair, and the bony part has the ruling of bone.

Our evidence is the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "Do not benefit from carrion in any way." This is general concerning it and every part of it, except what its specific evidence excludes. And among the decisive proofs for this are God's words: ﴿Who will give life to bones when they are decayed?﴾ [[See vol. 15, p. 58.]] and His words: ﴿Look at the bones, how We raise them﴾ [[See vol. 3, p. 288.]], and He said: ﴿Then We clothed the bones with flesh﴾ [[See vol. 12, p. 108.]], and He said: ﴿When we are bones and decayed dust?﴾ [[See vol. 91, p. 188.]] So the basis is bones, and life and spirit are in them as in flesh and skin. In the hadith of ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUkaym: "Do not benefit from carrion through any hide or sinew." If it is objected that it is established in the Sahih that the Prophet (ﷺ) said about Maymunah's sheep: "Would that you had benefited from its hide?" They said: "O Messenger of God, it is carrion." He said: "Only its eating is forbidden," and bone is not eaten. We reply: bone is eaten, especially the bone of a suckling lamb, a kid and birds, and the bone of a grown animal is roasted and eaten. What we mentioned earlier indicates that life is present in it, and what is pure by life and permitted by slaughter becomes impure by death. And God knows best.

The fourth issue: God's words ﴿from the skins of cattle﴾ are general concerning the skin of the living and the dead, so it is permissible to benefit from the skins of dead animals even if they are not tanned. This is also the view of Ibn Shihab al-Zuhri and al-Layth ibn Saʿd. Al-Tahawi said: we have not found any of the jurists permitting the sale of carrion skin before tanning except al-Layth. Abu ʿUmar said: he means among the jurists, the leading muftis of the cities after the Successors. As for Ibn Shihab, that is authentically transmitted from him, and it is the view that the majority of scholars adopted. Views opposite to these two have also been transmitted from them, but the first is more famous. I say: al-Daraqutni mentioned in his Sunan the hadith of Yahya ibn Ayyub from Yunus and ʿUqayl from al-Zuhri, and the hadith of Baqiyyah from al-Zubaydi, and the hadith of Muhammad ibn Kathir al-ʿAbdi and Abu Salamah al-Minqari from Sulayman ibn Kathir from al-Zuhri, and he said at the end of them: these chains are sound.

The sixth issue: The scholars differed over whether the skin of carrion becomes pure when tanned. Ibn ʿAbd al-Hakam transmitted from Malik something resembling the view of Ibn Shihab on this. Ibn Khuwayz Mindad mentioned it in his book from Ibn ʿAbd al-Hakam as well. Ibn Khuwayz Mindad said: this is the view of al-Zuhri and al-Layth. He said: the apparent position of Malik's school is what Ibn ʿAbd al-Hakam mentioned, namely that tanning does not purify carrion skin, but it permits its use in dry things, and one may not pray upon it or eat from it. In the Mudawwanah of Ibn al-Qasim: whoever usurps an untanned carrion skin and destroys it must pay its value, and he related this as Malik's view. Abu al-Faraj mentioned that Malik said: whoever usurps an untanned carrion skin belonging to a man, there is nothing owed on him. Ismaʿil said: unless it belonged to a Magian. Ibn Wahb and Ibn ʿAbd al-Hakam transmitted from Malik the permissibility of selling it, and this applies to the skin of every carrion except the pig alone, because slaughter has no effect on it, so tanning is more fitting. Abu ʿUmar said: every slaughtered skin may be used for ablution and other purposes. Malik disliked performing ablution from a vessel made of carrion skin after tanning, with variation in his statements, and once he said he disliked it only for himself personally. Prayer upon such a skin is disliked, and so is selling it, and a group of his companions followed him in this. But most of the people of Madinah permit and allow it, relying on the Messenger of God's (ﷺ) saying: "Any hide that has been tanned has become pure." On this view are most of the people of the Hijaz and Iraq among the scholars of jurisprudence and hadith. It is also the view chosen by Ibn Wahb.

The seventh issue: Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal, may God be pleased with him, held that it is not permissible to benefit from the skins of carrion in anything even if tanned, because it is like the flesh of carrion. The reports permitting benefit after tanning refute his view. He argued with the hadith of ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUkaym, related by Abu Dawud, who said: The letter of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was read to us in the land of Juhaynah, while I was a young man: "Do not benefit from carrion through any hide or sinew." In another report: "a month before his death." This was related by al-Qasim ibn Mukhaymirah from ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUkaym, who said: some elders of ours told us that the Prophet (ﷺ) wrote to them... Dawud ibn ʿAli said: I asked Yahya ibn Maʿin about this hadith, and he weakened it and said: it is worth nothing; he only says "some elders told me." Abu ʿUmar said: even if it were established, it would be possible that it contradicts the hadiths transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿA'ishah, Salamah ibn al-Muhabbaq and others, because it is possible that the meaning of the hadith of Ibn ʿUkaym, "Do not benefit from carrion through any hide," refers to before tanning. And since it can be understood as not contradicting, why should we take it as contradicting? We must apply both reports as far as possible. And the hadith of ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUkaym, even if it was a month before the Prophet's (ﷺ) death as the report says, it is possible that the incident of Maymunah and Ibn ʿAbbas's hearing from him, "Any hide that has been tanned has become pure," was a week before his death or less than a week. And God knows best.

The eighth issue: The well-known view among us is that the skin of a pig does not fall under the hadith and is not covered by its generality, and likewise the dog according to al-Shafiʿi. According to al-Awzaʿi and Abu Thawr: only the skin of an animal whose flesh is eaten becomes pure by tanning. Maʿn ibn ʿIsa transmitted from Malik that he was asked about the skin of a pig when tanned, and he disliked it. Ibn Wadah said: I heard Sahnun say there is no harm in it. Muhammad ibn ʿAbd al-Hakam, Dawud ibn ʿAli and his companions also said the same, based on his (peace be upon him) saying: "Any skin (maskin) that has been tanned has become pure." Abu ʿUmar said: it is possible that he intended by this statement the generality of skins whose use is customary, whereas the pig is not included in this meaning, because the use of its skin is not customary, since slaughter has no effect on it. Another evidence is what al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: the ihab is the skin of cattle, sheep and camels, and whatever else is called only "jild" (skin), not "ihab." I say: the skin of the dog and of every animal whose flesh is not eaten is also not customarily used, so it does not become pure. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Eating every fanged beast of prey is forbidden," so slaughter does not apply to them, just as slaughter does not apply to the pig. Al-Nasaʾi related from al-Miqdam ibn Maʿdi Karib who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) forbade silk, gold and the saddle-cushions of panther skins." [[That is, forbidden to spread their skins over saddles and riding gear for sitting on them, because of the pride it involves, or because it is a custom of the non-Arabs, or because the hair is impure and does not accept tanning. (From the commentary on Sunan al-Nasaʾi.) Al-mayathir: stuffed hides placed on a saddle.]]

The ninth issue: The jurists differed over what tanning is by which the skins of carrion become pure. The companions of Malik, and this is the well-known view of his school, said: anything that tans the hide, whether salt, qarazh, alum or otherwise, makes its use permissible. Abu Hanifa and his companions said the same, and it is the view of Dawud. Al-Shafiʿi has two opinions on this question: one of them is this, and the other is that only alum and qarazh purify, because that is the tanning known in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ). On this basis al-Khattabi, God knows best, explained what al-Nasaʾi related from Maymunah, the wife of the Prophet (ﷺ), that some men of Quraysh passed by the Messenger of God (ﷺ) dragging a sheep of theirs, like a horse, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to them: "If only you had taken its hide." They said: "It is carrion." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Water and qarazh purify it."

The tenth issue: God's words ﴿athāthan﴾. Athāth means household goods; its singular is athāthah. This is the view of Abu Zayd al-Ansari. Al-Umawi said: athāth means household goods, and its plural is ātthah and uthuth. Others said: athāth is all kinds of property, and it has no singular from its own form. Al-Khalil said: its root is from abundance and the gathering of some goods upon others until they become many, and from it comes sha'r athīth, meaning abundant hair. Aththth hair of so-and-so yaʾuththu athththan when it becomes abundant and dense. Imru' al-Qays said:

"And a branch adorning the back, jet-black and thick, abundant like the clustered date-cluster."

"It is also said: al-athath is that which is worn and spread out (as bedding). One says ta'assathtu when one acquires athath. And from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him), regarding "athathan," it means wealth (mal). The discussion of al-hin has already been mentioned [[See vol. 1, p. 321 and vol. 9, p. 360 onward.]], and here it is a time not fixed according to each person, either by his death or by the loss of those things which are athath. From this word is the saying of the poet:
Did the litters (of the women) stir your longing on the day they departed,
with the fine adornment of their athath?"

Concerning this verse there are six issues.

**The first issue:** His saying, exalted is He, ﴿shadows﴾ (*zilal*). *Zilal* refers to everything under which one seeks shade, such as houses and trees. His saying "of what He has created" (*mimma khalaqa*) encompasses all the shade-casting objects.

**The second issue:** His saying, exalted is He, "shelters" (*aknanan*). *Aknan* is the plural of *kinn*, which is that which protects from rain, wind and other things. Here it refers to caves in the mountains. God made them a refuge for creation, where they take shelter, fortify themselves, and withdraw from people. In the authentic collection it is reported that at the beginning of his mission, the Prophet (ﷺ) used to worship in the cave of Hira and would remain there for nights... (the hadith). In Sahih al-Bukhari it is related that he said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) left Mecca as an emigrant, fleeing from his people, fleeing with his religion, together with his companion Abu Bakr, until they reached a cave in Mount Thawr. They stayed there three nights. Abdullah ibn Abi Bakr, a young, intelligent, quick-witted lad, would spend the night with them there. He would leave them before dawn and be in Mecca with the Quraysh in the morning as one who had spent the night there. Whatever plot they were devising, he would hear it and remember it, and then bring them news of it when darkness fell. Amir ibn Fuhayra, the freedman of Abu Bakr, would graze a milch sheep for them and bring it to them at the time when part of the night had passed, so they would spend the night with its milk and its heated milk, until Amir ibn Fuhayra would call to them at the first light of dawn. He did this every night of those three nights... and he mentioned the hadith. It was narrated by al-Bukhari alone.

**The third issue:** His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and He has made for you garments that protect you from the heat﴾. This means shirts, the singular of which is *sirbal*.

"And garments that protect you from your violence" means coats of mail that protect people in war. From this is the saying of Ka'b ibn Zuhayr:

*Lofty of noses, heroes whose armour*
*Is of the weaving of David, are coats of mail in the battle.*

**The fourth issue:** If someone asks: Why did He say "from the mountains, shelters" and not mention the plains, and say "that protect you from the heat" without mentioning the cold? The answer is that they were people of mountains and not people of plains, and they were people of heat and not people of cold. So He mentioned to them the blessings that are specific to them, just as He singled them out by mentioning wool and other things. He did not mention cotton, linen or snow, as has been stated before, because these were not in their land. This was said by Ata al-Khurasani and others. [Editor's note: God mentioned those blessings, which indicate what corresponds to them, by way of sufficiency. Cotton is famous in Yemen, and from it come the Sahuli garments, and likewise Sahar, from which the shroud of the Prophet, peace be upon him, was made of two Saharian cloths. Likewise snow is found in the mountains of the Arabian lands.] Also, mention of one of two things indicates the other. From this is the saying of the poet:

*I do not know, when I head towards a land*
*Seeking good, which of the two will take hold of me:*
*Is it the good that I seek,*
*Or the evil that seeks me?*

**The fifth issue:** The scholars said: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and garments that protect you from your violence﴾ is evidence for the servants taking up the equipment of jihad, so that they may be helped by it in fighting enemies. The Prophet (ﷺ) wore armour to protect himself from injury, although he sought martyrdom. But it is not for the servant to seek it by surrendering to death, to spear thrusts, or to sword blows. Rather, he wears the war gear (*lamat harb*), which is his equipment, so that he may have strength to fight his enemy, and he fights so that the word of God may be supreme, and God then does what He wills.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 16, Verse 90:**

This passage contains six issues.

**The first issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands justice and excellence﴾. It is narrated from ʿUthman ibn Mazʿun that he said: "When this verse was revealed, I recited it to ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, and he was amazed and said: 'O family of Ghalib, follow him and you will prosper. By Allah, Allah sent him to command you with noble character.'"

In a hadith: "When Abu Talib was told, 'Your nephew claims that Allah revealed to him, "Indeed, Allah commands justice and excellence," [and the rest of the verse],' he said: 'Follow my nephew, for by Allah, he commands only the finest of character.'"

ʿIkrimah said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) recited to al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, 'Indeed, Allah commands justice and excellence,' up to its end. He said: 'O nephew, repeat it!' So he repeated it to him, and he said: 'By Allah, it has a sweetness, and it has a radiance, its root is fruitful and its branches bear fruit, and it is not the words of a human being!'"

Al-Ghaznawi mentioned that ʿUthman ibn Mazʿun was the one who recited it. ʿUthman said: "I did not embrace Islam at the outset except out of shyness before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), until this verse was revealed while I was with him, and faith settled in my heart. I recited it to al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, and he said: 'O nephew, repeat it!' So I repeated it, and he said: 'By Allah, it has a sweetness...'" and he mentioned the rest of the report.

Ibn Masʿud said: "This is the most comprehensive verse in the Qur'an for good to be enacted and for evil to be avoided."

Al-Naqqash related: "It is said: the zakat of justice is excellence (ihsan), the zakat of power is pardon, the zakat of wealth is kindness, and the zakat of status is writing on behalf of a man to his brothers."

**The second issue:** The scholars differed in interpreting "justice" (ʿadl) and "excellence" (ihsan). Ibn ʿAbbas said: "Justice is 'There is no god but Allah,' and excellence is performing the obligatory duties (fara'id)." It was also said: "Justice is the obligatory (fard), and excellence is the supererogatory (nafilah)." Sufyan ibn ʿUyayna said: "Justice here is the equality of the inner self, and excellence is that the inner self be better than the outward appearance." ʿAli ibn Abi Talib said: "Justice is fairness, and excellence is going beyond what is due."

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: "Justice is everything obligatory, in terms of beliefs and laws, in fulfilling trusts, abandoning oppression, being fair, and giving what is due. Excellence is doing everything recommended. Among things, some are entirely recommended and some are obligatory, except that the minimum of performance in them falls under justice, while the perfection beyond the minimum falls under excellence. As for the statement of Ibn ʿAbbas, it is open to scrutiny, because performing the obligatory duties is Islam as the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) explained it in the hadith of Gabriel's questioning, and that is justice. Excellence is rather the perfections and what is recommended, as the explanation of the Prophet (ﷺ) in the hadith of Gabriel's questioning requires, with his saying: 'It is that you worship Allah as if you see Him, and if you do not see Him, indeed He sees you.' If this is authentically from Ibn ʿAbbas, then he meant the obligations in their perfected form."

Ibn al-ʿArabi said: "Justice between the servant and his Lord is preferring His right over the servant's own portion, preferring His pleasure over his desire, refraining from what is forbidden, and complying with His commands. As for justice between a person and himself, it is restraining the self from what leads to its ruin. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And restrained the self from desire﴾ [79:40]. It is also turning away greed from what is not one's own and holding to contentment in every state and meaning. As for justice between a person and creation, it is giving sincere counsel, abandoning betrayal in matters great and small, being fair to them in every way, not causing harm to anyone by word or deed, either in secret or in public, and patiently enduring the trials one suffers from them. At the least, that is fairness and refraining from harm."

I say: This detailed explanation of justice is good and just. As for excellence, our scholars said: "Excellence (ihsan) is the verbal noun of 'ahsana, yuhsinu, ihsanan.' It is used in two senses. The first is transitive without a preposition, as in your saying: 'I beautified such-and-such,' meaning I made it good and perfected it; this is derived with the hamza from hassana al-shay'. The second is transitive with a preposition, as in your saying: 'I did good to so-and-so,' meaning I delivered to him what benefits him." I say: In this verse it is intended in both senses together. Allah, exalted is He, loves from His creation that some of them do good to others, to the extent that the bird in your cage and the cat in your house should not be neglected in your care and kindness. He, exalted is He, is independent of their kindness. From this comes the meaning of kindness, favours, bounty and graces. In the hadith of Gabriel it is in the first sense, not the second, for the first sense refers to perfecting worship and observing it through performing it correctly and completely, watching over the truth in it, and recalling His greatness and majesty at the beginning and throughout. This is what is meant by his saying: "that you worship Allah as if you see Him, and if you do not see Him, indeed He sees you."

People of the heart are in this vigilance in two states. In one, the witnessing of the Truth prevails over them, so it is as if they see Him. Perhaps the Prophet (ﷺ) pointed to this state with his saying: "The coolness of my eyes has been placed in prayer." In the other, they do not reach this level, but what predominates over them is that the Truth, glorified is He, is watching them and present to them. To this refers the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿Who sees you when you stand [in prayer], and your movements among those who prostrate﴾ [26:218–219]. And His saying: ﴿We were witnesses over you when you were engaged in it﴾ [10:61].

**The third issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and giving to relatives (dhi al-qurba)﴾, meaning kinsfolk. He says: "He gives them wealth, as He said: ﴿and give the kinsman his right﴾ [17:26]," meaning his support (silah). This is of the category of mentioning what is recommended after what is obligatory. Al-Shafiʿi used it as evidence for the obligation of giving to the mukatab (a slave contracted to purchase his freedom), as will be explained. He specifically mentioned relatives because their rights are more emphatic and their maintenance more obligatory, given the emphasis on the rights of kinship (rahim), whose name Allah derived from His own name and whose maintenance He made from His own maintenance. He said in the authentic hadith: "Are you not pleased that I join whoever joins you and sever whoever severs you?" (Sahih al-Bukhari, Tafsir, in the chapter on Surah Muhammad; and Sahih Muslim, Adab). This is especially so when they are poor.

**The fourth issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and forbids indecency, wrongdoing and oppression﴾. Al-fahsha' is al-fuhsh, which is every ugly thing, whether in speech or action. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "It is fornication." Al-munkar is what the Law has denounced by prohibiting it, and it encompasses all sins, vices and base conduct in their various kinds. It was said that it is polytheism (shirk). Al-baghy is pride, injustice, malice and transgression, and its reality is exceeding the limit. It falls under the category of munkar, but Allah, exalted is He, singled it out for mention out of concern with it because of the severity of its harm.

In a hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ): "No sin is punished more swiftly than oppression (baghy)." He (peace be upon him) also said: "The oppressor will be struck down." Allah has promised victory to whoever is wronged. In some of the revealed books it is said: "If one mountain oppressed another mountain, the oppressor from them would be crushed to dust."

**The fifth issue:** Imam Abu ʿAbd Allah Muhammad ibn Isma'il al-Bukhari entitled a chapter in his Sahih: "Chapter on the saying of Allah, exalted is He: 'Indeed, Allah commands justice and excellence and giving to relatives, and forbids indecency, wrongdoing and oppression; He admonishes you that you may remember'" [16:90], and His saying: "Your oppression is only against yourselves" [10:23], and "Whoever is wronged, Allah will surely help him" [22:60], and abandoning stirring up evil against a Muslim or a disbeliever. Then he mentioned the hadith of ʿAʾisha concerning the sorcery of Labid ibn al-Asam against the Prophet (ﷺ).

Ibn Battal said: "Al-Bukhari, may Allah be pleased with him, interpreted from these verses the abandonment of stirring up evil against a Muslim or a disbeliever, as the hadith of ʿAʾisha indicates, where he (peace be upon him) said: 'As for Allah, He has cured me, and as for me, I dislike stirring up evil among the people.'" The point of this, and Allah knows best, is that he interpreted in the saying of Allah, exalted is He, "Indeed, Allah commands justice and excellence," the recommendation of excellence toward the one who does evil and the abandonment of punishing him for his evil. If it is asked: "How does this interpretation fit the verses on oppression?" It is answered: The point of this, and Allah knows best, is that when Allah informed His servants that the harm of oppression returns upon the oppressor, by His saying: "Your oppression is only against yourselves," and guaranteed the victory of whoever is wronged, it was more fitting for the one wronged to thank Allah for what He guaranteed of His help, and to respond to that by pardoning the one who wronged him. This is what the Prophet (ﷺ) did with the Jew who bewitched him, although he had the right to retaliate against him by the saying: "And if you retaliate, then retaliate with the like of that by which you were harmed" [16:126]. Yet he preferred forgiveness, following His saying: "But whoever is patient and forgives, indeed that is of the matters requiring determination" [42:43].

**The sixth issue:** This verse includes the enjoining of good and the forbidding of evil, and the discussion of both has already been presented. It is narrated that a group of people brought their governor (ʿamil) before Abu Jaʿfar al-Mansur al-ʿAbbasi. The governor argued against them and prevailed over them, since they did not establish against him any great injustice or any oppression in anything. Then a young man from among the people stood up and said: "O Commander of the Faithful, indeed Allah commands justice and excellence, and he has been just but has not been excellent." Abu Jaʿfar was amazed at his correctness and dismissed the governor.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 16, verse 91:

There are three issues (masa'il) in this.

The first: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And fulfil the covenant of Allah﴾. It is a general term covering everything that is contracted by the tongue and that a person binds himself to, such as a sale, a tie of kinship, or a pact concerning a matter that accords with the religion. This verse is an elaboration (mudammin) of His saying: "Indeed, Allah commands justice and good conduct" (16:90), because its meaning is: do such-and-such, and refrain from such-and-such, so it is conjoined to that implied sense. It has been said that it was revealed concerning the pledge of allegiance (bay'ah) of the Prophet ﷺ to Islam. It has also been said that it was revealed concerning adherence to the alliance (hilf) that existed in the Jahiliyyah, and Islam came with its fulfilment; this was said by Qatadah, Mujahid and Ibn Zayd. The generality encompasses all of that, as we have explained.

The sound (Sahih) collection narrates from Jubayr ibn Mut'im, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "There is no alliance in Islam, and whatever alliance existed in the Jahiliyyah, Islam has only increased it in strength," meaning in supporting the truth, standing by it and in mutual aid. This is like the Alliance of the Virtuous (Hilf al-Fudul), which Ibn Ishaq mentioned. He said: Several clans of Quraysh gathered in the house of Abdullah ibn Jud'an because of his nobility and lineage [[In the Sirah of Ibn Hisham: "because of his nobility and customs."]], and they made a pact and covenanted together that they would not find anyone wronged in Makkah, from its people or from others, without standing with him until his wrong was restored to him. Quraysh named that alliance Hilf al-Fudul, that is, the Alliance of Virtues. Al-Fudul here is the plural of fadl for multiplicity, like fals and fulus.

Ibn Ishaq narrated from Ibn Shihab, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "I witnessed in the house of Abdullah ibn Jud'an an alliance that I would not love to have in exchange for red camels; were I invited to it in Islam, I would respond."

Ibn Ishaq said: Al-Walid ibn Utbah oppressed Husayn ibn Ali concerning some property of his, by virtue of al-Walid's authority, for he was governor of Madinah. Husayn ibn Ali said to him: "I swear by Allah, you will either give me justice regarding my right, or I will take my sword, then I will stand in the Mosque of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and then I will call upon the Alliance of the Virtuous." Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr said: "And I swear by Allah, if he calls upon it, I will take my sword and stand with him until he is given justice regarding his right, or we all die." The news reached al-Miswar ibn Makhramah, and he said the same. The news reached Abd al-Rahman ibn Uthman ibn Ubayd Allah al-Taymi, and he said the same. When this reached al-Walid, he did him justice.

The scholars said: This alliance which existed in the Jahiliyyah is the one that Islam confirmed, and the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, excepted it from the generality of his saying: "There is no alliance in Islam." The wisdom in this is that the Law came with taking retribution from the oppressor, taking the right from him and delivering it to the one wronged. Through the foundation of the Shariah, this was made a general obligation upon whoever among the responsible persons is able, and He made a way for them against the oppressors. He, exalted is He, said: "The way is only against those who wrong people and transgress in the earth without right; those will have a painful punishment" (42:42) [[See vol. 16, p. 44.]].

In the Sahih (from his saying [[min: wa]]): "Support your brother, whether he is an oppressor or oppressed." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, we support him when he is oppressed, but how do we support him when he is an oppressor?" He said: "You restrain him from his hands" (in another narration: "you prevent him from oppression"), for that is supporting him. And his peace be upon him earlier said: "When people see the oppressor and do not restrain his hands, Allah is about to encompass them all with a punishment from Him."

The second: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not break the oaths after their confirmation﴾. It means after their strengthening and emphasis. It is said: tawkid and ta'kid, and wakkada and akkada; these are two dialects.

The third: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you have indeed made Allah your surety over you﴾. It means a witness. It is also said: a guardian, and it is said: a guarantor.

He said "after their confirmation" to distinguish between an oath confirmed by resolve and the idle oath (laghw al-yamin). Ibn Wahb and Ibn al-Qasim said, from Malik: tawkid is a person swearing about a single matter repeatedly, repeating the oaths three times or more, such as saying: "By Allah, I will not diminish it from such-and-such; by Allah, I will not diminish it from such-and-such; by Allah, I will not diminish it from such-and-such." He said: the expiation for that is one, like the expiation for an oath. Yahya ibn Sa'id said: they are covenants, and a covenant is an oath, but the difference between them is that a covenant is not expiated. The Prophet ﷺ said: "On the Day of Resurrection a banner will be raised for every treacherous person at his backside, according to the measure of his treachery; it will be said: this is the treachery of so-and-so."

As for an oath by Allah, Allah, glorified is He, has prescribed expiation for it with one act, and what the oath was bound to becomes permissible. Ibn Umar said: tawkid is that one swears twice; if he swears once, there is no expiation for it. This has been mentioned in al-Ma'idah [[See vol. 6, p. 364.]].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 16, verse 92:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And do not be like her who undoes her spinning after it had been made strong, into threads (ankathan)﴾. The naqd (undoing) and the nakth (breaking) are one and the same; the noun is nikth and naqd, and the plural is ankath. This verse likens the one who swears, makes a covenant, confirms his pledge, and then breaks it, to the woman who spins her thread, twists it firmly, and then unravels it.

It is narrated that there was a foolish woman in Makkah called Rayta, daughter of Amr ibn Ka'b ibn Sa'd ibn Taym ibn Murrah, who used to do this, and the comparison was made with her. Al-Farra' said, and Abdullah ibn Kathir and al-Suddi related it, but they did not name the woman. Mujahid and Qatadah said: this is a parable (darb mathal), not referring to a specific woman.

Ankathan is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). And al-Dakhal (dakhal): al-daghal (deceit), al-khida' (trickery), and al-ghishsh (cheating). Abu Ubaydah said: every matter that is not sound is dakhal.

(That one community should be more numerous than another community.) The commentators said: this verse was revealed concerning the Arabs, among whom a tribe would make an alliance with another tribe, and then a larger and stronger tribe came, so one of the two allies entered into alliance with it (dakhalat-hā), betrayed the first, broke its covenant and returned to this greater one. This was said by Mujahid. So Allah, exalted is He, said: Do not break the covenants because one group is more numerous than another or has more wealth, so that you break your oaths when you see abundance and ease in the world possessed by your idolatrous enemies. The intent is the prohibition of returning to disbelief because of the multitude of the disbelievers and the abundance of their wealth. Al-Farra' said: the meaning is, do not betray a people because of your fewness and their multitude, or because of your multitude and their fewness, when you have confirmed the covenant with them by oaths.

(Arba) means akthar (more), from raba al-shay yarbu, when a thing increases. The pronoun in "bihi" may refer to the fulfilment of the covenant that Allah commanded. It may also refer to riba' (the excess or greater number), meaning that Allah, exalted is He, tested His servants with envy and with some of them seeking to dominate others, and He tested them thereby, distinguishing one who strives against his self and opposes it from one who follows it and acts according to the dictates of its desire. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿Allah only tests you thereby, and He will surely make clear to you on the Day of Resurrection that about which you used to differ﴾, concerning the resurrection and other matters.

"Concerning His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if Allah had willed, He would have made you one community﴾, that is, upon one religion.

(But He causes to go astray whom He wills) by forsaking them, as a matter of His justice concerning them.

(And He guides whom He wills) by granting them success, as a matter of His grace upon them. ﴿He is not questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned﴾. The verse refutes the Qadariyya (al-Qadariyya), as has already been mentioned. The lam in ﴿wa-la-yubayyinanna﴾ and ﴿wa-latus'alunna﴾ together with the heavy nun indicate an implied oath, meaning: "By Allah, He will surely make [it] clear to you, and you will surely be questioned."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 16, verse 94:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not take your oaths as means of deception among yourselves﴾. He repeated this for emphasis.

(Lest a foot slip after it was firm) — an intensification in prohibiting it, given the great weight it carries in the religion and how often it recurs in people's dealings. That is, do not conclude oaths while harboring deceit and corruption, lest a foot slip after it was firm, i.e., from the oaths after knowledge of Allah. This is a metaphor for one who is upright in condition and then falls into great evil and collapses into it, because when a foot slips it moves a person from a state of good to a state of evil. From this meaning is the saying of Kuthayyir:

"When we met, you stood firm, and I slipped."

The Arabs say of everyone afflicted after well-being, or who falls into a predicament: "His foot slipped," as in the saying of the poet:

"The race will be denied you if you were a leader... and you will be killed if both feet slip under you."

It is said of one who erred in something: "He slipped in it." Then, exalted is He, threatened afterward with punishment in this world and a great punishment in the Hereafter. This threat applies only to those who break the covenant of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), for whoever pledged allegiance to him and then broke his pledge has left the faith. For this reason He said: ﴿and taste the evil for what you have averted from the way of Allah﴾, i.e., because of your averting. The tasting of evil in this world is the disagreeable things that befall them.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 16, verse 95–96:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And do not exchange the covenant of Allah for a small price﴾. He forbade bribery and taking wealth in exchange for breaking the covenant, meaning: do not break your covenants for a small gain of this world. It is called "small" even if it is great, because it is subject to passing away, so in reality it is small. This is what is meant by His saying: "What you have will be exhausted, and what is with Allah is lasting." Thus He distinguished between the state of this world and the state of the Hereafter: this world is exhausted and transformed, whereas what is with Allah of the bounties of His grace and the bliss of His Garden is enduring and does not pass away, for those who fulfil the covenant and remain steadfast in the contract. How well has the one said:

"Wealth is exhausted, both its lawful and its unlawful, one day, and its sins remain for the morrow."

"The pious one is not truly pious toward his Lord... until his drink and his food are wholesome."

Another said:

"Suppose the world is driven to you willingly; is not its outcome a passing away?
And your worldly life is only like a cloud that shades you, then announces its departure."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We will surely reward those who are patient﴾, meaning patient upon Islam and the acts of obedience and against sins, meaning from the acts of obedience. He made it "best" because whatever else is good is permissible, while reward is only for acts of obedience, by way of Allah's promise. ʿĀṣim and Ibn Kathīr read "wa-linajziyanna" with the nūn, as an expression of magnification; the rest read it with the yāʾ. It was said that this verse, "And do not exchange," was revealed concerning Imru' al-Qays ibn ʿĀbis al-Kindī and his opponent Ibn Aswaʿ, who disputed over land. Imru' al-Qays wanted to swear an oath, but when he heard this verse he refrained and acknowledged his right to it. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 16, verse 97:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while he is a believer – We will surely cause him to live a good life﴾ is a conditional clause (shart) and its response (jawab).

Concerning "the good life" (al-hayat al-tayyibah) there are five opinions:

The first: it is lawful provision (al-rizq al-halal). This was said by Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ata' and al-Dahhak.

The second: contentment (al-qana'ah). This was said by al-Hasan al-Basri, Zayd ibn Wahb and Wahb ibn Munabbih, and al-Hakam narrated it from Ikrimah from Ibn Abbas. It is also the saying of Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him.

The third: that He grants him success in acts of obedience, for these lead him to the pleasure of Allah. al-Dahhak said this in meaning. He also said: Whoever does righteousness while he is a believer, in poverty or in ease, his life is good; and whoever turns away from the remembrance of Allah, does not believe in his Lord, and does not do righteousness, his livelihood is straitened (dank), with no good in it.

Mujahid, Qatadah and Ibn Zayd said: it is Paradise. al-Hasan also said this, and said: life is not made good for anyone except in Paradise.

It was also said: it is happiness (al-sa'adah), narrated from Ibn Abbas as well. Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: it is the sweetness of obedience. Sahl ibn Abd Allah al-Tustari said: it is that the servant's own management is removed from him and his management is returned to the Truth. Ja'far al-Sadiq said: it is the knowledge of Allah and sincerity in standing before Allah.

It was said: it is independence from creation and need of the Truth. It was said: it is contentment with the decree.

(And We will surely reward them their wage) meaning in the Hereafter,

(according to the best of what they used to do). He said "fa-lanuhyiyannahu" and then said "wa-lanajziyannahum," because "man" can apply to the singular and the plural, so He returned once to the wording and once to the meaning. This has been discussed earlier.

Abu Salih said: some people of the Torah, some people of the Gospel and some people of the idols sat together. These said: "We are the best," and those said: "We are the best," so it was revealed.

There is one issue here: this verse is connected to His saying, "And We have sent down to you the Book as an explanation of all things" (16:89). So when you begin to recite it, seek refuge in Allah from Satan lest he present himself to you and divert you from reflecting upon it and acting by what is in it. It does not mean "seek refuge after the recitation." Rather, it is like your saying, "When you eat, say Bismillah," meaning, when you intend to eat.

Jubayr ibn Mut'im narrated from his father, who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when he began the prayer say: 'Allahumma inni a'udhu bika min ash-shaytan, min hamzihi, wa nafkhihi, wa nafthihi'" [[al-Hamz: the prodding and pricking; and everything you push is hamaztahu. An-Nafkh: arrogance, because the arrogant person magnifies himself and gathers his self and his self, so he needs to puff up. An-Nafth: Ibn al-Athir said: its explanation came in the hadith that it is poetry, because it is blown from the mouth.]].

And Abu Sa'id al-Khudri narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to seek refuge in his prayer before the recitation.

Al-Kiya al-Tabari said: It has been reported from some of the early scholars (salaf) that seeking refuge is after the recitation absolutely, citing His saying, "So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan" (16:98). There is no doubt that the apparent meaning of this requires that seeking refuge be after the recitation, like His saying, "So when you have finished the prayer, remember Allah standing, sitting, and lying on your sides" (4:103) [[See vol. 5, p. 373.]]. However, other readings are possible, such as His saying, "And when you speak, be just" [[See vol. 7, p. 137.]], and "And when you ask them for something, ask them from behind a screen" (33:53) [[See vol. 14, p. 227.]]. It is not meant that one asks her from behind a screen after a previous request. Similar to this is the saying of someone: "When you speak, be truthful," and "When you enter the state of ihram, perform ghusl," meaning before ihram. The meaning in all of these is: when you intend that, (do it). Likewise, seeking refuge. This meaning has already been mentioned [[See vol. 6, p. 80.]], and the discussion of seeking refuge has been covered fully [[See vol. 1, p. 86.]].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 16, verse 99–100:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, he has no authority over those who believe﴾, i.e., by misguidance and disbelief; that is, you have no power to lead them to a sin that will not be forgiven. This was said by Sufyan. Mujahid said: he has no proof for what he calls them to of disobedience. It was also said: he has no authority over them in any way, because Allah, exalted is He, removed his authority over them when the enemy of Allah, Iblis, may Allah curse him, said: "And I will surely mislead them all, except Your sincere servants among them" [[See vol. 27 of this part and what follows.]]. Allah, exalted is He, said: "Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them, except those who follow you of the misguided." I say: We have explained that this is a general statement that admits specification, and he misled Adam and Eve, peace be upon them, by his authority; and he troubled the virtuous scholars' times with his saying: "Who created your Lord?" as has preceded at the end of al-A'raf [[See vol. 7, p. 348.]], its explanation.

(Indeed, his authority is only over those who take him as a protector) i.e., those who obey him. It is said: "tawallaytuhu" means I obeyed him, and "tawallaytu 'anhu" means I turned away from him.

(And those who associate others with Him) i.e., with Allah. This was said by Mujahid and al-Dahhak. It was also said: the pronoun "bihi" refers to Satan; this was said by al-Rabi' ibn Anas and al-Qutabi. The meaning is: those who, because of him, are associates (of Allah). It is said: "kafartu bihadhihi al-kalimah," meaning because of this word; and "sara fulan bika 'aliman," meaning because of you. That is: those who take Satan as protector are polytheists with Allah.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 16, verse 99–100:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, he has no authority over those who believe﴾, i.e., by misguidance and disbelief; that is, you have no power to lead them to a sin that will not be forgiven. (And those who associate others with Him) i.e., with Allah. This was said by Mujahid and al-Dahhak. It was also said: the pronoun "bihi" refers to Satan; this was said by al-Rabi' ibn Anas and al-Qutabi. The meaning is: those who, because of him, are associates (of Allah). It is said: "kafartu bihadhihi al-kalimah," meaning because of this word; and "sara fulan bika 'aliman," meaning because of you. That is: those who take Satan as protector are polytheists with Allah.

The commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 16, verses 101–102:

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And when We substitute a verse in place of another verse, and Allah knows best what He sends down﴾. It was said: the meaning is that We replaced a earlier law with a newly established law; this was said by Ibn Bahr. Mujahid said: that is, We lifted a verse and put another in its place. The majority (al-Jumhur) said: We abrogated (naskh) a verse with a verse harsher for them than it. Naskh and tabdil are the removal of a thing while placing something other than it in its place. The discussion of naskh has already been covered fully in al-Baqarah [see vol. 2, p. 61 and following].

(They say) means the disbelievers of Quraysh.

(You are only a fabricator) means a liar, an inventor, because of what they saw of the change of a ruling. So Allah said: (Rather, most of them do not know) that Allah legislates rulings and substitutes some for others. And His words: (Say: The Holy Spirit has brought it down) refers to Jibril, who brought down the whole Qur'an, its abrogating and abrogated parts. It is narrated with a sound chain from ʿAmir al-Shaʿbi, who said: Israfil was entrusted with Muhammad (ﷺ) for three years, bringing him a word and a word, then Jibril descended to him with the Qur'an. Also in Sahih Muslim it is related that a angel who had never descended to the earth came down to him with the surah "al-Hamd", as its explanation was already given under al-Fatihah [see vol. 1, p. 116].

(From your Lord in truth) means from the speech of your Lord.

(To make firm those who believe) means by what it contains of proofs and signs.

(And a guidance) means and it is guidance.

(And good tidings for the Muslims).
