Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 16, verse 103:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We know that they say, "It is only a human being who teaches him."﴾ There is disagreement about the name of the person they claimed was teaching him. It is said that he was a slave of al-Fakih ibn al-Mughirah, whose name was Jabr. He had been a Christian and had become a Muslim. Whenever they heard the Prophet (ﷺ) relate what had passed and what was yet to come, even though he was unlettered and could not read, they said: "It is only Jabr who teaches him, and he is a non-Arab (a'jami)." Then Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿The tongue of the one they point to is foreign, while this is a clear Arabic tongue.﴾ That is: how could Jabr teach him this speech, when Jabr is a non-Arab, the speech that neither humans nor jinn can produce the like of, even a single surah or anything beyond it?

Al-Naqqash mentioned that the master of Jabr used to beat him and say to him: "You are teaching Muhammad!" He would reply: "No, by Allah, rather he is teaching me and guiding me."

Ibn Ishaq said: The Prophet (ﷺ), as has reached me, often used to sit near al-Marwah beside a Christian boy called Jabr, a slave of the Banu al-Hadrami, who used to read the scriptures. The polytheists said: "By Allah, Muhammad is not taught what he brings except by Jabr the Christian."

Ikrimah said: His name was Ya'ish, a slave of the Banu al-Hadrami. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to teach him the Qur'an. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

Al-Tha'labi related from Ikrimah and Qatadah that he was a boy belonging to the Banu al-Mughirah named Ya'ish, who used to read the foreign scriptures. Quraysh said: "It is only a human being who teaches him," and so this was revealed.

Al-Mahdawi related from Ikrimah: He was a boy belonging to the Banu 'Amir ibn Lu'ayy, and his name was Ya'ish.

'Abd Allah ibn Muslim al-Hadrami said: We had two Christian boys from the people of 'Ayn al-Tamr, one named Yasar and the other named Jabr. So said al-Mawardi, al-Qushayri and al-Tha'labi, except that al-Tha'labi said: One of them was called Nabt and was known as Abu Fukayhah, and the other was Jabr. Both were sayqals (polishers of swords; sayqal: one who sharpens and polishes swords), working on swords, and they used to read a book of theirs. Al-Tha'labi said: They used to read the Torah and the Gospel. Al-Mawardi and al-Mahdawi said: the Torah. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would pass by them and hear their recitation, and the polytheists would say: "He is learning from them." So Allah revealed this verse and refuted them.

It was also said: They meant Salman al-Farisi, may Allah be pleased with him; this was said by al-Dahhak.

It was also said: A Christian in Mecca named Bal'am, who was a boy reading the Torah; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas. The polytheists used to see the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when he entered upon him and when he left from his presence, and they said: "It is only Bal'am who teaches him."

Al-Qutaybi said: In Mecca there was a Christian man called Abu Maysarah who spoke in Roman (Greek) language. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would sometimes sit with him, and the unbelievers said: "Muhammad only learns from him," and so this was revealed. In another report, it was 'Addas, the slave of 'Utbah ibn Rabi'ah. It was also said: 'Abis, the slave of Huwaytib ibn 'Abd al-'Uzza, and Yasar, Abu Fukayhah, a client of Ibn al-Hadrami; both of them had embraced Islam. And Allah knows best.

I say: All of these are possible, for the Prophet (ﷺ) may have sat with them at different times in order to teach them from what Allah had taught him, and that was in Mecca. Al-Nahhas said: These statements are not contradictory, since it is possible that they pointed to all of these people and claimed that they were teaching him. I say: As for what al-Dahhak mentioned, that it was Salman, this is far-fetched, because Salman came to the Prophet (ﷺ) only in Medina, whereas this verse is Meccan.

(The tongue of the one they point to is foreign) Al-ilhad (ilhad: inclination, deviation) means to incline; it is said: lahada and alhada, meaning he deviated from the right course. This has already been discussed in al-A'raf (see vol. 7, p. 328). Hamzah read yalhadun with a fatha on the ya' and the ha', meaning: the tongue of the one they incline towards and point to is foreign.

Al-'ujmah (ujmah: concealment, and the opposite of clarity) means concealment. A man is a'jam and a woman 'ajam, meaning one who does not speak clearly. From this comes 'ujm al-dhanab (the tail's hidden end), because it is concealed. Al-'ajma' is the beast, because it does not make itself clear. A'jamtu al-kitab means I removed its obscurity (ujmah). The Arabs call anyone who does not know their language and does not speak their speech a'jami.

Al-Farra' said: The a'jam is one whose tongue has a foreignness in it even if he is of the Arabs, while the a'jami or 'ajami is one whose origin is from the 'Ajam (non-Arab peoples). Abu 'Ali said: The a'jami is one who does not speak clearly, whether he is of the Arabs or of the 'Ajam, and likewise the a'jam; and the a'jami is one ascribed to the 'Ajam even if he is eloquent.

By "tongue" He means the Qur'an, because the Arabs call a qasidah (ode) or a verse a "tongue." The poet said:

"A tongue of evil you present to us,
and you betrayed, and I did not think you would betray."

By "tongue" he means the qasidah.

﴿And this is a clear Arabic tongue﴾: that is, the most eloquent form of Arabic.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who do not believe in the signs of Allah﴾, that is, these polytheists who do not believe in the Qur'an (﴿Allah will not guide them, and for them is a painful punishment.﴾)

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 16, verse 105:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Only those fabricate lies who do not believe in the signs of Allah, and it is they who are the liars﴾ (105).

(His saying, exalted is He:) ﴿Only those fabricate lies who do not believe in the signs of Allah⦄ This is a response to their description of the Prophet (ﷺ) as a fabricator.

(And it is they who are the liars) This is an intensification in describing them as liars, meaning: every lie is small in comparison to their lying. It is said: "Fulan lied" (kadhaba fulan), but it is not said "he is a liar" (innahu kadhib) in the sense of an attribute, because the verb may be intransitive or not. As for the epithet (al-na't), it is a permanent attribute. For this reason it is said: "Adam disobeyed his Lord and went astray" (ʿasa Adamu rabbahu fa-ghawa), but it is not said: "He is disobedient and astray" (innahu ʿasin ghawin). So when it is said: "Fulan lied, so he is a liar" (kadhaba fulan fa-huwa kadhib), it is an intensification in describing him with lying. This was said by al-Qushayri.

There are twenty-one issues concerning this verse:

The First: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever disbelieves in Allah﴾. This is connected to His saying: "And do not break your oaths after confirming them." It is an intensification in describing (them) with lying, because its meaning is: do not turn back from the pledge to the Messenger (ﷺ), that is, whoever disbelieves after his belief and apostatizes, upon him is the wrath of Allah.

Al-Kalbi said: It was revealed concerning Abdullah ibn Abi Sarh, Muqays ibn Dababa, Abdullah ibn Khatal [[In the originals: "Abdullah ibn Ams ibn Khatal," which is a distortion.]], and Qays ibn al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, who disbelieved after their faith. Then he said: (Except one who has been forced).

Al-Zajjaj said: "Whoever disbelieves in Allah after his belief" is a substitute for "those who fabricate lies." That is, only those who disbelieve in Allah after their belief fabricate lies, because he saw that the speech was not complete up to the end of the exception, so he attached it to what came before it.

Al-Akhfash said: "Man" (whoever) is a beginning (subject), and its predicate is omitted; it has been sufficed by the predicate of the second "man," as in your saying: "Whoever comes to us, whoever is good, we honor him."

The Second: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿except one who has been forced﴾. This verse was revealed concerning Ammar ibn Yasir, according to the view of the scholars of tafsir (Qur'anic exegesis), because he came close to some of what they had urged him toward.

Ibn Abbas said: The polytheists seized him, and they seized his father and his mother Sumayya, and Suhayb, Bilal, Khabbab and Salim, and they tortured them. Sumayya was tied between two camels, and her private part was struck with a spear. It was said to her: "You embraced Islam only for the sake of men." So she was killed, and her husband Yasir was killed; they were the first two martyrs in Islam.

As for Ammar, he gave them what they wanted with his tongue, under compulsion. He complained of that to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: "How do you find your heart?"
He said: "Content with faith."
The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "If they return (to it), then return (to what you said)."

Mansur ibn al-Mu'tamir narrated from Mujahid, who said: The first female martyr in Islam was the mother of Ammar; Abu Jahl killed her. And the first male martyr was Mihja', the freed slave of Umar.

Mansur also narrated from Mujahid, who said: The first to openly manifest Islam were seven: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), Abu Bakr, Bilal, Khabbab, Suhayb, Ammar, and Sumayya the mother of Ammar.

As for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), Abu Talib protected him; as for Abu Bakr, his people protected him. The others were seized, and they clothed them in iron armor, then they exposed them to the sun until the hardship reached them to the utmost degree from the heat of the iron and the sun. When it was evening, Abu Jahl came to them with a spear, and he began to revile them and rebuke them. He came to Sumayya and began to revile her and to speak obscenely (yarfuth) [[Rafath: obscene speech.]], then he thrust into her private part until the spear came out of her mouth, and he killed her, may Allah be pleased with her.

He said: The others said what they were asked, except Bilal, for his soul was made light for him for the sake of Allah. They began to torture him and say to him: "Return from your religion." He would say: "One! One!" until they grew weary of him. Then they bound him, put a rope of palm fiber around his neck, and handed him over to their children, who played with him between the two mountains [[Al-Akhshabān: the two mountains surrounding Mecca, namely Abu Qubays and al-Ahmar.]] of Mecca, until they grew weary of him and left him. He said: Ammar said: "We all spoke with what they said, were it not that Allah rescued us, except Bilal, for his soul was made light for him for the sake of Allah, so he was despised by his people until they grew weary of him and left him."

The correct view is that Abu Bakr bought Bilal and freed him.

Ibn Abi Najih narrated from Mujahid that some people of Mecca embraced faith, and some of the Companions of Muhammad (ﷺ) in Medina wrote to them: "Emigrate to us, for we will not consider you of us until you emigrate to us." So they set out intending Medina, but Quraysh overtook them on the road, tempted them, and they disbelieved under compulsion. It was concerning them that this verse was revealed.

Isma'il ibn Ishaq mentioned both narrations from Mujahid.

Al-Tirmidhi narrated from Aisha, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Ammar was never given a choice between two matters without choosing the more rightly guided of them." This is a hasan gharib hadith.

It is also narrated from Anas ibn Malik, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Paradise longs for three: Ali, Ammar, and Salman ibn Rabi'a."

Al-Tirmidhi said: This is a gharib hadith; we only know it from the hadith of al-Hasan ibn Salih.

The Third: Since Allah, Mighty and Majestic, permitted disbelief in Him, which is the foundation of the Shari'a, under compulsion, and did not hold (the person) accountable for it, the scholars extended to the branches of the Shari'a all of it. So if compulsion falls upon them, one is not held accountable for them, and no ruling is consequent upon them. With this came the well-known report from the Prophet (ﷺ): "My nation has been relieved of error, forgetfulness, and what they have been forced to do," etc.

Although the chain of this report is not sound, its meaning is sound by consensus of the scholars, as stated by al-Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-Arabi.

Abu Muhammad Abd al-Haqq mentioned that its chain is sound. He said: Abu Bakr al-Asili mentioned it in al-Fawa'id, and Ibn al-Mundhir in Kitab al-Iqna'.

The Fourth: The people of knowledge have agreed that whoever is compelled to disbelieve, to the point that he fears death for himself, there is no sin upon him if he disbelieves while his heart is content with faith. His wife is not separated from him, and he is not judged by the ruling of disbelief. This is the view of Malik, the Kufans, and al-Shafi'i, except Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, for he said: If he manifests polytheism, he is an apostate outwardly, and between him and Allah he remains upon Islam. His wife is separated from him, he is not prayed over if he dies, and he does not inherit from his father if he dies a Muslim.

This is a view that the Book and the Sunna refute. Allah said: ﴿except one who has been forced﴾, the verse. And He said: ﴿except that you fear from them a fear﴾. And He said: ﴿Indeed, those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves, (the angels) say, "In what were you?" They say, "We were oppressed in the land."﴾, the verse. And He said: ﴿except the oppressed among men, women, and children﴾, the verse.

So Allah excused the oppressed who refrain from abandoning what Allah has commanded, and the one under compulsion is only oppressed, not refraining from doing what he was commanded. This is what al-Bukhari said.

The Fifth: A group of scholars held that the concession (ruksha) came only in speech, and that in action there is no concession, such as being compelled to prostrate to other than Allah, or to pray facing other than the qibla, or to kill a Muslim, strike him, or consume his property, or to commit fornication, drink wine, or consume usury. This is related from al-Hasan al-Basri, may Allah be pleased with him.

This is also the view of al-Awza'i and Sahnun among our scholars.

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: If it is said to a captive: "Prostrate to this idol, or I will kill you," and he said: If the idol is facing the qibla, then let him prostrate, with his intention being for Allah, Exalted is He; but if it is not facing the qibla, then he should not prostrate, even if they kill him.

The correct view is that he prostrates even if it is not facing the qibla. How worthy he is of prostrating then! For in the Sahih, it is reported from Ibn Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to pray on his mount while traveling from Mecca to Medina, facing wherever his face was turned. He said: And concerning it was revealed: ﴿Wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah﴾. In another narration: "And he would perform the witr on it, except that he would not perform the obligatory prayer on it."

If this is permissible during travel in a state of safety, for the hardship of dismounting for voluntary prayer, then how about this (situation)?

Those who restricted the concession to speech argued with the saying of Ibn Mas'ud: "There is no speech by which I can ward off two lashes from a ruler except that I would speak it."

So he restricted the concession to speech and did not mention action. This is no proof, because it may be that he made speech an example, and he meant that action has the same ruling.

Another group said: Compulsion in action and in speech is the same, when one conceals faith. This is related from Umar ibn al-Khattab and Makhul, and it is the view of Malik and a group of the people of Iraq.

Ibn al-Qasim narrated from Malik that whoever is compelled to drink wine, abandon the prayer, or break the fast in Ramadan, the sin is lifted from him.

The Sixth: The scholars have agreed that whoever is compelled to kill another, it is not permissible for him to proceed to kill him, nor to violate his sanctity by flogging or otherwise. He should endure the trial that has befallen him, and it is not lawful for him to ransom himself with another's life. He asks Allah for well-being in this world and the Hereafter.

Opinions differed concerning fornication. Mutarrif, Asbagh, Ibn Abd al-Hakam, and Ibn al-Majishun said: No one should do that, and even if he is killed, he should not do it. If he does it, he is sinful and the prescribed punishment (hadd) is incumbent upon him. Abu Thawr and al-Hasan also said this.

Ibn al-Arabi said: The correct view is that proceeding to fornication is permissible and there is no prescribed punishment upon him, contrary to those who made it obligatory upon him. This is because he considered it a natural desire for which compulsion cannot be conceived, and he overlooked the cause that stirs up the desire, which is the constraint toward it, and this is what removed its ruling. The prescribed punishment is only obligatory for a desire stirred by a voluntary cause. He analogized the thing to its opposite, so he did not arrive at the correct position from his own reasoning.

Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said in his Ahkam: Our companions differed as to when a man is compelled to fornicate. Some of them said: He is liable to the prescribed punishment, because he only does that by his own choice. Others said: There is no prescribed punishment upon him.

Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: And this is the correct view.

Abu Hanifa said: If someone other than the ruler compels him, he is flogged. If the ruler compels him, then by analogy he should be flogged, but I deem it preferable that he not be flogged.

His two companions disagreed with him and said: There is no prescribed punishment upon him in either case, and they did not consider the erection (of the organ). They said: Whenever he knows that he will be freed from being killed by committing fornication, it is permissible for him to have an erection.

Ibn al-Mundhir said: There is no prescribed punishment upon him, and there is no difference between the ruler and others in this.

The Seventh: The scholars differed concerning the divorce and manumission of one under compulsion. Al-Shafi'i and his companions said: Nothing is binding upon him.

Ibn Wahb mentioned from Umar, Ali, and Ibn Abbas that they did not consider his divorce to be anything.

Ibn al-Mundhir mentioned it from Ibn al-Zubayr, Ibn Umar, Ibn Abbas, Ata', Tawus, al-Hasan, Shurayh, al-Qasim, Salim, Malik, al-Awza'i, Ahmad, Ishaq, and Abu Thawr.

A group permitted his divorce; this is related from al-Sha'bi, al-Nakha'i, Abu Qilaba, al-Zuhri, and Qatada, and it is the view of the Kufans.

Abu Hanifa said: The divorce of one under compulsion is binding, because nothing is lost in it except consent, and its occurrence is not a condition for divorce, like the one who jokes.

This is an invalid analogy, for the one who jokes intends to effect the divorce and consents to it, whereas the one under compulsion does not consent and has no intention regarding divorce. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Actions are only by intentions."

In al-Bukhari it is stated: Ibn Abbas said, concerning one whom robbers compel so that he divorces: "It is nothing." Ibn Umar, Ibn al-Zubayr, al-Sha'bi, and al-Hasan also said this.

Al-Sha'bi said: If robbers compel him, it is not a divorce; if a ruler compels him, it is a divorce.

Ibn Uyayna explained it, saying: The robber proceeds to kill him, whereas the ruler does not kill him.

The Eighth: As for the sale of one under compulsion and one who is coerced, it has two states.

**Part 2 of 3**

**The first issue:** If a person sells his property to settle a right that is owed by him, that sale is valid and binding, and there is no retraction from it according to the jurists (fuqaha'), because he is obliged to discharge the right to its owner from something other than the property sold. Since he did not do that, his selling was a choice on his part, and so it binds him.

As for the sale of one who is compelled through injustice or coercion, that sale is not valid against him. He has the right to take back his goods without paying a price, and he may pursue the buyer for the price from that wrongdoer. If the goods have been lost, he may recover either the price or the value, whichever is greater, from the wrongdoer, provided the buyer was unaware of his injustice.

Mutarrif said:
Whoever among the buyers knows the condition of the one compelled is liable for what he bought of his slaves and goods, like a usurper (ghasib). Whatever the buyer does with them, such as manumission ('itq), conditional manumission upon death (tadbir), or endowment (tahbis), does not bind the one who was compelled, and he has the right to take back his property.

Sahnun said:
Our companions (the Malikis) and the people of Iraq (the Hanafis) agreed that the sale of one compelled to injustice and oppression is not valid.

Al-Abhari said:
It is a consensus (ijma').

**The ninth issue:** As for the marriage of one who is compelled, Sahnun said: Our companions agreed that the marriage of a compelled man and a compelled woman is void, and they said: it is not permissible to remain in it, because it was never validly concluded.

Muhammad ibn Sahnun said: The people of Iraq permitted the marriage of one compelled, and they said: If a man is compelled to marry a woman for ten thousand dirhams, while her proper dower (sadaq al-mithl) is one thousand dirhams, the marriage is valid, he is bound to pay the one thousand, and the excess is annulled. Muhammad said: Just as they annulled the amount exceeding the thousand, so it is binding on them to annul the marriage made under compulsion. Their view contradicts the established Sunnah in the hadith of Khansa' bint Khidham al-Ansariyya, and the Prophet's (ﷺ) command to seek the consent of women concerning their own marriage, which has already been mentioned. Therefore there is no basis for their view.

**The tenth issue:** If the man who was compelled to marry has intercourse with her, while not being compelled to intercourse and having consented to the marriage, then according to us the marriage is binding upon him with the stated dower, and the hadd punishment is averted from him. If he says: "I had intercourse with her without my consent to the marriage," then he is liable to the hadd punishment and to the stated dower, because he claims to void the stated dower. The woman is punished if she proceeded knowing that he was compelled to the marriage. As for a woman compelled to marriage and to intercourse, there is no hadd punishment on her, she is entitled to the dower, and the one who had intercourse is punished with the hadd. Know this. Sahnun said this.

**The eleventh issue:** If a woman is compelled to fornication, there is no hadd punishment upon her, based on His saying, "except one who is compelled" (16:106), and the Prophet's (peace be upon him) saying: "Indeed Allah has overlooked for my community error, forgetfulness, and what they have been compelled to do." Also based on the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Then indeed your Lord, after their compulsion, is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ (24:33), meaning the slave girls. In this sense Umar ruled concerning a slave girl whom a slave had compelled, and he did not inflict the hadd upon her. The scholars agree that there is no hadd upon a woman who was compelled.

Malik said: If a woman is found pregnant, has no husband, and says "I was compelled," that is not accepted from her, and she is liable to the hadd, unless she has proof, or she comes bleeding showing that she was violated, or something similar. He relied on the hadith of Umar ibn al-Khattab that he said: "Stoning is in the Book of Allah for whoever among men and women commits adultery, if they are muhsan (married), when the evidence is established, or there is pregnancy, or confession." Ibn al-Mundhir said: I hold the first view.

**The twelfth issue:** They differed concerning the obligation of the dower for a compelled woman. Ata' and al-Zuhri said: she is entitled to the dower of her equal (sadaq al-mithl). This is also the view of Malik, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Ishaq, and Abu Thawr. Al-Thawri said: If the hadd is carried out upon the one who committed adultery with her, the dower is void. This was transmitted from al-Sha'bi, and it is the view of the companions of Malik and the companions of opinion (Hanafis). Ibn al-Mundhir said: The first view is correct.

**The thirteenth issue:** If a person is compelled to renounce Islam with respect to his family, for what is not lawful, and he renounces it, and he does not kill himself in defending them, nor does he bear harm in rescuing them, then the basis for this is what al-Bukhari transmitted from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Ibrahim (peace be upon him) migrated with Sarah and entered a town in which there was a king among the kings, or a tyrant among the tyrants. He sent to him: 'Send her to me.' So he sent her. He approached her, but she stood up and performed ablution and prayed, and she said: 'O Allah, if I have believed in You and Your Messenger, do not give this disbeliever power over me.' So he was seized (ghutta) until he kicked with his leg."[^1] This hadith also indicates that since no blame fell upon Sarah, likewise no blame falls upon a woman who is compelled, and there is no hadd for what is greater than seclusion. And Allah knows best.

**The fourteenth issue:** As for the oath of one who is compelled, it is not binding according to Malik, al-Shafi'i, Abu Thawr, and most scholars. Ibn al-Majishun said: It makes no difference whether he swore concerning what is obedience to Allah or concerning what is disobedience, when he was compelled to swear. Asbagh said the same. Mutarrif said: If he is compelled to swear concerning what is disobedience to Allah, or concerning an act in which there is neither obedience nor disobedience, then the oath is void. If he is compelled to swear concerning what is obedience, such as when a ruler seizes a corrupt man and compels him to swear by divorce that he will not drink wine, or will not commit corruption, or will not cheat in his work, or a father makes his son swear as discipline, then the oath is binding, even if the one compelled erred in what he was obligated to. Ibn Habib said the same.

Abu Hanifa and those who followed him among the Kufans said: If he swore not to do something and then did it, he breaks the oath. They said: Because the one compelled may use tawriya (equivocation) in his entire oath, and since he did not use equivocation, and his intention did not turn to the opposite of what he was compelled to, he has intended the oath. The earlier scholars argued: When he is compelled to it, his intention is contrary to his words, because he is averse to what he has sworn to.

**The fifteenth issue:** Ibn al-'Arabi said: Among the strange matters is that our scholars differed on whether compulsion to break an oath (hinth) takes effect or not. This is an Iraqi question that spread to us from them. Would that this question had never existed, nor they! What difference, O company of our companions, is there between compulsion to swear, in that it is not binding, and breaking under compulsion, in that it does not take effect? So fear Allah and review your insights, and do not be deceived by this opinion, for it is a blemish upon understanding.

**The sixteenth issue:** If a man is compelled to swear, or else his property is taken, like tax collectors (ashab al-maks), oppressive collectors, and aggressors, Malik said: He has no taqiyyah (dissimulation) in that, and a person only averts by his oath harm to his body, not to his property. Ibn al-Majishun said: He does not break the oath even if he averts harm from his property and did not fear for his body. Ibn al-Qasim held the view of Mutarrif, and he related it from Malik. Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam and Asbagh said the same.

I say: The view of Ibn al-Majishun is sound, because defending one's property is like defending one's self. This is also the view of al-Hasan and Qatada, which will come. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed your blood, your property, and your honor are sacred to you." And he said: "Every Muslim is sacred to a Muslim: his blood, his property, and his honor." Abu Hurayra narrated that a man came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah, what do you think if a man comes wanting to take my property?" He said: "Do not give him your property." He said: "What do you think if he fights me?" He said: "Fight him." He said: "What if he kills me?" He said: "Then you are a martyr." He said: "What if I kill him?" He said: "He is in the Fire." Muslim transmitted it.[^2] The discussion of this has already passed.

Mutarrif and Ibn al-Majishun said: If the one swearing hastens to swear to the unjust ruler before he is asked, in order to ward off by it what he fears for his property and body, and he swears to him, then the oath binds him. Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam and Asbagh said the same. Ibn al-Majishun also said concerning one whom a wrongdoer seized and who swore to him by an absolute divorce (talaq al-battah) without being made to swear, and then he left him while he was lying, and he swore only out of fear of being beaten, killed, or having his property taken: if he volunteered the oath out of overwhelming fear and hope of escaping his injustice, then he has entered into compulsion and there is nothing upon him. But if he did not swear with hope of escape, then he is a breaker of the oath (hanith).

**The seventeenth issue:** The scholars who verify matters said: If the one compelled utters disbelief, it is not permissible for him to let it pass upon his tongue except as ma'arid (allusive speech), for in ma'arid there is a broad latitude away from lying. If he does not do that, he is a disbeliever, because compulsion has no authority over ma'arid. An example: if he is told, "Disbelieve in Allah," and he says "bi-l-lahi" (with the Allah) while adding a yā' (lahi with a yā' to make "lāhī," meaning a sport or plaything), and similarly if he is told, "Disbelieve in the Prophet," and he says, "huwa kafir bi-l-nabiyy," with the letter hamza unpronounced and shaddah, meaning "he is a disbeliever in the high place" (nabiyy as "elevated ground"). This is also used of a plaited palm-leaf thing resembling a table, so he intends one of the two meanings in his heart, clears himself of disbelief, and clears himself of its sin.[^3] If he is told, "Disbelieve in the Prophet" with the hamza pronounced, and he says, "He is a disbeliever in the Prophet," meaning the informer (mukhbir), whoever he is, like Tulayha[^4] and Musaylima the liar. Or he means by it the Prophet about whom the poet said:

*So he became crushed pebbles*
*in place of the Prophet from the sand heap.*[^5]

---

[^1]: The author mentioned this hadith in abridged form; see al-Qastallani's commentary, Kitab al-Buyu', vol. 4, p. 122, Bulaq edition. *Ghatta* here means severe squeezing and pressing, and *rakada* means striking with the foot.

[^2]: Supported by what Ahmad and al-Tirmidhi transmitted from Ibn 'Umar: "Whoever is killed defending his property is a martyr." Kashf al-Khafa', vol. 2, p. 296.

[^3]: Ma'arid: equivocation by means of one thing in place of another. "A'rada al-kalam" and "mu'arada" and "ma'arid" mean speech whose parts resemble one another in meaning.

[^4]: Tulayha ibn Khuwaylid ibn Nawfal al-Asadi apostatized after the Prophet (ﷺ) and claimed prophethood, then later embraced Islam.

**Eighteenth:** The scholars agreed that whoever is compelled to disbelieve and chooses to be killed has a greater reward with God than one who takes the concession (*rukhsa*). They differed regarding one compelled to do something other than killing, something unlawful for him. The companions of Malik said: taking the strict course in that case, and choosing killing or beating, is better with God than taking the concession. Ibn Habib and Sahnun mentioned this. Ibn Sahnun reported from the people of Iraq that if he is threatened with killing, mutilation, or beating that he fears could destroy him, then he may do what he is compelled to, such as drinking wine or eating pork. But if he refuses until he is killed, we fear he would be sinful, since he is like one under necessity (*mudtarr*).

Khabbab ibn al-Aratt narrated: We complained to the Messenger of God ﷺ while he was reclining on a cloak of his in the shade of the Ka'ba. I said: "Will you not seek victory for us? Will you not supplicate for us?" He said: "Among those before you, a man would be seized, a pit dug for him in the earth, and he would be placed in it. Then a saw would be brought and placed on his head, and he would be split in two. Combs of iron would be scraped against him, beneath his flesh and bones, and that would not turn him from his religion. By God, this matter will surely be completed [[He means Islam.]] until a rider travels from San'a to Hadramawt fearing none but God and the wolf for his sheep. But you are hasty."

His description ﷺ of the earlier nations is in praise of them and of their patience in the face of hardship for the sake of God. It also notes that they did not disbelieve outwardly while concealing faith, in order to ward off punishment from themselves. This is the proof for one who prefers beating, killing, and humiliation over the concession and dwelling in the Gardens. More detailed explanation of this will come in the commentary on Surah al-Buruj [[See vol. 19, p. 284.]], God willing.

Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn Muhammad ibn al-Faraj al-Baghdadi mentioned: Shurayh ibn Yunus narrated to us from Isma'il ibn Ibrahim, from Yunus ibn Ubayd, from al-Hasan, that spies of Musaylima seized two men from the companions of the Prophet ﷺ and took them to Musaylima. He said to one of them: "Do you testify that Muhammad is the Messenger of God?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Do you testify that I am the Messenger of God?" He said: "Yes." So he released him. He said to the other: "Do you testify that Muhammad is the Messenger of God?" He said: "Yes." He said: "And do you testify that I am the Messenger of God?" He said: "I am deaf, I do not hear." So he brought him forward and struck his neck. The first man came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: "I am ruined!" He said: "What has ruined you?" Then he related the hadith. He said: "As for your companion, he persisted in his faith [[The wording in al-Durr al-Manthur is: "As for your companion, he went on in his faith."]], and as for you, you took the concession, according to what you are upon this hour." He said: "I testify that you are the Messenger of God." He said: "You are upon what you are upon."

**The concession** applies to one whom an oppressive ruler compels to swear on his own behalf, or to swear that he will point out a man or a man's property. Al-Hasan said: if he fears for himself and his property, let him swear and not expiate the oath. Qatada's view is the same if he swears regarding himself or his own property. What the scholars hold on this has already been mentioned.

Musa ibn Mu'awiya mentioned that Abu Sa'id ibn Ashras, a companion of Malik, was made to swear by the ruler in Tunis that he had not sheltered a man the ruler wanted to kill and did not know where he was. Ibn Ashras swore to him, though that day he knew the man's location and had sheltered him. The ruler made him swear by divorce three times, and Ibn Ashras swore. Then he said to his wife: "Withdraw," and she withdrew from him. Ibn Ashras then rode until he reached al-Buhlul ibn Rashid in Qayrawan and informed him of the matter. Al-Buhlul said to him: "Malik said that you have broken your oath (*hanith*)." Ibn Ashras said: "I too heard Malik say that, but I intended only the concession," or words to this effect. Al-Buhlul ibn Rashid then said to him: "al-Hasan al-Basri said there is no breaking of the oath upon you." Ibn Ashras returned to his wife and adopted the view of al-Hasan.

Abd al-Malik ibn Habib mentioned: Mu'bad narrated to me from al-Musayyab ibn Sharik, from Abu Shayba, who said: I asked Anas ibn Malik about a man who is seized in place of another man: "Do you think he should swear to protect him with his oath?" He said: "Yes. Swearing seventy oaths and breaking them is dearer to me than pointing out a Muslim."

Idris ibn Yahya said: al-Walid ibn Abd al-Malik would order spies to inform on people and bring him news. One of them sat in the circle of Raja' ibn Hayawa and heard some of those present speaking ill of al-Walid, and he reported this to him. Al-Walid said: "O Raja'! You were spoken of with evil in your gathering, and you did not change it?" He said: "That was not so, O Commander of the Faithful." Al-Walid said to him: "Say: 'By God, there is no god but He.'" He said: "By God, there is no god but He." Al-Walid ordered the spy to be beaten seventy lashes. The spy would meet Raja' and say: "O Raja', rain is sought through you, and I have seventy lashes on my back!" Raja' would say: "Seventy lashes on your back are better for you than that a Muslim man be killed."

**Nineteenth:** The scholars differed about the limit of compulsion (*hadd al-ikrah*). It is reported from Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, that he said: "A man is not safe for himself when you frighten him, bind him, or beat him." Ibn Mas'ud said: "No speech would avert two lashes from me except that I would speak it." Al-Hasan said: "Taqiyya (concealment of faith under threat) is permissible for the believer until the Day of Resurrection, except that God does not make taqiyya permissible in killing." Al-Nakha'i said: "Shackles are compulsion, and imprisonment is compulsion." This is the view of Malik as well, except that he said: a frightening threat is compulsion even if it is not carried out, provided the oppressor's wrongdoing is certain and he will carry out what he threatens. For Malik and his companions, there is no fixed measure for beating and imprisonment; rather, it is whatever causes pain in beating, and whatever imprisonment brings constriction upon the one compelled. For Malik, the compulsion of the ruler and of others is compulsion.

The Kufans were inconsistent: they did not regard imprisonment and shackles as compulsion to drink wine or eat carrion, because death is not feared from them, yet they regarded them as compulsion in acknowledging that someone is owed a thousand dirhams by him. Ibn Sahnun said: their consensus that pain and severe suffering constitute compulsion shows that compulsion can occur without the loss of life.

Malik held that whoever is compelled to swear by a threat, imprisonment, or beating may swear, and there is no breaking of the oath upon him. This is also the view of al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Abu Thawr, and most scholars.

**Twentieth:** Among this category is what is established: "Indeed, in *ma'arid* (allusive speech) there is ample alternative to lying." Al-A'mash narrated from Ibrahim al-Nakha'i that he said: "There is no harm if a report reaches you about something said against you, and you say: 'By God, God knows what I said about you of such a thing.'" Abd al-Malik ibn Habib said: its meaning is that God knows what you said, and in its outward form it is a denial of having said it. No breaking of the oath falls upon one who says this in his oath, nor is there a lie in his speech.

Al-Nakha'i said: They had a kind of speech from the riddles of oaths by which they warded off harm from themselves. They did not regard it as lying, nor did they fear breaking an oath by it. Abd al-Malik said: They called that *ma'arid* of speech, provided it was not used for deceit or trickery in a matter of right.

Al-A'mash said: When someone came to Ibrahim al-Nakha'i whom he disliked going out to meet, he would sit in the mosque of his house and say to his slave girl: "Tell him: he is, by God, in the mosque." Mughira narrated from Ibrahim that he permitted a man of the army (*al-ba'th*: the troops) to say, when they were reviewed before their commander: "By God, I am not guided except by what another has guided me to, and I do not ride except on what another has carried me on," and similar words.

Abd al-Malik said: By "another" he means God Almighty, who guides him and carries him. So they did not regard it as a breaking of the oath upon the man in this, nor as a lie in his speech. But they disliked that this be said in deceit, oppression, or the denial of a right. Whoever dared to do so and acted thus sinned in his deception, and no expiation was obligatory upon him for his oath.

**Twenty-first:** God's words: ﴿But whoever opens his breast to disbelief﴾, that is, expands it to accept disbelief. None is able to do that except God. This refutes the Qadariyya (those who deny God's predestination of human acts). *Sadran* (breast) is in the accusative as an object.

﴿Upon them is wrath from God, and for them is a great punishment﴾, which is the punishment of Hell.

"His saying, the Exalted: ﴿That﴾, i.e., that wrath.

(Because they preferred the worldly life) i.e., they chose it over the Hereafter.

(And that Allah) "That" (anna) is in the genitive position, coordinated with "because that they" (bi-annahum).

(Does not guide the disbelieving people.) Then He described them, saying: (Those are the ones whom Allah has sealed upon their hearts) i.e., so that they do not understand the admonitions,

(and their hearing) from the words of Allah the Exalted,

(and their sight) from looking at the signs.

(And those are the heedless) of what is intended for them.

(Undoubtedly, in the Hereafter they are the losers) This has been mentioned before [[see vol. 9, p. 20.]]."

Al-Qurtubi, *al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran*, on Surah 16, verse 110:

Allah's words: ﴿Then indeed your Lord, for those who emigrated after they were tried and then strove and were patient, indeed your Lord thereafter is Forgiving and Merciful﴾. All of this concerns ʿAmmar, on account of jihad; al-Nahhas mentioned it. Qatadah said: it was revealed concerning a people who went out as emigrants to al-Madinah after the polytheists had tried them and tortured them, and their mention has already preceded in this surah [[See p. 180 of this part.]]. It was also said: it was revealed concerning Ibn Abi Sarh, who had apostatized and joined the polytheists, so the Prophet (ﷺ) ordered his killing on the day of the Conquest of Makkah. He sought protection through Uthman, and the Prophet (ﷺ) granted him protection. al-Nasa'i mentioned it from Ikrimah, from Ibn Abbas, who said: In Surah al-Nahl, ﴿Whoever disbelieves in Allah after his faith, except one who is compelled while his heart is secure in faith, [but whoever opens his breast to disbelief]—upon them is wrath from Allah, and for them is a great punishment﴾ was abrogated, and an exception was made from it, and He said: ﴿Then indeed your Lord, for those who emigrated after they were tried and then strove and were patient, indeed your Lord thereafter is Forgiving and Merciful﴾. He is Abdullah ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Sarh, who was over Egypt. He used to write for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), but Satan caused him to slip, so he joined the disbelievers. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ordered that he be killed on the day of the Conquest, but Uthman ibn Affan interceded for him, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) granted him protection.

The Qur'anic verse: ﴿On the Day when every soul comes pleading for itself﴾. That is, God is Forgiving and Merciful regarding that. Or: remind them.

"On the Day when every soul comes pleading for itself" means: disputing and arguing on its own behalf. It is reported in a khabar (report) that on the Day of Resurrection everyone will say, "Myself, myself!", because of the intensity of the terror of that Day, except Muhammad (ﷺ), for he will intercede for his community.

In the hadith of Umar, he said to Ka'b al-Ahbar: "O Ka'b, make us fear, stir us, narrate to us, awaken us." Ka'b said to him: "O Commander of the Faithful, by Him in whose hand my soul is, if you were to arrive on the Day of Resurrection with the deeds of seventy prophets, there would come upon you moments in which you would be concerned with nothing but yourself. Indeed, Hell has a roar, and no angel brought near and no chosen prophet will remain without falling to his knees, to the extent that Abraham the Friend will rely upon his intimate friendship (khullah) and say: 'O Lord, I am Your friend Abraham; today I ask for nothing but myself!'" Umar said: "O Ka'b, where do you find that in the Book of God?" Ka'b said: it is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿On the Day when every soul comes pleading for itself, and every soul will be paid in full for what it did, and they will not be wronged﴾.

Ibn Abbas said concerning this verse: "The dispute among people on the Day of Resurrection will not cease until the soul disputes with the body. The soul will say: 'Lord, the soul is from You; You created it. I had no hand with which to strike, no foot with which to walk, no eye with which to see, no ear with which to hear, and no intellect with which to understand, until You came and I entered this body. So multiply upon it the kinds of punishment and save me.' The body will say: 'Lord, You created me with Your hand, and I was like a piece of wood: I had no hand with which to strike, no foot with which to walk, no eye with which to see, and no ear with which to hear. Then this came, like a ray of light, and through it my tongue spoke, through it my eye saw, through it my foot walked, and through it my ear heard. So multiply upon it the kinds of punishment and save me from it.'" He said: "Then God will strike for them both a parable: a blind man and a lame man who entered a garden with fruit. The blind man cannot see the fruit, and the lame man cannot reach it. The lame man called to the blind man, 'Come (ائتني) and carry me, and I will eat and feed you.' So he drew near and carried him, and they partook of the fruit. Upon whom, then, will the punishment fall?" [They both said: "Upon them both."] He said: "Upon both of you together is the punishment." This was related by al-Tha'labi.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 16, verse 112:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And Allah presents a parable: a town⁠﴾. This is connected to the mention of the polytheists. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had invoked against the polytheists of Quraysh and said: "O Allah, tighten Your grip upon Mudar, and make for them years like the years of Yusuf." So they were afflicted with famine until they ate bones, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent food to them, which was distributed among them.

(﴿It was secure﴾) its people were not raided.

(﴿Its provision came to it abundantly from every place﴾) from land and sea. Its parallel is His saying: "to which are brought the fruits of every thing" [see vol. 13, p. 299], and so on.

(﴿But it denied the favours of Allah⁠﴾) al-An'um (the favours) is the plural of al-ni'mah (favour), like al-ashudd, the plural of al-shiddah (severity). It is also said: it is the plural of nu'ma, like bu's and ab'us. This ingratitude is a denial of Muhammad (ﷺ).

(﴿So Allah made it taste﴾) that is, He made its people taste.

(﴿the garment of hunger and fear⁠﴾) He called it a garment because the signs of emaciation, pallor of complexion and evil condition appear upon them like a garment.

(﴿for what they used to do⁠﴾) that is, for their disbelief and sins. Hafs ibn Ghiyath, Nasr ibn 'Asim, Ibn Abi Ishaq, al-Hasan, and Abu 'Amr, as related from him by 'Abd al-Warith and 'Ubayd and 'Abbas, read "wal-khawfu" (and fear) in the accusative, as the object of the verb "adhaqaha" (He made it taste), coordinated with "libasa al-ju'" (the garment of hunger) [that is, Allah made it taste the garment of hunger and made it taste the fear]. This refers to the Prophet (ﷺ) sending his expeditions (sarayah) which used to encircle them. The original meaning of "dhawq" (tasting) is with the mouth, then it is used figuratively and placed in the position of trial. He cited Makkah as an example for other lands, meaning that although it enjoys the neighbourhood of the House of Allah and the maintenance of its mosque, when its people disbelieved, famine struck them, so how much more so would other towns be (affected). It has also been said that it is Madinah, which believed in the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), then disbelieved in the favours of Allah by the killing of 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, and by the trials that occurred there after the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). This is the view of 'Aishah and Hafsah, the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ). It has been said: it is a parable struck for any town that was in this condition among the other towns.

Almighty God says: ﴿And there had certainly come to them a messenger from among themselves, but they denied him﴾. This indicates that the town is Makkah. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatadah.

(So the punishment seized them) and it was the famine (al-jou') that befell Makkah. It was also said: the hardships, and the famine among them.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 16, verse 114:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So eat of what Allah has provided for you﴾, meaning: eat, O assembly of Muslims, of the spoils of war (al-ghana'im). It has also been said: the address is to the polytheists, because the Prophet ﷺ sent them food out of compassion for them. This was because, when they were afflicted with hunger for seven years, and the Arabs cut off the supply of provisions from them by the command of the Prophet ﷺ, they ate burnt bones, carrion, dead dogs, hides, and al-'ilhiz, which is wool treated with blood. Then the chiefs of Makkah spoke to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ when they were in dire straits, and said: "This is the punishment of the men, so what of the women and children?" Abu Sufyan said to him: "O Muhammad, you came commanding the joining of ties of kinship and forgiveness, and your people have perished, so pray to Allah for them." So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ prayed for them, and he permitted the people to bring food to them, even though they were still polytheists.
The discussion of it has already been given in full in "al-Baqarah" [[See vol. 2, p. 216 and following.]].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 16, verse 116–117:

There are two issues here. The first concerns His saying, ﴿for what your tongues describe﴾. Here "ma" (what) is a verbal-source particle (maṣdariyyah), meaning "for the description" (li-waṣf). It was also said that the lam is the lam of cause and purpose, meaning: do not say for the sake of your describing "the lie" by dropping the preposition, i.e. for what your tongues describe of falsehood. It was also read "al-kadhib" (the lie) with a ḍammah on the kaf, the dhal and the ya', as a qualifier of "al-alsinah" (the tongues), and this has been mentioned before [[See p. 120 of this part.]]. Al-Hasan read here specifically "al-kadhib" with a fatḥah on the kaf and a kasrah on the dhal and the ba', as a qualifier of "ma" (what), the sense being: and do not say, to the lie that your tongues describe, "This is lawful and this is unlawful, to fabricate against Allah the lie" (﴿This is lawful and this is unlawful, to fabricate against Allah the lie﴾). The verse is addressed to the disbelievers who declared unlawful the baḥā'ir (she-camels slit-eared) and the sawā'ib (freed camels), and made lawful what is in the bellies of livestock even if it was carrion. So his saying "This is lawful" refers to the carrion of the bellies of livestock and everything else they made lawful, and his saying "This is unlawful" refers to the baḥā'ir, the sawā'ib, and everything else they made unlawful.

﴿Indeed, those who fabricate against Allah the lie will not succeed. A brief enjoyment, and for them is a painful punishment﴾. That is, what they enjoy of the pleasures of this world will soon vanish. Al-Zajjaj said: their enjoyment is a brief enjoyment. It was also said: for them is a brief enjoyment, then they will be returned to a painful punishment.

The second issue: Abu Muhammad al-Darimi narrated in his Musnad: Harun related to us from Hafs, from al-A'mash, who said: "I never heard Ibrahim (al-Nakha'i) ever say 'lawful' or 'unlawful'; rather he used to say: 'They disliked' and 'They preferred'." Ibn Wahb said: Malik said: "It was not the practice of the people of fatwa to say 'This is lawful and this is unlawful'; rather they would say: 'Beware of such-and-such,' and 'I would not do this.'" The meaning of this is that declaring something lawful or unlawful belongs only to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and it is not for anyone to say or state this about any specific thing, unless the Exalted Creator informs about it. Whatever ijtihad leads to as being unlawful, one says: "I dislike [such-and-such]." And Malik acted this way following those of earlier piety. If it is said: Malik did say concerning one who tells his wife "You are unlawful to me" that she is unlawful and it counts as three (divorces)? The answer is that when Malik heard 'Ali ibn Abi Talib say it, he followed him. The evidence for prohibition may become strong for a mujtahid, so there is no harm in his saying it, just as he says that riba (usury) is unlawful in other than the six commodities [[They are gold, silver, wheat, barley, dates and salt.]]; and Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, often uses such absolute expressions, and that is unlawful in ribawi goods and in what opposes the public interests and departs from the path of the objectives, due to the strength of the evidences in that.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 16, verse 118:

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And to those who became Jews⁠﻿ We had forbidden⁠﻿ ...﴾ He made clear that the cattle and the tilled produce are permissible (halal) for this community, whereas for the Jews some things were forbidden to them from among them.

﴿We forbade what We have related to you before⁠﻿﴾ — that is, in Surat al-An'am [[See vol. 7, p. 124.]].

﴿And We did not wrong them⁠﻿﴾ — that is, by forbidding what We forbade them; rather they wronged themselves, so We forbade them those things as a punishment for them, as was mentioned earlier in Surat al-Nisa' [[See vol. 6, p. 12.]].

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Then indeed your Lord, for those who did evil in ignorance⦅ –⦆﴾ [the Arabic text as given: "ثُمَّ إِنَّ رَبَّكَ لِلَّذِينَ عَمِلُوا السُّوءَ"]. "Evil" (al-su') means shirk (associating partners with Allah), as reported from Ibn 'Abbas. This has already been discussed in Surat an-Nisa' [see vol. 5, p. 92].

Note on the rendering above: the quoted verse should read, in plain meaning, "Then indeed your Lord, toward those who did evil…" Corrected translation of the Qur'anic quotation:

﴿Then indeed your Lord – for those who committed evil⦅ –⦆﴾

Translation of the commentary:

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Then indeed your Lord, for those who committed evil﴾. That is, shirk (associating others with Allah), as Ibn 'Abbas said. This has already been discussed in Surat an-Nisa' [see vol. 5, p. 92].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 16, verse 120:

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, Abraham was a nation, devoutly obedient to Allah, inclining toward truth (ḥanīfan)﴾. He, peace be upon him, called the polytheists of the Arabs to the creed (millah) of Abraham, since he was their father and the builder of the House through which their honor lies. And "ummah" (nation) here means a man who gathers within himself all goodness, and its meanings have already been discussed [[See vol. 2, p. 127.]]. Ibn Wahb and Ibn al-Qasim related from Malik, who said: It reached me that ʿAbdullah ibn Masʿud said: "May Allah have mercy on Muʿadh! He was a nation, devoutly obedient (qānitan)." It was said to him: "O Abu ʿAbd al-Rahman, Allah the Mighty and Majestic mentioned by this Abraham, peace be upon him." Ibn Masʿud said: "Indeed, the ummah is one who teaches people goodness, and the qanit is the one who is obedient (muṭīʿ)." Qunut (devout obedience) has already been discussed in al-Baqarah [[vol. 2, p. 86 and vol. 3, p. 213]], and "ḥanīfan" (inclining toward truth) in al-Anʿam [[It is mentioned in al-Anʿam in two places (vol. 7, pp. 28, 152), and the author did not explain its derivation in them, but spoke about it in surah al-Baqarah, vol. 2, p. 139, so refer to it.]].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 16, verse 121–122:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Grateful for His bounties﴾, meaning he was grateful.

(لِأَنْعُمِهِ) al-an'um is the plural of ni'mah (bounty). This has already been discussed. And (اجْتَباهُ) means He chose him (akhtarahu).

(وَهَداهُ إِلى صِراطٍ مُسْتَقِيمٍ. وَآتَيْناهُ فِي الدُّنْيا حَسَنَةً) It has been said: the good child. It has also been said: the good praise. It has been said: prophethood. It has been said: the prayer linked with the prayer upon Muhammad (ﷺ) in the tashahhud. It has been said: there is no people of any religion except that they claim allegiance to him. It has been said: the continuation of his hospitality and the visiting of his grave. All of these Allah gave him, and He increased them for him (ﷺ).

(وَإِنَّهُ فِي الْآخِرَةِ لَمِنَ الصَّالِحِينَ). The "min" here carries the meaning of "ma'a" (with), meaning with the righteous, because he was also with the righteous in this world. This has already been discussed in al-Baqarah. [[See vol. 2, p. 133.]]

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 16, verse 121–122:

It has been said: the prayer linked with the prayer upon Muhammad (ﷺ) in the tashahhud. It has been said: there is no people of any religion except that they claim allegiance to him. It has been said: the continuation of his hospitality and the visiting of his grave. All of these Allah gave him, and He increased them for him (ﷺ).

(وَإِنَّهُ فِي الْآخِرَةِ لَمِنَ الصَّالِحِينَ). The "min" here carries the meaning of "ma'a" (with), meaning with the righteous, because he was also with the righteous in this world. This has already been discussed in al-Baqarah. [[See vol. 2, p. 133.]]

Ibn 'Umar said: He was commanded to follow him (Ibrahim) in the rites of the Hajj, just as Jibril (Gabriel) taught Ibrahim, peace be upon them both.

Al-Tabari said: He was commanded to follow him in disavowing the idols and adorning himself with Islam.

It was also said: He was commanded to follow him in his entire religion (millah, religious creed and way) except for what he was commanded to abandon. This was said by some of al-Shafi'i's companions, as related by al-Mawardi.

The correct view is that one follows him in the foundations of the Shari'a (sacred law) and not in its derivative rulings (furu', detailed legal rules), based on the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿For each of you We have made a law and a way﴾.

Issue (mas'ala): In this verse there is evidence for the permissibility of a more excellent person following a lesser one, if the lesser one is correct (the text reads: "for what preceded [[So in Ya. In Awj and Waw: 'in the originals.']] [to the correct view [[So in Ya. In Awj and Waw: 'in the originals.']]]"), and of acting upon it, and there is no blame (darak, responsibility) upon the superior in that, because the Prophet (ﷺ) is the most excellent of the prophets, peace be upon them, and he was commanded to take them as models, when He said: ﴿So follow their guidance﴾ [[See vol. 7 p. 35.]]. And here He said: ﴿Then We revealed to you, "Follow the religion of Ibrahim, a man of pure faith"﴾.

The Qurtubi commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Qur'an) on surah 16, verse 124:

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿The Sabbath was only prescribed for those who differed about it﴾. That is, it was not part of the law (shari'a) of Ibrahim, nor part of his religion. Rather, his religion was tolerant (samhan), with no severity in it. The Sabbath was a severity upon the Jews, in that it required abandoning work and refraining from earning a livelihood, because of their disagreement about it. Then 'Isa, peace be upon him, came on a Friday and said: "Devote yourselves to worship one day in every seven days." They said: "We do not want their festival to come after our festival," so they chose Sunday.

The scholars differed about how the disagreement that occurred among them came about. One group said: Musa, peace be upon him, commanded them to observe Friday, specified it for them, and informed them of its merit over other days. They argued with him that Saturday was better, so Allah said to him: "Leave them and what they have chosen for themselves." It was also said: Allah the Exalted did not specify it for them. Rather, He commanded them to honour one day in the week, and their ijtihad (independent reasoning) differed in determining it. So the Jews designated Saturday, because Allah finished the creation on it. The Christians designated Sunday, because Allah began the creation on it. Each of them was then bound by what his ijtihad led him to. Allah specified Friday for this community without leaving them to their own ijtihad, as a favour and blessing from Him, and so it became the best of nations.

The Sahih relates from Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "We are the last but the first on the Day of Resurrection, and we are the first to enter Paradise, though they were given the Book before us and we were given it after them. They differed about it, so Allah guided us to the truth regarding what they differed about. This is their day about which they differed, and Allah guided us to it" – he said: "It is Friday. So today is ours, tomorrow is for the Jews, and the day after tomorrow is for the Christians."

His saying, "This is their day about which they differed," strengthens the view of the one who said that He did not specify it for them. For if He had specified it for them and they had opposed it stubbornly, it would not be said that they "differed"; rather it should have been said that they "opposed it and were obstinate." Another thing that strengthens this is his saying, peace be upon him: "Allah led astray from Friday those who were before us." This is explicit in meaning. In some of its chains it has come: "This is their day which Allah prescribed for them, about which they differed." This is evidence for the first view.

It has also been related: "Allah prescribed Friday for those before us, but they differed about it, and Allah guided us to it. So people are followers of us."

His saying the Exalted: ﴿upon those who differed about it﴾ means: about the day of Friday, as we have explained, they differed concerning their prophets Musa and 'Isa.

The connection with what precedes it is that the Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded to follow the truth, and Allah warned the community against differing over it, lest He impose severity upon them as He imposed it upon the Jews.

There is one issue here. This verse was revealed in Mecca at a time when the command was to maintain a truce with the Quraysh, and He commanded him to call to the religion of Allah and His law with gentleness and kindness, without harshness or rebuke. And thus the Muslims should be admonished until the Day of Resurrection. So it is muhkam (decisive, not abrogated) with regard to the sinful among the monotheists, and mansukh (abrogated) by fighting with regard to the disbelievers. It has also been said: whoever among the disbelievers can be reached by these methods, and whose faith is hoped for through them without fighting, then the verse is muhkam with regard to him. And Allah knows best.

**First issue:** Most scholars of tafsir (Qur'anic exegesis) agree that this verse is Medinan. It was revealed concerning the mutilation of Hamzah on the day of Uhud, and this is recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari and in the books of the Prophetic biography (kitab al-siyar). Al-Nahhas held that it is Meccan, and that its meaning connects well with the Meccan verses before it, since it moves through the ranks from the one who is invited and admonished, to the one who is argued with, to the one who is repaid for his deeds. But what the majority narrated is more authentic. Al-Daraqutni narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: When the polytheists turned away from the slain of Uhud, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) turned and saw a sight that grieved him. He saw Hamzah with his belly ripped open, his nose cut off, and his ears severed. He said: "Were it not that the women would grieve, or that it would become a sunnah after me, I would have left him until Allah raises him from the bellies of beasts and birds. I will mutilate in his place seventy men." Then he called for a cloak and covered his face with it, but his feet were exposed, so he covered his feet with idhkhir (a fragrant grass). Then he placed him forward and said the takbir over him ten times. Then men were brought one by one and placed beside Hamzah, until he had prayed over him seventy times, and the slain were seventy. When they had been buried and he had finished with them, this verse was revealed: ﴿Invite to the way of your Lord with wisdom and good admonition … ﴾ up to ﴿But if you are patient, it is better for the patient. Be patient, and your patience is not but by Allah.﴾ So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was patient and did not mutilate anyone. Isma'il ibn Ishaq recorded it from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, but the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas is more complete. Al-Tabari related from a group that they said: This verse was revealed concerning the one who has been wronged, that he may not take from his wrongdoer, when he is able to, except the equivalent of his wrong, and that he should not go beyond it to others. Al-Mawardi related this from Ibn Sirin and Mujahid.

**Second issue:** The scholars differed concerning a person who was wronged by another man who took his property, and then the wrongdoer was entrusted with property by the one he wronged. Is it permissible for the wronged man to betray him in the amount by which he was wronged? A group said he may do so, among them Ibn Sirin, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, Sufyan and Mujahid, and they argued with this verse and the generality of its wording. Malik and a group with him said it is not permissible for him to do so, and they argued with the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Return the trust to the one who entrusted you, and do not betray the one who betrayed you." Al-Daraqutni narrated it. This has already been discussed fully in al-Baqarah [See vol. 2, p. 355]. In the Musnad of Ibn Ishaq it occurs that this hadith was narrated concerning a man who committed adultery with the wife of another man. Then the other man was able to reach the wife of the second man, by leaving her with him while he traveled. That man sought the advice of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on the matter, and he said to him: "Return the trust to the one who entrusted you, and do not betray the one who betrayed you." On this basis, the view of Malik concerning property is strengthened, because betrayal attaches to that act, and it is a vice from which one cannot be free, so one should avoid it for oneself. If he is able to take redress from property of one who did not entrust it to him, then it seems that this is permissible, as if Allah had judged in his favour, just as if he were able to take by the judgment of a judge. It has also been said that this verse is abrogated (mansukhah); it was abrogated by ﴿But be patient, and your patience is not but by Allah.﴾

**Third issue:** This verse is evidence for the permissibility of equivalence in retaliation (qisas). Whoever kills with an iron implement is killed with it, and whoever kills with a stone is killed with it, and the due amount must not be exceeded. This meaning has already been discussed fully in al-Baqarah [See vol. 3, p. 355], and praise be to Allah.

**Fourth issue:** Allah the Exalted called the harms inflicted in this verse "punishment" ('uqubah), whereas punishment in its true sense is the second (the retaliation). He did this so that the two expressions would be parallel and the wording of the speech would be harmonious. This is the reverse of His saying: ﴿They schemed, and Allah schemed﴾ [See vol. 4, p. 98], and His saying: ﴿Allah mocks them﴾ [See vol. 1, p. 207]. For the second here is the figurative (majaz) and the first is the literal (haqiqah), as Ibn 'Atiyyah said.

There is one issue (mas'alah) in this passage. Ibn Zayd said: it is abrogated (mansukhah) by fighting. But the majority of scholars hold that it is non-abrogated (muhkamah), meaning: be patient by pardoning, rather than retaliating with the same kind of punishment they inflicted through mutilation.

﴿And do not grieve over them﴾: that is, over the dead of Uhud, for they have passed on to the mercy of Allah.

﴿And do not be in distress﴾: ضيق (ḍayq) is the plural of ضيقة (ḍayqah). The poet said:

*"He removed the distress from us and widened..."*

[This is the second half of a verse by al-A'sha. Its first half, as given in the lisan and in his diwan, is: "Then surely your Lord, in His mercy..."]

The reading of the majority is with a fatha on the ḍād (ḍaqa). Ibn Kathir read it with a kasra on the ḍād (ḍiyq), and it is also reported from Nafi', but this is an error on the part of the one who transmitted it. Some lexicographers said: the kasra and the fatha on the ḍād are two dialectal forms of the verbal noun. Al-Akhfash said: al-ḍiyq and al-ḍayq are the verbal noun of ḍaqa, yaḍīqu. The meaning is: your chest should not be constricted by their disbelief. Al-Farra' said: al-ḍayq is what your chest is constricted by, while al-ḍiyq is what occurs in something that can widen or narrow, such as a house or a garment. Ibn al-Sikkit said: they are the same; it is said: "In his chest there is ḍayq and ḍiyq." Al-Qutaybi said: ḍayq is a lightened form of ḍayyiq, meaning "do not be in a constricted matter," and it was lightened, like hayyin and hayn. Ibn Arafah said: it is said that a man ḍāqa when he was stingy, and aḍāqa when he became poor.

As for His saying, ﴿Indeed, Allah is with those who fear Him and those who are doers of good﴾: that is, those who avoid immoral acts and major sins, with help, assistance, favor, righteousness, and support. The meaning of ihsan (doing good) has already been explained.

It was said to Hiram ibn Hibban [In Usd al-Ghaba it is written "Hayyan," with a ya. Likewise in J. In al-Taj and W it is "Hibban," with a single letter ba.] at the time of his death: "Give us counsel." He said: "I counsel you with the verses of Allah and the last verses of the surah, 'Call to the way of your Lord...,' to its end."

The Surah of al-Nahl is complete, and all praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds.
